model.goal: Build a conditional macroeconomic prediction from choices and consistency.
assumptions: A model deliberately omits some features.
Predictions are conditional on the stated market and behavioral assumptions.

derive.title: Choose a question
derive.why: Ask how employment responds to productivity before deciding which details matter.

derive.title: Specify behavior
derive.why: Households choose work and firms choose employment under their constraints.

derive.title: Require compatibility
derive.why: A wage must make planned labor supply equal planned labor demand.

derive.title: State a conditional answer
derive.why: Changing the mechanism can change the prediction.
derive.question: Why is a demand shift alone not an equilibrium prediction?
derive.answer: The resulting wage and employment also depend on labor supply and market clearing.

graph.title: Read the choice blocks
graph.why: The first block contains behavior, not an observed correlation.

graph.title: Connect choices
graph.why: Market clearing links separate plans.

graph.title: Reach a prediction
graph.why: Follow the arrows only under the stated assumptions.
graph.question: Where would sticky wages enter this reasoning?
graph.answer: They change the market-adjustment mechanism between choices and the final outcome.

increase.title: Raise productivity
increase.why: At a given wage, more productive labor raises the firm's desired hiring.

increase.title: Reconcile plans
increase.why: With upward-sloping supply, a higher wage brings additional workers.

increase.title: Conclude conditionally
increase.why: Competitive employment and output rise in this example.
increase.question: Which assumption makes the employment conclusion conditional?
increase.answer: The supply response and competitive wage adjustment; a fixed wage or a different supply schedule needs a new solution.

decrease.title: Reduce productivity
decrease.why: The same worker now adds less output at the old employment level.

decrease.title: Recompute demand
decrease.why: Firms cut desired hiring at the old wage; wage adjustment reconciles plans.

decrease.title: Resolve the outcome
decrease.why: With upward supply, wage and employment fall.
decrease.question: Can the final wage be inferred from productivity alone?
decrease.answer: No. Its size requires both demand and supply equations.

edge.title: Identify the failed assumption
edge.why: Suppose wages cannot adjust immediately.

edge.title: Replace the clearing step
edge.why: Evaluate desired hiring and offered work separately at the fixed wage.

edge.title: Allow disequilibrium
edge.why: Excess labor supply can remain instead of a new clearing wage.
edge.question: Must the flexible-wage prediction still hold?
edge.answer: No. The changed adjustment rule produces a different short-run result.

variables.goal: Distinguish what a model takes as given from what it solves.

symbols.meaning: investment taken as given in the illustrative expanded model
government purchases taken as given in that model

assumptions: Illustration: C = a + bY, with a = 10 and b = 0.6.
Variable status is relative to a particular model.

derive.title: List the inputs
derive.why: These three quantities are specified outside this consumption equation.

derive.title: Apply the rule
derive.why: The equation maps the inputs to a consumption choice.

derive.title: Solve the output
derive.why: Consumption is endogenous in this small model.

derive.title: Check model scope
derive.why: A larger goods-market model may solve income jointly with consumption.
derive.question: Is Y inherently exogenous?
derive.answer: No. Y is exogenous here but can be endogenous in a larger model.

graph.title: Reveal givens
graph.why: The input node fixes the experiment.

graph.title: Reveal mechanism
graph.why: The rule node links the quantities.

graph.title: Reveal solution
graph.why: The output node shows what was actually determined.
graph.question: Which node would change if a were estimated rather than fixed?
graph.answer: Its status would depend on the estimation model; in this behavioral equation a remains a parameter.

increase.title: Raise specified income
increase.why: Hold a and b fixed to isolate the income effect.

increase.title: Propagate through the rule
increase.why: An input change produces an endogenous response.

increase.title: Read new consumption
increase.why: The increase is smaller than the income increase.
increase.question: Does C become exogenous because we calculated it?
increase.answer: No. It is still the model's solved outcome.

decrease.title: Lower specified income
decrease.why: The same equation is retained.

decrease.title: Apply the coefficient
decrease.why: The sign follows from positive b.

decrease.title: Read lower spending
decrease.why: Only the input changed.
decrease.question: Would a negative b give this same direction?
decrease.answer: No. The sign of the parameter is part of the maintained behavioral assumption.

edge.title: Expand the model
edge.why: Add Y = C + I + G, with I and G specified.

edge.title: Solve jointly
edge.why: Income is now determined by consistency with spending.

edge.title: Inspect a singular case
edge.why: The usual division is unavailable.
edge.question: At b = 1, is the familiar solution formula valid?
edge.answer: No. The equations need separate inspection; they can be inconsistent or fail to determine a unique income.

autonomous.goal: Separate movements along a relationship from shifts of that relationship.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in the two-determinant extension
positive interest sensitivity in that extension

assumptions: Illustration C = a + bY, initially a = 20 and b = 0.5.
The intercept is autonomous with respect to Y, not necessarily every possible influence.

derive.title: Fix the rule
derive.why: The slope measures the response to income.

derive.title: Evaluate a point
derive.why: A point combines one income with its implied consumption.

derive.title: Change income alone
derive.why: Keep the intercept fixed to move along the curve.

derive.title: Change the intercept
derive.why: An autonomous change alters consumption at every income.
derive.question: If Y rises by 20 and a is unchanged, what is ΔC?
derive.answer: 10, a movement along the original curve.

graph.title: Draw the original line
graph.why: Intercept 20 and slope 0.5 locate the baseline.

graph.title: Add a parallel line
graph.why: An intercept rise leaves the slope unchanged.

graph.title: Compare at one income
graph.why: Use a common horizontal coordinate to identify a shift.
graph.question: Why is moving from (100,70) to (120,80) not this shift?
graph.answer: It follows the original line because income changed.

increase.title: Raise autonomous spending
increase.why: The change does not require income to rise.

increase.title: Recalculate at fixed income
increase.why: Every predicted consumption value is 10 higher.

increase.title: Retain the slope
increase.why: The marginal response to income is unaffected.
increase.question: Does a rise imply a larger MPC?
increase.answer: No. MPC is b, which remains 0.5.

decrease.title: Reduce the intercept
decrease.why: Remove 10 units of spending at each income.

decrease.title: Evaluate the lower line
decrease.why: The entire schedule shifts down.

decrease.title: Keep the comparison clean
decrease.why: A simultaneous income rise could offset this decrease.
decrease.question: If Y also rises by 20, what is total ΔC?

edge.title: Change the slope instead
edge.why: A slope change is not a parallel autonomous shift. In the extension C = a + bY − dr, an r change also shifts the graph against Y while the Y slope b stays fixed.

edge.title: Redo the difference
edge.why: The effect depends on income and is zero at Y = 0.

edge.title: Identify the pivot
edge.why: The two schedules share the intercept but diverge as income rises.
edge.question: Can a slope change be represented by shifting the old line up by 10 everywhere?
edge.answer: No. At Y = 100 the difference is 10, but at Y = 200 it is 20.

real-nominal.goal: Convert money amounts into purchasing power before interpreting changes.

symbols.meaning: a new value, as in W′ or P′
nominal and real gross domestic product
proportional nominal-value, price and real-value growth rates
current prices, current quantities and fixed base-period prices for each good

assumptions: P is strictly positive.
The plotted W values are illustrative fixed nominal wages.

derive.title: Price the basket
derive.why: Nominal pay equals purchasing power times the basket price.

derive.title: Divide by the price
derive.why: This removes the currency unit and leaves baskets per hour.

derive.title: Evaluate the baseline
derive.why: One hour buys 50 baskets.

derive.title: Apply the distinction to GDP
derive.why: Nominal GDP uses current prices, whereas constant-price real GDP holds the valuation prices fixed to track production.

derive.title: Derive exact real growth
derive.why: Take the ratio of new real value to old real value. This applies when the matching price index satisfies nominal value = price index × real value.

derive.title: Distinguish changes
derive.why: Equal proportional wage and price changes cancel exactly.
derive.question: If both double, what happens to the real wage?
derive.answer: It is unchanged, because 2W/(2P) = W/P.

graph.title: Hold the wage fixed
graph.why: Higher prices trace a downward curved relationship.

graph.title: Add a higher nominal wage
graph.why: At each price, purchasing power doubles.

graph.title: Compare paired changes
graph.why: The baseline and scaled points have equal real wages.
graph.question: Why does a move along the baseline reduce w?
graph.answer: W stays 100 while the denominator P rises.

increase.title: Raise only the price
increase.why: The nominal amount purchases fewer baskets.

increase.title: Recompute the ratio
increase.why: Real pay halves.

increase.title: Separate wage inflation
increase.why: A simultaneous wage rise must be compared proportionally.
increase.question: If a nominal amount rises by 20% and the matching price index rises by 10%, what is exact real growth?
increase.answer: 1.20/1.10 − 1 = 1/11, about 9.091%. Subtracting 10% from 20% gives only an approximation.

decrease.title: Lower nominal pay at fixed price
decrease.why: Keep the denominator unchanged.

decrease.title: Recompute purchasing power
decrease.why: The lower nominal wage buys half as much.

decrease.title: Compare a price decline
decrease.why: A sufficiently large price fall could instead increase real pay.
decrease.question: If W falls to 50 and P falls to 0.5, what is w?
decrease.answer: 100 baskets per hour; real pay rises despite the nominal pay cut.

edge.title: Check the denominator
edge.why: The price index must represent a positive basket cost.

edge.title: Reject division by zero
edge.why: W/P no longer supplies a finite real wage.

edge.title: Avoid a unit illusion
edge.why: Changing a price-index base rescales measured real quantities without changing actual purchasing opportunities.
edge.question: Is a higher numerical real-wage index proof of a welfare gain if the index base changed?
edge.answer: No. Compare consistently normalized real values or actual baskets.

stocks-flows.goal: Reconcile a dated balance sheet with activity over an interval.

symbols.meaning: other net stock adjustments, zero in the baseline reconciliation

assumptions: Illustration excludes transfers and other balance-sheet adjustments.
A stock has a date; a flow has a time interval.

derive.title: Start with a dated stock
derive.why: This is wealth at the opening date.

derive.title: Add accumulated saving
derive.why: Unconsumed current resources add to wealth over the period.

derive.title: Add valuation changes
derive.why: An asset-price loss changes wealth without being current saving.

derive.title: Close the balance sheet
derive.why: Separate the mechanisms rather than calling the entire stock change saving.
derive.question: What is the change in wealth, and is it equal to saving?
derive.answer: Wealth rises by 5; saving is 8 because valuation subtracts 3.

graph.title: Show opening wealth
graph.why: The first node is dated, not an annual rate.

graph.title: Reveal interval contributions
graph.why: Saving and revaluation are distinct additions to the reconciliation.

graph.title: Show closing wealth
graph.why: The endpoint adds the contributions once.
graph.question: Would adding total income as well as saving double-count resources?
graph.answer: Yes, if income has already been used to compute saving net of consumption.

increase.title: Increase saving by 4
increase.why: Hold the initial balance and valuation fixed.

increase.title: Update the stock
increase.why: Additional saving raises ending wealth one for one.

increase.title: Keep units consistent
increase.why: Saving of 12 per year refers to the chosen annual interval.
increase.question: Does doubling the interval necessarily double the saving flow?
increase.answer: Only if the saving rate stays constant over that interval.

decrease.title: Make valuation more negative
decrease.why: The asset loses more market value.

decrease.title: Recalculate ending wealth
decrease.why: Wealth falls despite positive saving.

decrease.title: Distinguish behavior from prices
decrease.why: The household did not necessarily consume more.
decrease.question: Can falling wealth alone establish negative saving?
decrease.answer: No. The valuation loss can exceed positive saving.

edge.title: Identify missing adjustments
edge.why: An inheritance arrives during the interval.

edge.title: Extend the reconciliation
edge.why: The earlier accounting assumption excluded this transfer.

edge.title: Classify before adding
edge.why: A balance-sheet addition is not automatically earned income or saving.
edge.question: Why can the short formula fail to reconcile observed wealth?
edge.answer: It omits a relevant transfer or other stock adjustment.

[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3A - Rewriting Budget Constraints with Initial Wealth.pdf

wealth.goal: Distinguish gross assets, liabilities, net wealth, and saving.
assumptions: All assets and debts use the same valuation date and currency.
Debt repayment from existing cash involves no new income or consumption.

derive.title: Value assets
derive.why: Include financial and real assets at the chosen valuation.

derive.title: Value obligations
derive.why: Debt is an offsetting claim on future resources.

derive.title: Subtract liabilities
derive.why: Gross assets alone overstate net ownership.

derive.title: Trace a repayment
derive.why: Using cash to retire debt reduces both sides.
derive.question: Does repayment from existing cash create 10 of net wealth?
derive.answer: No. The net position remains 120.

graph.title: Reveal the gross balance sheet
graph.why: Assets and debt must both appear.

graph.title: Compute net ownership
graph.why: Subtract the liability node from the asset node.

graph.title: Add a transaction
graph.why: The repayment node changes composition, not net wealth.
graph.question: Which additional node could represent actual wealth creation through saving?
graph.answer: The income-and-saving node: new unconsumed resources can raise net wealth before repayment.

increase.title: Raise asset prices
increase.why: The debt amount is unchanged.

increase.title: Revalue net wealth
increase.why: Net wealth rises by the capital gain.

increase.title: Separate the income concept
increase.why: A valuation gain is not necessarily current disposable income.
increase.question: Must the 30 wealth gain imply 30 of saving?
increase.answer: No. Saving and revaluation are distinct.

decrease.title: Borrow and immediately consume 10
decrease.why: The borrowed cash is spent, so it does not remain as an asset.

decrease.title: Recompute net wealth
decrease.why: Debt-financed consumption reduces the net position.

decrease.title: Inspect the alternative transaction
decrease.why: Borrowing and retaining the cash would raise A and D equally.
decrease.question: Does borrowing itself always lower net wealth?
decrease.answer: No. The use of the proceeds determines whether the added liability has an offsetting asset.

edge.title: Allow negative net wealth
edge.why: The definition does not require wealth to be positive.

edge.title: Apply the same subtraction
edge.why: Net debtor status is economically meaningful.

edge.title: Separate liquidity from solvency
edge.why: Large net wealth can coexist with little spendable cash.
edge.question: Does NW > 0 guarantee the household can meet today's payment?
edge.answer: No. Asset liquidity and payment timing also matter.

graphs.goal: Read intercepts, slopes, movements, and shifts without confusing them.

symbols.meaning: vertical intercept and slope of C = a + bY

assumptions: The graph is a conditional consumption schedule, not a time series.
Numerical illustration C = 20 + 0.5Y.

derive.title: Name both axes
derive.why: A point describes income and consumption together.

derive.title: Locate the intercept
derive.why: This is spending at zero measured income in the illustration.

derive.title: Calculate the slope
derive.why: An extra 20 of income raises C by 10.

derive.title: Find the other intercept
derive.why: Set the vertical variable to zero and solve for the horizontal one. For a = 20 and b = 0.5, this is −40, outside the nonnegative-income plotting domain.

derive.title: Identify the experiment
derive.why: Holding a fixed traces the curve; changing a creates a new curve.
derive.question: Can a point above the old curve be explained by higher Y alone?
derive.answer: No. At that same Y, the old relationship predicts a lower C.

graph.title: Construct from two points
graph.why: A straight line is fixed by its intercept and slope.

graph.title: Reveal a second relationship
graph.why: The higher intercept produces a distinct parallel line.

graph.title: Use a common coordinate
graph.why: Compare vertically at Y = 100 to isolate the shift.
graph.question: Which comparison isolates an income movement?
graph.answer: The two baseline points (100,70) and (120,80).

increase.title: Increase the horizontal variable
increase.why: Do not change the equation.

increase.title: Move along the line
increase.why: The positive slope determines the vertical response.

increase.title: Hold other influences fixed
increase.why: An observed increase could combine both movement and shift.
increase.question: Can two observations alone prove the intercept was unchanged?
increase.answer: No. That is an assumption unless other evidence identifies it.

decrease.title: Lower a non-axis determinant
decrease.why: Income is held fixed while spending propensity shifts.

decrease.title: Draw the lower schedule
decrease.why: At each Y, predicted consumption is 10 lower.

decrease.title: Compare matching incomes
decrease.why: The downward shift is not movement to lower Y.
decrease.question: What would a fall in Y on the original curve look like?
decrease.answer: A move left and down along the baseline, retaining its intercept.

edge.title: Recognize a flat relationship
edge.why: Changing income no longer changes consumption in this specification.

edge.title: Redo the slope calculation
edge.why: The curve would be horizontal at C = a.

edge.title: Keep shifts possible
edge.why: Changing a still moves that horizontal curve.
edge.question: Does a zero slope mean no variable can change consumption?
edge.answer: No. It only eliminates the response to the plotted horizontal variable.

optimization.goal: Solve an interior optimum and then check whether it is feasible.
assumptions: Derived illustration Y = 10N − N² on 0 ≤ N ≤ 5; wage initially 4.
No fixed cost affects the employment choice; the illustration restricts employment to 0 ≤ N ≤ 5, where output remains nondecreasing.

derive.title: Write the objective
derive.why: Revenue and wage cost are expressed in the same real unit.

derive.title: Differentiate
derive.why: Marginal profit measures the gain from slightly more labor.

derive.title: Set marginal gain to zero
derive.why: At the candidate, another small unit neither raises nor lowers profit.

derive.title: Check maximum and feasibility
derive.why: Concavity and feasibility make the stationary point the maximum.
derive.question: Why is a zero first derivative alone insufficient?
derive.answer: It could be a minimum, or an infeasible candidate; curvature and constraints must also be checked.

graph.title: Draw profit against employment
graph.why: The vertical coordinate is total profit, not MPN.

graph.title: Mark the peak
graph.why: The slope is positive before the peak and negative after.

graph.title: Add the high-wage case
graph.why: The entire feasible curve slopes downward.
graph.question: Where is the best feasible high-wage choice?
graph.answer: N = 0, where profit is 0.

increase.title: Raise the wage
increase.why: The marginal labor cost now exceeds initial productivity.

increase.title: Redo the derivative
increase.why: For every N ≥ 0, additional employment lowers profit.

increase.title: Choose the boundary
increase.why: The stationary solution N = −1 is infeasible.
increase.question: Why not report the algebraic solution −1?
increase.answer: Negative employment is outside the feasible set.

decrease.title: Lower the wage
decrease.why: Each unit of employment becomes cheaper.

decrease.title: Solve the new marginal condition
decrease.why: Employment rises because MPN must fall to the lower wage.

decrease.title: Check the domain
decrease.why: The new candidate remains an interior maximum.
decrease.question: What is the new maximum profit?

edge.title: Identify a binding lower bound
edge.why: At zero employment, MPN is at most the wage.

edge.title: Replace equality with a boundary test
edge.why: No feasible increase from zero improves profit.

edge.title: State the constrained optimum
edge.why: The interior equality MPN = w need not hold.
edge.question: At w = 10, is zero still optimal?
edge.answer: Yes. The derivative is zero at zero and negative for every positive N.
