chain-rule.goal: Differentiate utility when consumption changes with leisure.

symbols.meaning: partial derivatives with respect to the first and second arguments of a function, rather than period labels
consumption and leisure evaluated in period 2

assumptions: Illustration U(c,l) = cl, h = 6, w = 2, m = 0.
The chain rule applies to differentiable functions; the budget makes c depend on l.

derive.title: Substitute the constraint
derive.why: One more leisure hour lowers earned consumption.

derive.title: Track the direct effect
derive.why: At fixed consumption, more leisure raises utility.

derive.title: Track the indirect effect
derive.why: Lost earnings reduce consumption and therefore utility.

derive.title: Read subscripts by their role
derive.why: The subscript on u identifies the argument being differentiated; the subscripts inside the parentheses identify the date. This is consumption marginal utility evaluated in period 2.

derive.title: Add both channels
derive.why: A total derivative includes both routes.
derive.question: At l = 2, what is dU/dl?
derive.answer: 4: the direct benefit is 8 and the indirect cost is −4.

graph.title: Draw utility after substitution
graph.why: This is utility along the feasible budget, not an indifference curve.

graph.title: Add a tangent at l = 2
graph.why: Its slope equals the total derivative 4.

graph.title: Locate the stationary point
graph.why: The total marginal gain becomes zero.
graph.question: Does U_l vanish at this optimum?
graph.answer: No. U_l = c = 6; it is balanced by the indirect cost 2l = 6.

increase.title: Increase leisure near l = 2
increase.why: Direct leisure benefit exceeds consumption loss.

increase.title: Recompute a finite change
increase.why: The derivative predicts approximately 0.4, not the exact finite difference.

increase.title: Explain the approximation
increase.why: Curvature changes the slope over the interval.
increase.question: Why is the exact utility gain below 0.4?
increase.answer: The slope falls as leisure increases.

decrease.title: Reduce leisure near l = 4
decrease.why: At this point more leisure would reduce utility.

decrease.title: Use a negative change
decrease.why: Giving up some leisure raises utility through consumption.

decrease.title: Keep signs separate
decrease.why: A negative derivative times a negative small change gives a positive gain.
decrease.question: Does dU/dl < 0 mean utility falls when leisure falls?
decrease.answer: No. Locally it means utility rises when leisure falls.

edge.title: Identify the failed shortcut
edge.why: Treating c as fixed ignores the budget.

edge.title: Redo the derivative
edge.math: U_l = c, but dU/dl = U_l − wU_c
edge.why: Partial and total derivatives answer different questions.

edge.title: Check the zero-total case
edge.why: Neither partial marginal utility has to be zero.
edge.question: Can a person value both goods at an interior optimum?
edge.answer: Yes. The budget tradeoff balances two positive marginal utilities.

total-differential.goal: Derive an indifference-curve slope by keeping utility constant.

symbols.meaning: marginal rate of substitution of leisure for consumption
a differentiable implicit relationship between variables x and y

assumptions: Illustration u = ln(c) + 2ln(l), with c > 0 and l > 0.
The budget in the plot is c = 22 − 3l; it is not tangent at the marked point.

derive.title: Write the total differential
derive.why: Both consumption and leisure can change simultaneously.

derive.title: Hold utility constant
derive.why: An indifference curve contains bundles with the same utility.

derive.title: Isolate the slope
derive.why: The lost consumption compensates for extra leisure.

derive.title: Generalize the implicit slope
derive.math: H(x,y) = 0 ⇒ H_x dx + H_y dy = 0 ⇒ dy/dx = −H_x/H_y
derive.why: The same rearrangement works for any differentiable implicit relation when H_y is nonzero.

derive.title: Evaluate the example
derive.why: This is a local tradeoff.
derive.question: For a small dl = 0.1, what dc approximately preserves utility?
derive.answer: dc ≈ −0.5; an exact finite change requires the full indifference curve.

graph.title: Construct the indifference curve
graph.why: This curve passes through (4,10).

graph.title: Add the budget
graph.why: The budget also passes through that bundle but has slope −3.

graph.title: Compare local slopes
graph.why: The bundle is feasible but not tangent.
graph.question: Would a small leisure increase along the budget raise utility?
graph.answer: Yes. The household would sacrifice up to 5 consumption units per leisure unit but only pays 3.

increase.title: Increase leisure on the same indifference curve
increase.why: Utility is held fixed, so consumption must adjust.

increase.title: Solve exactly
increase.why: Consumption falls from 10 by 3.6.

increase.title: Distinguish local from finite
increase.why: The initial slope times a change of 1 would predict −5 only approximately.
increase.question: Why is −5 not the exact consumption change?
increase.answer: MRS changes along the curved indifference curve.

decrease.title: Reduce leisure at constant utility
decrease.why: Consumption must compensate for lost leisure.

decrease.title: Solve the new bundle
decrease.why: Required consumption rises by about 7.778.

decrease.title: Read increasing scarcity
decrease.why: Less leisure makes another leisure unit more valuable relative to consumption.
decrease.question: Is the increase in c symmetric to the l = 4 to 5 decrease?
decrease.answer: No. Curvature makes equal leisure changes asymmetric.

edge.title: Identify a failed differentiability condition
edge.why: Switch explicitly to this kinked utility illustration. The marginal-rate-of-substitution derivative is not unique where c = l.

edge.title: Replace the tangent calculation
edge.why: Check feasible movements on both sides. More leisure reduces c below the kink level; less leisure reduces l below it. Either move lowers min(c,l).
edge.math: c = l and c + 2l = 20 ⇒ c = l = 20/3

edge.title: Preserve the economic question
edge.why: The optimum is still the best feasible bundle, even without smooth tangency.
edge.question: Must every optimum satisfy one smooth MRS = w equality?
edge.answer: No. Kinks and boundaries require the corresponding feasibility and one-sided tests.

production.goal: Translate a production function into feasible output, holding the correct inputs fixed.
assumptions: Illustration Y = A√(KN), initially A = 1 and K = 100.
Inputs are nonnegative; marginal calculations use positive inputs.

derive.title: List productive inputs
derive.why: Capital and labor enter a technological relationship, not a spending identity.

derive.title: Fix capital and productivity
derive.why: Only labor varies along this short-run curve.

derive.title: Calculate output
derive.why: The point gives total output, not output from the last worker.

derive.title: Compare a finite addition
derive.why: Eleven extra labor units produce ten extra output units.
derive.question: Is the slope equal to Y/N?
derive.answer: No. Y/N is average product; the slope is marginal product.

graph.title: Start at the origin
graph.why: This particular technology needs both inputs.

graph.title: Trace diminishing increments
graph.why: The curve rises but becomes flatter.

graph.title: Add a productivity change
graph.why: Higher A raises output at every positive N.
graph.question: Which quantity was held fixed to interpret this as a productivity shift?
graph.answer: K remains 100.

increase.title: Raise labor alone
increase.why: The technology itself does not change.

increase.title: Move along production
increase.why: Output rises because more input is used.

increase.title: Separate a technology increase
increase.why: The same output increase can come from a different mechanism.
increase.question: Is identical output evidence of identical productivity?
increase.answer: No. Input use and productivity can offset each other.

decrease.title: Reduce productivity
decrease.why: Hold K and N fixed.

decrease.title: Recompute output
decrease.why: Each unchanged input combination produces less.

decrease.title: Preserve the movement distinction
decrease.why: A labor reduction would instead move left on the old curve.
decrease.question: Would Y = 40 alone identify a productivity decline?
decrease.answer: No. On the baseline, N = 16 also produces 40.

edge.title: Set an essential input to zero
edge.why: At N = 0 the baseline curve reaches the origin. If K = 0 instead, the added horizontal curve shows zero output at every N; do not confuse these two different zero-input experiments.

edge.title: Evaluate total output directly
edge.why: The production function itself remains well defined.

edge.title: Separate level from derivative
edge.why: A finite zero output can coexist with an unbounded one-sided marginal product.
edge.question: Does an infinite boundary derivative mean infinite total output at zero labor?
edge.answer: No. Total output is zero; the slope describes very small additions.

marginal-products.goal: Differentiate output with respect to one input while holding the other fixed.
assumptions: Y = A√(KN), with A,K,N > 0.
The MPN plot fixes A = 1 and K = 100.

derive.title: Hold capital fixed
derive.why: Capital is a constant in the labor derivative.

derive.title: Apply the power rule
derive.why: The exponent falls by one and its original value becomes a multiplier.

derive.title: Differentiate in the other direction
derive.why: Now labor is held fixed instead.

derive.title: Evaluate marginal labor productivity
derive.why: One additional small labor unit adds approximately one output unit.
derive.question: Is the exact output gain from N = 25 to 26 equal to 1?
derive.answer: No. It is 10(√26 − 5), about 0.9902, because MPN falls over the interval.

graph.title: Plot the derivative, not output
graph.why: The vertical axis is output per additional unit of labor.

graph.title: Add a comparison wage
graph.why: This horizontal line supplies a possible marginal cost.

graph.title: Locate the crossing
graph.why: This can determine desired labor for a competitive firm.
graph.question: Why can output rise while this curve falls?
graph.answer: Total output rises, but each extra worker adds less than the previous one.

increase.title: Increase labor
increase.why: Capital and productivity remain unchanged.

increase.title: Recompute the derivative
increase.why: More labor shares the fixed capital.

increase.title: Keep total and marginal separate
increase.why: Output doubles while marginal labor product halves.
increase.question: Does diminishing MPN imply output falls?
increase.answer: No. Positive MPN still makes total output rise.

decrease.title: Reduce labor
decrease.why: The fixed capital becomes more abundant per worker.

decrease.title: Recompute marginal product
decrease.why: The remaining labor becomes more productive at the margin.

decrease.title: Check the total level
decrease.why: Total output falls even though MPN rises.
decrease.question: Can higher MPN accompany lower output?
decrease.answer: Yes, when labor is reduced while capital is fixed.

edge.title: Approach zero labor
edge.why: The derivative formula contains √N in the denominator.

edge.title: Take the correct limit
edge.why: A steep initial slope does not imply large output at the origin.

edge.title: Avoid substituting into a singular expression
edge.why: Use one-sided limits or the original function at the boundary.
edge.question: Can MPN at N = 0 be read as the finite number 0?
edge.answer: No. The right-hand derivative is unbounded for this illustration.

complementarity.goal: Explain how one input changes the marginal productivity of the other.
assumptions: Illustration Y = A√(KN), with positive inputs.
Technological complementarity concerns marginal products, not whether the firm can ever substitute inputs.

derive.title: Start with labor's marginal product
derive.why: Capital remains visible in labor's derivative.

derive.title: Differentiate with respect to capital
derive.why: Extra capital raises the productivity of an additional worker.

derive.title: Check the symmetric channel
derive.why: Extra labor raises capital's marginal productivity.

derive.title: Apply a finite capital change
derive.why: The shift comes from capital, with A fixed.
derive.question: Does positive complementarity contradict diminishing MPN?
derive.answer: No. MPN falls as N rises at fixed K, but rises as K rises at fixed N.

graph.title: Draw the baseline MPN
graph.why: It slopes down because only N varies along it.

graph.title: Add the capital-rich schedule
graph.why: Higher K shifts MPN upward at every positive N.

graph.title: Compare at a fixed wage
graph.why: A higher MPN supports more desired labor.
graph.question: What are the old and new employment intersections?
graph.answer: 25 and 36, with the wage unchanged.

increase.title: Increase capital
increase.why: Each worker has more productive capital.

increase.title: Raise total output
increase.why: At N = 25, output rises from 50 to 60.

increase.title: Raise marginal labor product
increase.why: The production curve becomes steeper there.
increase.question: Is the output increase caused by higher A in this experiment?
increase.answer: No. A is fixed; capital accumulation causes the change.

decrease.title: Destroy some capital
decrease.why: Workers have fewer tools or machines.

decrease.title: Recompute MPN
decrease.why: The whole marginal-product curve shifts down.

decrease.title: Resolve desired hiring at w = 1
decrease.why: A firm reduces employment to restore MPN = w.
decrease.question: Does capital loss merely move along the old MPN curve?
decrease.answer: No. It changes the marginal-product relationship itself.

edge.title: Change the technology
edge.why: Suppose Y = K + N instead of the Cobb–Douglas illustration.

edge.title: Recalculate the cross partial
edge.why: The previous positive complementarity condition fails.

edge.title: State the revised implication
edge.why: Additional capital raises output but not labor's marginal product in this alternative technology.
edge.question: Is complementarity guaranteed merely because both inputs appear in Y?
edge.answer: No. It must be checked from the cross partial or the technology.

productivity.goal: Distinguish productivity shifts from movements caused by input changes.
assumptions: Illustration Y = A√(KN), K = 100.
A multiplies the entire production function.

derive.title: Isolate technology
derive.why: A measures output efficiency conditional on inputs.

derive.title: Differentiate with respect to A
derive.why: More efficiency raises output at a fixed positive input bundle.

derive.title: Connect to the marginal product
derive.why: Productivity also scales labor's marginal contribution.

derive.title: Compute a proportional change
derive.math: A: 1 → 1.2 ⇒ Y and MPN rise 20% at fixed K,N
derive.why: The proportional statement requires the inputs to stay fixed.
derive.question: Must equilibrium output rise by exactly 20%?
derive.answer: No. Employment may also adjust, changing the total equilibrium effect.

graph.title: Draw the original technology
graph.why: The capital stock is fixed at 100.

graph.title: Add higher efficiency
graph.why: The curves share the origin and separate for positive labor.

graph.title: Compare at N = 25
graph.why: A vertical comparison isolates the direct productivity effect.
graph.question: Is this shift parallel?
graph.answer: No. The absolute increase is 2√N, which grows with N.

increase.title: Raise productivity
increase.why: Labor becomes more valuable to the firm at each N.

increase.title: Shift labor demand upward
increase.why: At a fixed wage, the old hiring level leaves positive marginal profit.

increase.title: Restore the marginal condition
increase.why: Hiring rises until MPN falls back to the wage.
increase.question: Why is employment's percentage rise larger than 20% here?
increase.answer: Solving N = (5A/w)² makes employment proportional to A² at this fixed wage.

decrease.title: Lower productivity
decrease.why: The same inputs produce less.

decrease.title: Recompute the production schedule
decrease.why: At N = 25 output falls from 50 to 40.

decrease.title: Trace the additional equilibrium channel
decrease.why: Lower MPN also tends to reduce labor demand under competitive hiring.
decrease.question: Is the fixed-N fall the entire general-equilibrium effect?
decrease.answer: No. Employment and the real wage may change as well.

edge.title: Set productivity to zero
edge.why: Positive output and positive marginal products disappear in this multiplicative model.

edge.title: Recompute rather than divide
edge.why: A formula obtained by dividing by A is invalid here.

edge.title: Consider hiring at a positive wage
edge.why: Employment has a cost but generates no output.
edge.question: What does a profit-maximizing firm choose if w > 0?
edge.answer: Zero employment, absent other obligations or objectives.

scale.goal: Test returns to scale by changing every input in the same proportion.
assumptions: Compare Y = AK^αN^γ with positive A and inputs.
The plot normalizes each separate technology's baseline output to 100.

derive.title: Scale both inputs
derive.why: A remains fixed; both K and N change.

derive.title: Collect the scale terms
derive.why: The sum of exponents determines the output response.

derive.title: Classify the technology
derive.math: α + γ = 1: constant; > 1: increasing; < 1: decreasing returns
derive.why: This differs from varying one input with the other fixed.

derive.title: Evaluate doubling
derive.why: Constant returns preserve output per scaled input bundle.
derive.question: Can a constant-returns technology still have diminishing MPN?
derive.answer: Yes. Cobb–Douglas with each exponent between 0 and 1 has both properties.

graph.title: Draw constant returns
graph.why: The straight line passes through (1,100).

graph.title: Add other exponent sums
graph.why: The curves represent different illustrative technologies.

graph.title: Compare at z = 2
graph.why: The benchmark is twice the baseline output.
graph.question: Which curve exceeds 200 when inputs double?
graph.answer: The exponent-sum 1.2 curve: 100×2^1.2 ≈ 229.74.

increase.title: Increase every input by 50%
increase.why: Keep technology unchanged.

increase.title: Apply constant returns
increase.why: Output rises by 50% for exponent sum 1.

increase.title: Contrast increasing returns
increase.why: A larger scale gives a more-than-proportional output increase.
increase.question: Does raising only N by 50% test returns to scale?
increase.answer: No. K must also rise by 50%.

decrease.title: Halve every input
decrease.why: Both inputs shrink proportionally.

decrease.title: Evaluate constant returns
decrease.why: Output halves.

decrease.title: Evaluate increasing returns
decrease.why: Output falls by more than half.
decrease.question: For decreasing returns with exponent sum 0.8, is output above or below half?

edge.title: Change only one input
edge.why: The all-input scaling condition fails.

edge.title: Redo the algebra
edge.why: With only labor changing, its exponent γ determines the response. The plotted illustration uses γ = 0.5; the dashed all-input experiment is a separate reference.

edge.title: Use the correct label
edge.why: This is a change in labor input at fixed capital.
edge.question: If γ = 0.5 and labor doubles, is √2 output evidence of decreasing returns to scale?
edge.answer: No. It establishes the one-input response only.

factor-shares.goal: Derive factor-payment shares under competitive Cobb–Douglas production.

symbols.meaning: labor exponent in the generalized edge case; γ = 1−α in the baseline

assumptions: Y = AK^αN^(1−α), with 0 < α < 1 and positive inputs.
Both factors receive their competitive marginal products; there are no additional fixed claims.

derive.title: Differentiate the technology
derive.why: Rewriting derivatives using Y makes shares visible.

derive.title: Apply competitive payments
derive.why: Factor prices equal marginal products under the stated market assumptions.

derive.title: Multiply by quantities
derive.why: Total factor income equals price times quantity.

derive.title: Add the payments
derive.why: Constant returns exhaust output.
derive.question: With α = 0.35 and Y = 200, what are the factor payments?
derive.answer: Capital receives 70 and labor receives 130.

graph.title: Reveal total output
graph.why: The accounting pool is 200.

graph.title: Allocate marginal-product payments
graph.why: Apply 35% to capital and 65% to labor.

graph.title: Check exhaustion
graph.why: The two shares sum to one under constant returns.
graph.question: Does the residual node prove every real firm has zero accounting profit?
graph.answer: No. The conclusion belongs to this competitive factor-payment model and its treatment of capital costs.

increase.title: Raise productivity at fixed inputs
increase.why: Output and both marginal products rise proportionally.

increase.title: Recompute incomes
increase.why: Payment levels rise by 10%.

increase.title: Check the shares
increase.why: The exponents have not changed.
increase.question: Does a productivity rise change the labor share in this technology?
increase.answer: No. Its level rises while its share remains 1−α.

decrease.title: Reduce output through lower A
decrease.why: Keep the exponents and competitive payment rule.

decrease.title: Reduce factor payments
decrease.why: Both shares apply to a smaller output total.

decrease.title: Distinguish level from fraction
decrease.why: Lower labor income need not mean a lower labor share.
decrease.question: What is labor's new share?

edge.title: Remove constant returns
edge.why: The exhaustion assumption fails.

edge.title: Sum marginal-product payments
edge.why: Payments need not equal output.

edge.title: Reassess equilibrium feasibility
edge.why: With increasing returns, paying both marginal products exceeds output in this simple specification.
edge.question: May we keep the zero-residual conclusion automatically?
edge.answer: No. It relied on the exponents summing to one and the competitive setup.

labor-demand.goal: Explain why a competitive firm's labor demand is its marginal-product schedule.

symbols.meaning: production function before multiplication by productivity A

assumptions: K is fixed; output and labor markets are competitive.
Illustration Y = A√(100N), with A = 1 and N > 0.

derive.title: Write real profit
derive.why: The wage is a cost per labor unit.

derive.title: Find marginal profit
derive.why: Hiring is profitable while its added output exceeds its cost.

derive.title: Set the interior condition
derive.why: The last unit has zero marginal net gain.

derive.title: Use diminishing MPN
derive.why: Crossing from positive to negative marginal profit identifies the maximum.
derive.question: If MPN = 1.2 and w = 1, should a price-taking firm reduce labor?
derive.answer: No. It should expand hiring until the gap closes, subject to feasibility.

graph.title: Draw marginal benefit
graph.why: The curve descends as labor becomes abundant relative to capital.

graph.title: Draw marginal cost
graph.why: A competitive firm can hire at a given wage.

graph.title: Mark desired employment
graph.why: The intersection gives the optimal quantity at this wage.
graph.question: Why is the area or height of total output not the hiring rule?
graph.answer: The hiring decision compares marginal, not total, benefit with marginal cost.

increase.title: Increase the wage
increase.why: Labor demand itself is unchanged because A and K are fixed.

increase.title: Inspect old employment
increase.why: The last workers now cost more than their contribution.

increase.title: Reduce hiring
increase.why: Moving left raises MPN to the new wage.
increase.question: Is this a leftward shift of labor demand?
increase.answer: No. It is a movement along the unchanged MPN schedule.

decrease.title: Decrease the wage
decrease.why: At old employment, marginal benefit exceeds cost.

decrease.title: Expand hiring
decrease.why: Additional labor lowers MPN along the same curve.

decrease.title: Find the new optimum
decrease.why: The firm hires more at the cheaper wage.
decrease.question: What stays unchanged during this movement?
decrease.answer: Productivity, capital, and therefore the labor-demand schedule.

edge.title: Use a technology with finite initial MPN
edge.why: Unlike the square-root example, its first-worker benefit is bounded.

edge.title: Let wage exceed that bound
edge.why: The interior equality would imply negative employment.

edge.title: Choose the feasible corner
edge.why: The firm's optimality condition becomes a boundary inequality.
edge.question: Must a firm always hire until MPN = w?
edge.answer: Only at an interior optimum. A zero-hiring corner can have MPN < w.

labor-demand-algebra.goal: Solve a Cobb–Douglas labor-demand equation and check comparative-static powers.
assumptions: Y = AK^αN^(1−α), A,K,w > 0, and 0 < α < 1.
The plot uses α = 0.5, K = 100 and A = 1.

derive.title: Differentiate output
derive.why: The exponent on labor becomes negative.

derive.title: Set marginal product equal to wage
derive.why: This is the interior profit condition.

derive.title: Isolate the labor power
derive.why: All terms are positive, so the power operation is well defined.

derive.title: Raise to the reciprocal power
derive.why: The capital term simplifies because (K^α)^(1/α) = K.
derive.question: At α = 0.5, A = 1, K = 100 and w = 1, what is Nᵈ?

graph.title: Draw the inverse demand
graph.why: The graph expresses wage as a function of labor.

graph.title: Select a wage
graph.why: Solving the same equation gives direct labor demand.

graph.title: Verify the solution
graph.why: Direct and inverse forms identify the same crossing.
graph.question: What common algebra error would give 25 instead?
graph.answer: Forgetting the reciprocal exponent or failing to square the entire ratio.

increase.title: Raise the wage by 100%
increase.why: The wage appears in the denominator.

increase.title: Apply the exponent
increase.why: Employment falls by 75%, not 100%.

increase.title: Distinguish exact from local elasticity
increase.why: An elasticity gives a local percentage response.
increase.question: Can we use −2×100% as an exact finite employment change?
increase.answer: No. The exact ratio is one quarter; a −200% employment prediction is infeasible.

decrease.title: Reduce productivity by 20%
decrease.why: At any wage, desired employment falls.

decrease.title: Apply the exact power
decrease.why: The 20% productivity loss lowers employment by 36% at fixed wage.

decrease.title: Verify numerically
decrease.why: Substituting into 4/√N returns w = 1.
decrease.question: Does the real wage have to fall in this firm-level experiment?
decrease.answer: No. It is treated as given; market equilibrium would additionally solve supply.

edge.title: Inspect α = 0
edge.why: The formula's reciprocal exponent becomes undefined.

edge.title: Return to the technology
edge.why: Labor's marginal product is constant.

edge.title: Solve separately
edge.why: If w > A choose zero; if w = A any feasible N is equally profitable; if w < A and no cap exists there is no finite optimum.
edge.question: Why not take the old demand formula literally at α = 0?
edge.answer: Its derivation divided by and inverted a positive α, an assumption that has failed.

implicit-function.goal: Differentiate an equilibrium condition without first solving its level.

symbols.meaning: production function before multiplication by productivity A

assumptions: The interior condition is AF_N(K,N) = w.
A > 0, F_NN < 0 and derivatives exist; K and w are held fixed for dN/dA.

derive.title: Start from the condition
derive.why: N depends on the parameter being changed.

derive.title: Differentiate both routes
derive.why: A affects marginal product directly and indirectly through changed employment.

derive.title: Isolate the response
derive.why: The negative denominator reverses the minus sign.

derive.title: Compare another parameter
derive.why: A higher wage requires a lower employment level.
derive.question: Why must the derivative of N be included when differentiating with respect to A?
derive.answer: Because desired N changes as A changes; holding it fixed would omit the equilibrium adjustment.

graph.title: Draw the original condition
graph.why: The intersection represents AF_N = w.

graph.title: Increase the parameter A
graph.why: The marginal-product curve shifts upward while wage stays fixed.

graph.title: Locate the new solution
graph.why: Moving right restores equality.
graph.question: How does the graph confirm the sign of dN/dA?
graph.answer: The new intersection has larger N: 36 rather than 25.

increase.title: Increase capital slightly
increase.why: Complementarity raises MPN at the old N.

increase.title: Differentiate implicitly
increase.why: Employment must adjust to keep the wage condition satisfied.

increase.title: Read the sign
increase.why: Positive complementarity and diminishing MPN imply more labor.
increase.question: In the Cobb–Douglas direct formula, what is dN/dK?
increase.answer: N/K, consistent with labor demand being proportional to capital.

decrease.title: Lower productivity slightly
decrease.why: At unchanged N, marginal product falls.

decrease.title: Use the derivative with the change
decrease.why: A positive derivative times a negative parameter change gives a negative response.

decrease.title: Restore equality
decrease.why: Reducing employment raises MPN back toward the given wage.
decrease.question: Is the derivative itself negative because A fell?
decrease.answer: No. dN/dA stays positive locally; dA is negative.

edge.title: Identify a zero denominator
edge.why: The local slope needed for the usual implicit solution vanishes.

edge.title: Return to the original equation
edge.why: This explicit linear-technology case has F_NN = 0. The equality is satisfied at every employment level, so it does not identify a unique N.
edge.math: Y = N; MPN = 1; w = 1 ⇒ every feasible N satisfies MPN = w

edge.title: Avoid an invalid derivative
edge.why: A division by zero is a warning that local uniqueness or regularity fails.
edge.question: May we report a finite dN/dw from the usual formula?
edge.answer: No. The underlying condition must be analyzed separately.

time-budget.goal: Convert a time allocation into a feasible consumption–leisure budget.
assumptions: h = 16, w = 5 and m = 20 in the illustration.
No saving in this one-period worker problem; 0 ≤ l ≤ h and c ≥ 0.

derive.title: Account for time
derive.math: N + l = h ⇒ N = h − l
derive.why: An hour used for leisure cannot also be sold as labor.

derive.title: Value work
derive.why: Only worked hours earn the wage.

derive.title: Add nonlabor resources
derive.math: c = w(h − l) + m = wh + m − wl
derive.why: Nonlabor income does not require current work.

derive.title: Identify feasible endpoints
derive.why: The time limit truncates the mathematical line.
derive.question: Is the horizontal intercept 20 a feasible leisure choice here?
derive.answer: No. h = 16 is the maximum leisure even though the line would reach c = 0 at l = 20.

graph.title: Draw the budget line
graph.why: Its slope is the consumption cost of leisure.

graph.title: Add the time ceiling
graph.why: The feasible line ends at nonlabor income, not at its extended horizontal intercept.

graph.title: Mark no work
graph.why: This endpoint remains feasible because m is positive.
graph.question: What happens to consumption if leisure falls by one hour?
graph.answer: It rises by 5, the wage earned from that hour.

increase.title: Increase leisure by two hours
increase.why: Start from (l,c) = (10,50), hold the wage and nonlabor income fixed, and increase leisure by two hours.

increase.title: Reduce work
increase.why: The fixed time endowment requires this adjustment.

increase.title: Compute the consumption cost
increase.why: The household moves down and right on the same line.
increase.question: Is this an inward shift of the budget?
increase.answer: No. It is movement along an unchanged opportunity set.

decrease.title: Reduce leisure by three hours
decrease.why: Start from (l,c) = (10,50). Reducing leisure by three hours converts those hours into market work.

decrease.title: Increase earned income
decrease.why: Nonlabor income remains 20.

decrease.title: Move up the same line
decrease.why: The choice changes while prices and endowments stay fixed.
decrease.question: Can this continue beyond l = 0?
decrease.answer: No. Negative leisure violates the time constraint.

edge.title: Reach the time ceiling
edge.why: No more work hours can be released.

edge.title: Use the endpoint budget
edge.why: Wage income is zero at no work.

edge.title: Reject an infeasible intercept
edge.why: When m > 0, h + m/w exceeds h for w > 0.
edge.question: Why must the graph stop at h even though the algebraic line continues?
edge.answer: The time budget, not the consumption equation alone, defines feasible leisure.

leisure-foc.goal: Balance the utility benefit of leisure against its lost earnings.
assumptions: Illustration u = ln(c) + ln(l), h = 16, w = 5, m = 20.
Smooth concave utility, c,l > 0 and an interior work choice are required for tangency.

derive.title: Substitute the budget
derive.why: The constraint turns the problem into a single choice.

derive.title: Differentiate the objective
derive.why: The wage converts lost consumption utility into the cost of leisure.

derive.title: Set marginal gain to zero
derive.why: The household's willingness to trade equals the market tradeoff.

derive.title: Solve with the budget
derive.why: The choice is feasible and leaves six work hours.
derive.question: Why is c/l, not l/c, the MRS here?
derive.answer: MRS = u_l/u_c = (1/l)/(1/c) = c/l, consumption sacrificed per extra leisure hour.

graph.title: Draw feasible bundles
graph.why: All chosen resources must fit this line.

graph.title: Add the attained indifference curve
graph.why: Its slope at the optimum is −c/l = −5.

graph.title: Locate tangency
graph.why: The best feasible interior bundle balances marginal values.
graph.question: At a feasible bundle with MRS > 5, which direction improves utility locally?
graph.answer: Increase leisure: the willingness to pay exceeds its market cost.

increase.title: Raise leisure slightly from below ten
increase.why: Leisure is relatively scarce along this budget.

increase.title: Compare marginal gains
increase.why: The direct leisure benefit exceeds the lost consumption benefit.

increase.title: Move toward tangency
increase.why: The improvement continues until the gap closes.
increase.question: Why stop at l = 10?
increase.answer: Beyond that point the lost consumption utility exceeds the additional leisure utility.

decrease.title: Start above ten leisure hours
decrease.why: The household has relatively abundant leisure and little consumption.

decrease.title: Give up a little leisure
decrease.why: The negative derivative times the negative change raises utility.

decrease.title: Return toward the optimum
decrease.why: Work and consumption rise until MRS matches w.
decrease.question: Does reducing leisure always improve utility?
decrease.answer: No. It helps here because the starting point lies beyond the interior optimum.

edge.title: Increase m enough to bind time
edge.why: The unconstrained formula proposes l = 18.

edge.title: Apply the feasible bound
edge.why: The household cannot choose eighteen leisure hours.

edge.title: Use an inequality at the corner
edge.why: The household would like more leisure but cannot obtain it.
edge.question: Is MRS = w required at this corner?
edge.answer: No. The time constraint prevents the marginal adjustment needed for tangency.

nonlabor-income.goal: Trace an income change separately from a change in the opportunity cost of leisure.
assumptions: Both consumption and leisure are normal goods.
Illustration u = ln(c) + ln(l), h = 16, w = 5; interior results apply until l = h.

derive.title: Write full resources
derive.why: Changing m alters wealth but not the relative price w.

derive.title: Use the interior tangency
derive.why: Equal log weights split full expenditure equally.

derive.title: Solve leisure
derive.why: Higher nonlabor resources permit more leisure.

derive.title: Convert to labor
derive.why: The labor response is negative in this illustration.
derive.question: With w = 5, how much does interior work fall when m rises by 20?
derive.answer: Two hours.

graph.title: Draw the original budget
graph.why: Its slope is −5 and the optimum is (10,50).

graph.title: Add a higher-income budget
graph.why: The entire budget shifts upward by 20 without rotating.

graph.title: Add the new optimum
graph.why: The higher indifference curve is tangent at (12,60).
graph.question: Why is there no substitution effect from this change?
graph.answer: The relative price of leisure, w, has not changed.

increase.title: Raise m
increase.why: Earned opportunities remain the same.

increase.title: Recompute the choice
increase.why: Both normal goods rise.

increase.title: Reduce hours worked
increase.why: The extra leisure comes from less market work.
increase.question: Does this require the wage to fall?
increase.answer: No. The wage remains 5.

decrease.title: Reduce m
decrease.why: The household loses resources without a price change.

decrease.title: Recompute consumption and leisure
decrease.why: Both normal goods decline.

decrease.title: Supply more labor
decrease.why: Working more partly offsets the lost nonlabor income.
decrease.question: Is the increase in work a substitution effect?
decrease.answer: No. It is the income effect of being poorer at the same wage.

edge.title: Reach the no-work threshold
edge.why: The interior solution first reaches l = 16.

edge.title: Raise m beyond the threshold
edge.why: The unrestricted l = 18 is infeasible.

edge.title: Cap leisure
edge.why: Further income raises consumption, not leisure beyond h.
edge.question: Does dN/dm remain −1/(2w) after the corner binds?
edge.answer: No. Locally work stays zero.

wage-effects.goal: Separate compensated substitution from the income effect of a wage change.
assumptions: Illustration u = ln(c) + ln(l), h = 16, m = 20.
A Hicks-compensated line has the new slope and is tangent to the original indifference curve; all marked choices are interior.

derive.title: Write the wage-dependent budget
derive.why: A wage change alters both the price of leisure and earnings from available time.

derive.title: Isolate substitution
derive.why: Holding utility fixed, a higher wage makes leisure more expensive.

derive.title: Identify the worker's income effect
derive.why: At the original positive work hours, a higher wage increases attainable resources.

derive.title: Combine two channels
derive.why: Substitution lowers leisure; a normal-good income effect raises it.
derive.question: Is the total work response theoretically guaranteed positive?
derive.answer: No. The two effects oppose; this numerical log example happens to increase work.

graph.title: Draw the original budget and choice
graph.why: The baseline optimum is (10,50).

graph.title: Rotate through no work
graph.why: The new line shares (16,20) because wage income is zero there.

graph.title: Add the compensated comparison
graph.why: The line parallel to the new budget touches the old indifference curve.
graph.question: Which movement isolates substitution?
graph.answer: From the old choice to the compensated choice, with utility held fixed.

increase.title: Raise w from 5 to 10
increase.why: The budget becomes steeper around the no-work endpoint.

increase.title: Separate the two moves
increase.why: Substitution reduces leisure; the income effect restores some of it.

increase.title: Compute the net effect
increase.why: Substitution dominates in this illustration.
increase.question: Does the upward income effect undo all the substitution effect here?
increase.answer: No. Final leisure 9 is below the original 10.

decrease.title: Cut w from 5 to 2.5
decrease.why: Leisure becomes cheaper, while the worker becomes poorer.

decrease.title: Trace compensation
decrease.why: Substitution raises leisure; the negative income effect reduces it.

decrease.title: Compute the net result
decrease.why: Final leisure rises in this example.
decrease.question: Must every worker cut work after a wage cut?
decrease.answer: No. A stronger income effect could instead raise work.

edge.title: Remove nonlabor income
edge.why: The original numerical resource assumption changes.

edge.title: Resolve the log example
edge.why: The opposing effects exactly cancel in hours worked.

edge.title: State the zero response
edge.why: A wage increase still changes consumption and utility.
edge.question: Does unchanged work prove there were no substitution or income effects?
edge.answer: No. The two nonzero effects can cancel.

aggregate-supply.goal: Build aggregate labor supply from hours and participation decisions.
assumptions: Aggregate supply sums heterogeneous individuals.
An upward-sloping aggregate curve is a maintained course-model relationship, not a universal theorem for every worker.

derive.title: Sum individual hours
derive.why: Both existing workers and potential entrants matter.

derive.title: Separate intensive adjustment
derive.why: An employed person may vary hours as wages change.

derive.title: Separate participation
derive.why: A higher wage can bring people above their reservation wage.

derive.title: Combine responses
derive.why: Aggregate hours can rise even if some individuals reduce hours.
derive.question: Why does an ambiguous individual wage effect not automatically imply a downward aggregate curve?
derive.answer: Participation and heterogeneous responses can outweigh individual reductions.

graph.title: Draw an illustrative supply curve
graph.why: Higher wages correspond to more total labor in this example.

graph.title: Add labor demand
graph.why: Demand provides the other side of the labor market.

graph.title: Locate compatible plans
graph.why: Supply alone does not determine equilibrium employment.
graph.question: Does a wage increase along supply mean supply itself shifted?
graph.answer: No. A shift requires a change in a determinant other than the plotted wage.

increase.title: Increase the available working population
increase.why: At a given wage, additional people can supply hours.

increase.title: Shift aggregate supply right
increase.why: The illustrative addition is 24 hours at each wage.

increase.title: Hold demand fixed
increase.why: The wage falls as firms absorb additional labor.
increase.question: Why does equilibrium employment rise by only eight rather than twenty-four?
increase.answer: The lower wage reduces hours supplied along the new schedule.

decrease.title: Reduce labor availability
decrease.why: Fewer potential workers can supply hours at each wage.

decrease.title: Shift supply left
decrease.why: The inverse schedule lies above the old one.

decrease.title: Find the new crossing
decrease.why: Employment falls and the wage rises.
decrease.question: Can this be explained as movement along the original supply curve alone?
decrease.answer: No. The underlying population or participation condition changed.

edge.title: Allow some backward-bending individuals
edge.why: For a worker, the income effect can dominate substitution.

edge.title: Sum actual individual responses
edge.why: Do not impose the sign before examining the mix.

edge.title: Qualify the aggregate conclusion
edge.why: The illustrative upward curve is an assumption for this market exercise.
edge.question: Does one backward-bending individual prove aggregate supply bends backward?
edge.answer: No. The aggregate sign depends on all hours and participation responses.

labor-equilibrium.goal: Solve a clearing real wage and explain adjustment away from it.
assumptions: Illustrative demand w = 30 − N/4 and supply w = N/8.
Competitive wages adjust and the schedules are locally valid.

derive.title: Write both plans
derive.why: Each side conditions on the same real wage.

derive.title: Impose consistency
derive.why: Actual equilibrium employment must satisfy both plans.

derive.title: Solve the price
derive.why: The wage clears the labor market.

derive.title: Recover the quantity
derive.why: Substitution into demand gives the same quantity.
derive.question: What does disagreement between the two substituted quantities reveal?
derive.answer: An algebra error or a proposed wage that does not clear the market.

graph.title: Reveal demand
graph.why: At higher wages firms want fewer hours.

graph.title: Add supply
graph.why: At higher wages households offer more hours in this model.

graph.title: Mark their intersection
graph.why: Both planned quantities equal 80 at wage 10.
graph.question: Why is the intersection a consistency condition, not simply an average of wages?
graph.answer: It equates quantities supplied and demanded at one common wage.

increase.title: Set wage temporarily above equilibrium
increase.why: Evaluate both schedules at that same price.

increase.title: Calculate excess supply
increase.why: Offered labor exceeds firms' desired hiring by 24.

increase.title: Explain adjustment
increase.why: Competitive wage pressure is downward until the gap closes.
increase.question: Does the high wage create equilibrium employment of 96?
increase.answer: No. Firms only want 72 at that wage; the plans are inconsistent.

decrease.title: Set wage below equilibrium
decrease.why: The old schedules remain unchanged.

decrease.title: Calculate excess demand
decrease.why: Firms want 24 more labor units than workers offer.

decrease.title: Explain upward pressure
decrease.why: Competition for scarce labor tends to raise the wage.
decrease.question: Is 88 equilibrium employment on the old supply curve?
decrease.answer: No. At wage 8 households supply only 64.

edge.title: Prevent wage adjustment
edge.why: The flexible-price clearing assumption fails.

edge.title: Keep both planned quantities
edge.why: The excess supply cannot be erased by declaring the market cleared.

edge.title: Use a rationing mechanism
edge.why: If firms determine hiring, employment can be 72 with unmet work offers.
edge.question: Must the competitive equilibrium point be reached immediately?
edge.answer: No. A fixed or rigid wage requires an explicit disequilibrium or rationing account.

labor-shocks.goal: Trace demand and supply shifts through wages, employment, and production.
assumptions: Illustration Y = A(30N − N²/8), so MPN = A(30 − N/4).
Baseline A = 1; supply Nˢ = 8w. This normalization differs from the square-root firm example.

derive.title: Derive demand from technology
derive.why: Productivity changes the entire marginal-product schedule.

derive.title: Combine with supply
derive.why: The wage and employment adjust together.

derive.title: Solve employment
derive.why: The solution respects both plans.

derive.title: Recover wage and output
derive.why: Output changes through technology and the new employment.
derive.question: At A = 1, what are N, w and Y?

graph.title: Show the initial crossing
graph.why: Demand and supply meet at (80,10).

graph.title: Add higher-productivity demand
graph.why: Supply is the unchanged reference curve.

graph.title: Mark the new crossing
graph.why: Both equilibrium values rise.
graph.question: Why is this not a movement along the old labor-demand curve?
graph.answer: A changed the marginal-product relationship itself.

increase.title: Increase A to 1.2
increase.why: At the old wage firms want more labor.

increase.title: Let the wage adjust
increase.why: A higher wage induces more supplied hours and tempers demand expansion.

increase.title: Compute the final outcome
increase.why: Output rises through both A and N.
increase.question: Why does holding N at 80 understate the final output here?
increase.answer: Supply is upward-sloping, so equilibrium employment also rises.

decrease.title: Reduce A to 0.8
decrease.why: The marginal product of unchanged labor falls.

decrease.title: Resolve the crossing
decrease.why: The lower wage partially moderates the employment loss.

decrease.title: Recompute output
decrease.why: Both reduced efficiency and lower employment lower production.
decrease.question: Does the wage decline fully restore initial employment?
decrease.answer: No. The new demand curve intersects supply at a smaller N.

edge.title: Add an opposing supply shock
edge.why: Suppose productivity falls while labor supply also contracts.

edge.title: Separate the signs
edge.why: Both shocks reduce employment; their wage effects oppose.

edge.title: Solve before assigning a wage sign
edge.why: This particular combination raises wage above 10 despite lower productivity.
edge.question: Is the wage direction generally determined without shock magnitudes?
edge.answer: No. Demand contraction lowers wage, while supply contraction raises it.

unemployment.goal: Classify people before calculating labor-market rates.
assumptions: Use the lecture's U.S./BLS illustration: the adult population is aged 16 or above; employed includes part-time work and temporary absence from a job; unemployed means not employed but actively searching during the preceding four weeks. These course categories are not asserted as a universal definition for every country.
Illustration E = 180, U = 20 and POP = 250; this is not current empirical data.

derive.title: Classify the labor force
derive.why: People outside the labor force are excluded from this denominator.

derive.title: Compute unemployment
derive.why: The rate measures unsuccessful labor-force participants.

derive.title: Compute participation
derive.why: The denominator now includes adults outside the labor force.

derive.title: Compute employment ratio
derive.why: The identity connects the two different margins.
derive.question: Why is 20/250 not the unemployment rate?
derive.answer: It uses adult population rather than the labor force as denominator.

graph.title: Start with the population
graph.why: The 250 adults divide into employed, unemployed and outside the labor force.

graph.title: Reveal mutually exclusive categories
graph.why: Add 180, 20 and 50 to recover 250.

graph.title: Build the correct denominators
graph.why: Only employed and unemployed enter LF.
graph.question: Which category includes a discouraged non-searcher under this framework?
graph.answer: Outside the labor force, not unemployed.

increase.title: Move ten employed people into unemployment
increase.why: Assume all continue actively seeking work.

increase.title: Keep labor force unchanged
increase.why: This transition is within the labor force.

increase.title: Recompute rates
increase.why: Unemployment rises while participation stays fixed.
increase.question: Must rising unemployment mean participation rose?
increase.answer: No. This example changes employment status without changing LF.

decrease.title: Let ten unemployed people stop searching
decrease.why: They move outside the labor force.

decrease.title: Compute the new unemployment rate
decrease.why: Both numerator and denominator fall.

decrease.title: Check actual employment
decrease.why: No additional person obtained a job.
decrease.question: Does the lower unemployment rate prove improved job creation?
decrease.answer: No. Here it reflects withdrawal from active search.

edge.title: Remove all labor-force participants
edge.why: The unemployment-rate denominator vanishes.

edge.title: Recalculate what remains defined
edge.why: Participation and employment ratios remain meaningful.

edge.title: Do not report a spurious zero rate
edge.why: No labor-force share can be calculated.
edge.question: Is unemployment necessarily 0% when nobody participates?
edge.answer: No. The rate is undefined because its denominator is zero.

natural-okun.goal: Separate unemployment types and apply the lecture's empirical growth relationship carefully.

symbols.meaning: change in unemployment in percentage points

assumptions: Lecture illustration g_Y ≈ 3 − 2Δu is an empirical rule, not an accounting identity.
Natural unemployment includes frictional and structural unemployment; it need not be constant across time.

derive.title: Classify the unemployment gap
derive.why: A positive gap indicates unemployment above its natural benchmark.

derive.title: Keep levels separate from changes
derive.why: Okun's displayed growth relation uses a change, not the unemployment level.

derive.title: Apply the empirical coefficients
derive.why: The intercept is growth consistent with no unemployment-rate change in this calibration.

derive.title: Use percentage-point units
derive.why: A one-point increase is not a 1% proportional increase.
derive.question: Should we substitute 6 into Δu because the new rate is 6%?
derive.answer: No. The relevant change is one percentage point.

graph.title: Plot change in unemployment horizontally
graph.why: The vertical coordinate is output growth, not output's level.

graph.title: Mark the zero-change benchmark
graph.why: Stable unemployment is compatible with positive growth.

graph.title: Read positive and negative changes
graph.why: The negative slope associates stronger growth with falling unemployment.
graph.question: Where does the line predict zero output growth?
graph.answer: At Δu = 1.5 percentage points.

increase.title: Increase unemployment by one point
increase.why: For example, 4% becomes 5%.

increase.title: Insert the change
increase.why: Growth is below the 3% benchmark.

increase.title: Interpret the level carefully
increase.why: Output still grows in this example.
increase.question: Does rising unemployment always imply negative GDP growth?
increase.answer: No. Growth can be positive but too weak to keep unemployment stable.

decrease.title: Reduce unemployment by one point
decrease.why: For example, 6% becomes 5%.

decrease.title: Keep the minus signs
decrease.why: The negative change raises predicted growth above the benchmark.

decrease.title: Avoid a causal shortcut
decrease.why: The empirical association does not isolate a policy mechanism.
decrease.question: Does the equation prove forcibly lowering measured unemployment causes 5% growth?
decrease.answer: No. It summarizes a relationship and does not establish that intervention's causal effect.

edge.title: Question the stable calibration
edge.why: Productivity, participation, hours or structural conditions may change. The displayed line is the original lecture calibration retained only as a reference; no unestimated replacement coefficients are implied.

edge.title: Reassess the relationship
edge.why: The intercept, slope or natural unemployment benchmark may change.

edge.title: Use the appropriate interpretation
edge.why: A fitted rule can have residuals and should not be imposed as an exact law.
edge.question: Does full employment mean u = 0?
edge.answer: No. Frictional and structural unemployment can remain at u = u*.

saving-identities.goal: Build private, government and national saving without double-counting taxes.
assumptions: Closed economy; T is defined consistently as net taxes.
Illustration Y = 200, C = 120, T = 40 and G = 50.

derive.title: Compute private saving
derive.why: Households save disposable income not consumed.

derive.title: Compute government saving
derive.why: Government spending exceeds net tax receipts.

derive.title: Add the sectors
derive.why: A tax payment is an outflow for one sector and an inflow for the other.

derive.title: Cancel internal transfers
derive.why: Taxes cancel from the accounting expression.
derive.question: Does cancellation prove taxes cannot affect national saving?
derive.answer: No. Taxes can change behavior such as C, which remains in the identity.

graph.title: Start from total income
graph.why: The resource pool is 200.

graph.title: Reveal both saving components
graph.why: Private saving is positive while government saving is negative.

graph.title: Combine the components
graph.why: National saving is their sum, 30.
graph.question: Why should taxes not be subtracted again from national saving?
graph.answer: Their effect is already included in both sector balances and cancels on consolidation.

increase.title: Raise government purchases by ten
increase.why: Initially hold Y, C and T fixed.

increase.title: Lower government saving
increase.why: More current public use leaves fewer saved resources.

increase.title: Recompute national saving
increase.why: Private saving stays 40 in this accounting experiment.
increase.question: Is a larger tax receipt sufficient to establish this same outcome?
increase.answer: No. A tax change must also account for the private-sector balance and consumption response.

decrease.title: Reduce consumption by ten
decrease.why: Keep Y, T and G fixed.

decrease.title: Raise private saving
decrease.why: Unconsumed disposable income rises.

decrease.title: Add unchanged government saving
decrease.why: National saving rises by ten.
decrease.question: Why does lower private consumption increase national saving here?
decrease.answer: It frees current output from consumption while income and government purchases stay fixed.

edge.title: Change taxes with consumption held fixed
edge.why: This isolates the mechanical accounting transfer.

edge.title: Recompute both sectors
edge.why: The sector changes offset exactly.

edge.title: Check the unchanged total
edge.why: Behavioral tax effects require a separate consumption model.
edge.question: If the tax increase also reduces C by four, what happens to S at fixed Y,G?
edge.answer: National saving rises by four, through lower C.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 1.pdf

desired-actual.goal: Distinguish an accounting identity from equality of planned saving and investment.
assumptions: Closed economy; inventories count as investment.
Illustration output 100, consumption 60, government purchases 20 and planned investment 15.

derive.title: Sum planned spending
derive.why: Planned purchases are below current production.

derive.title: Account for unsold output
derive.why: Goods produced but not sold are still part of investment accounting.

derive.title: Recover actual investment
derive.why: Actual investment includes the inventory surprise.

derive.title: Compare plans and identities
derive.why: The identity holds even when firms' plans are not satisfied.
derive.question: Does actual S = I prove goods-market equilibrium?
derive.answer: No. Unplanned inventories can make the identity hold away from desired equilibrium.

graph.title: Reveal production and spending plans
graph.why: The gap is five units.

graph.title: Reveal the balancing inventory item
graph.why: Unsold output fills the accounting gap.

graph.title: Separate two conclusions
graph.why: Actual accounting balances; desired spending does not equal production.
graph.question: Which node signals disequilibrium?
graph.answer: The planned-equilibrium comparison, because desired investment is 15 while saving is 20.

increase.title: Increase planned investment to twenty
increase.why: Hold Y, C and G fixed.

increase.title: Close the spending gap
increase.why: All output is now purchased as planned.

increase.title: Remove the surprise
increase.why: Actual and planned investment coincide.
increase.question: What is national saving now?
increase.answer: Still 20; the change makes planned investment equal it.

decrease.title: Reduce planned investment to ten
decrease.why: Planned spending falls further below output.

decrease.title: Calculate unsold production
decrease.why: The unplanned inventory addition becomes larger.

decrease.title: Preserve actual accounting
decrease.why: The identity still holds despite worse plan inconsistency.
decrease.question: Did actual saving fall just because planned investment fell?
decrease.answer: Not at the fixed Y, C and G specified here.

edge.title: Let planned spending exceed production
edge.why: The earlier positive-inventory case no longer applies.

edge.title: Use inventory depletion
edge.why: Previously stored goods can satisfy excess purchases if stocks are available.

edge.title: Reconcile actual investment
edge.why: If inventories are unavailable, quantities must be rationed or production/prices adjust.
edge.question: Does a negative inventory surprise violate I = S?
edge.answer: No. It is part of actual investment and preserves the identity.

[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 3.pdf

lifecycle.goal: Explain why consumption can be smoother than income while assets rise and fall.
assumptions: Derived three-stage illustration: incomes 30,70,20; equal-length periods; zero interest; no initial or terminal assets.
Borrowing and lending are available. The illustration motivates the lecture's two-period analysis.

derive.title: Add lifetime resources
derive.why: Temporary income changes need not dictate same-period consumption.

derive.title: Choose a smooth illustrative path
derive.why: Equal consumption uses exactly the lifetime resources.

derive.title: Compute dated saving
derive.why: Consumption above income requires borrowing or asset drawdown.

derive.title: Accumulate assets
derive.why: Middle-stage saving repays early borrowing and funds retirement.
derive.question: Is retirement saving negative because lifetime planning failed?
derive.answer: No. Planned dissaving is how accumulated resources finance later consumption.

graph.title: Plot the income profile
graph.why: Income peaks in the middle stage.

graph.title: Add consumption
graph.why: The flat illustrative path spreads resources across stages.

graph.title: Plot the difference
graph.why: Saving equals the vertical income–consumption gap.
graph.question: At which stage is saving largest?
graph.answer: The middle stage: 70 − 40 = 30.

increase.title: Raise middle-stage income by thirty
increase.why: Lifetime resources become 150.

increase.title: Spread the additional resources
increase.why: Under this equal-consumption illustration, all stages benefit.

increase.title: Recompute saving
increase.why: Extra current saving can fund higher consumption elsewhere.
increase.question: Does higher middle-stage income raise middle-stage consumption by the entire thirty?
increase.answer: No. Only ten is consumed there under the stated smoothing rule.

decrease.title: Reduce retirement income by fifteen
decrease.why: Lifetime resources fall to 105.

decrease.title: Adjust consumption across life
decrease.why: Anticipation allows an earlier response.

decrease.title: Recompute assets
decrease.why: More assets are carried into retirement despite lower lifetime consumption.
decrease.question: Why can expected future income loss increase middle-stage saving?
decrease.answer: The household prepares for the larger later income shortfall.

edge.title: Prohibit early borrowing
edge.why: The original first-stage choice a_1 = −10 becomes infeasible.

edge.title: Respect current resources
edge.why: The perfectly flat path of 40 cannot be implemented.

edge.title: Reoptimize later consumption
edge.why: Under equal-weight concave preferences and zero interest, the first-period cap binds and the remaining ninety units are split equally across the last two periods. The new saving path never requires early borrowing.
edge.question: Does lifetime wealth alone determine current consumption when borrowing is constrained?
edge.answer: No. The timing of accessible resources matters.

[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 2.pdf

budget.goal: Eliminate saving to derive the intertemporal consumption constraint.
assumptions: Two periods; no initial assets in this walk; no terminal assets or bequest.
Borrowing and lending use the same R > 0. Illustration y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75 and R = 1.25.

derive.title: Write the current resource flow
derive.why: Saving is what current income leaves after consumption.

derive.title: Carry saving forward
derive.why: A negative s₁ represents repayment of borrowing next period.

derive.title: Substitute out saving
derive.why: The two dated budgets become one relationship.

derive.title: Divide by the gross return
derive.why: Future quantities are converted into current units.
derive.question: What is W in the illustration?

graph.title: Draw the future-value form
graph.why: The slope is minus the gross real return.

graph.title: Locate the income bundle
graph.why: Consuming income each period involves zero saving.

graph.title: Add an illustrative interior choice
graph.why: It saves 20 now and receives 25 next period.
graph.question: How does the choice's future consumption reconcile?

increase.title: Increase current income by eighteen
increase.why: Present-value resources rise by eighteen.

increase.title: Shift the budget outward
increase.why: The slope stays fixed because R is unchanged.

increase.title: Track the intercepts
increase.why: Current resources can also be carried forward.
increase.question: Why does the vertical intercept rise by 22.5 rather than eighteen?
increase.answer: The extra current income earns the gross return 1.25.

decrease.title: Reduce future income by 22.5
decrease.why: The present value of the loss is eighteen.

decrease.title: Shift the budget inward
decrease.why: The household has fewer lifetime resources.

decrease.title: Retain the intertemporal price
decrease.why: An income loss does not itself change the borrowing/lending rate.
decrease.question: Would losing eighteen of current income produce the same budget line?
decrease.answer: Yes, because the two losses have the same present value.

edge.title: Add a borrowing restriction
edge.why: The linear lifetime budget is no longer the only feasibility condition.

edge.title: Intersect both constraints
edge.why: In this separate illustration, y₁ = 80 and y₂ = 125 give the same W = 180.

edge.title: Exclude inaccessible bundles
edge.why: The lifetime-feasible choice (100,100) requires borrowing and is disallowed.
edge.question: Does equal lifetime wealth guarantee identical feasible current consumption?
edge.answer: No. Borrowing limits make income timing relevant.

[EC2102 Lecture Slides] 3 - The Goods Market - part 2.pdf

pv-fv.goal: Move resources between dates using the gross return consistently.
assumptions: The dates are one period apart and R > 0.
The plot values a fixed future payment of 100.

derive.title: Start from accumulation
derive.why: A current unit becomes R future units.

derive.title: Reverse the operation
derive.why: Discounting asks how much current saving produces a future amount.

derive.title: Evaluate a positive rate
derive.why: Eighty now finances one hundred next period.

derive.title: Keep dates comparable
derive.why: Add cash flows only after converting them to the same date.
derive.question: Is PV = FV − r·FV exact?
derive.answer: No. Exact discounting divides by 1+r; simple subtraction is generally different.

graph.title: Plot the fixed-payment value
graph.why: Only the discount rate varies.

graph.title: Add the face-value reference
graph.why: At zero interest, current and future values coincide.

graph.title: Locate positive and negative rates
graph.why: Higher r lowers PV throughout the domain r > −1.
graph.question: Why is the curve not a straight line?
graph.answer: The rate enters a denominator; the sensitivity changes with r.

increase.title: Increase the real rate
increase.why: Less current saving is needed to deliver a fixed future amount.

increase.title: Recompute the value
increase.why: The future payment is unchanged.

increase.title: Interpret the opportunity cost
increase.why: Current resources earn a larger future return.
increase.question: Does a lower PV mean the promised future payment fell?
increase.answer: No. Its current equivalent fell because the rate rose.

decrease.title: Reduce the real rate below zero
decrease.why: The gross return remains positive at 0.8.

decrease.title: Recompute present value
decrease.why: More than one hundred now is needed to preserve one hundred later.

decrease.title: Retain exact arithmetic
decrease.why: Negative real interest is allowed here as long as R > 0.
decrease.question: Must a future positive payment always have PV below its face amount?
decrease.answer: No. At a negative real rate, PV exceeds FV.

edge.title: Approach the excluded boundary
edge.why: The discount factor becomes unbounded.

edge.title: Inspect the limit
edge.why: A finite current amount earns almost no future resources.

edge.title: Do not divide at R = 0
edge.why: The ordinary present-value budget requires a positive gross return.
edge.question: Can we substitute r = −1 into FV/(1+r)?
edge.answer: No. The expression divides by zero and the standard transformation fails.

budget-geometry.goal: Construct budget intercepts, slopes and pivots from dated resources.
assumptions: No initial wealth; common positive borrowing/lending gross return.
Baseline y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75 and R = 1.25.

derive.title: Use future-value form
derive.why: All vertical amounts are future goods.

derive.title: Set current consumption to zero
derive.why: The household saves all current income.

derive.title: Set future consumption to zero
derive.why: The household borrows against all future resources.

derive.title: Read the slope
derive.why: One extra current good sacrifices 1.25 future goods.
derive.question: Is the slope minus r or minus 1+r?
derive.answer: Minus 1+r, because the principal as well as interest must be repaid.

graph.title: Join the intercepts
graph.why: The straight budget links (0,225) and (180,0).

graph.title: Mark the no-trade endowment
graph.why: The point (120,75) lies on the same line.

graph.title: Mark saving versus borrowing
graph.why: Points left of the endowment save; points right borrow.
graph.question: Does the chosen point (100,100) represent saving or borrowing?
graph.answer: Saving: current consumption is below current income by twenty.

increase.title: Raise the gross return
increase.why: Keep both dated incomes fixed.

increase.title: Rotate around the endowment
increase.why: The line becomes steeper while still passing through (120,75).

increase.title: Compare the two sides
increase.why: Saving bundles gain future resources; borrowing bundles require greater repayment.
increase.question: Is a rate increase an outward parallel budget shift?
increase.answer: No. It is a pivot, benefiting one side of the endowment and worsening the other.

decrease.title: Reduce the gross return
decrease.why: The slope becomes less negative.

decrease.title: Recompute intercepts
decrease.why: The pivot keeps the endowment fixed.

decrease.title: Compare feasible trades
decrease.why: Borrowers can obtain more current goods for a given future sacrifice; savers earn less.
decrease.question: Why can one intercept rise while the other falls?
decrease.answer: The relative intertemporal price changes rather than lifetime resources shifting uniformly.

edge.title: Place choice at the endowment
edge.why: Switch to this explicit zero-saving endowment. The initial optimum is exactly (100,100), rather than the original saver example's (120,75) income bundle.

edge.title: Inspect a rate pivot
edge.why: The no-trade bundle stays feasible, but the budget's slope changes. The first-order endowment wealth effect is zero initially; the substitution incentive remains.

edge.title: Do not infer an unchanged optimum
edge.why: Solving the unchanged log preferences under the new rate gives positive saving and a different consumption allocation, despite the fixed endowment point.
edge.question: Does zero initial saving guarantee consumption stays at the endowment after a rate change?
edge.answer: No. The intertemporal substitution incentive still changes.

preferences.goal: Connect diminishing marginal utility, indifference curves and intertemporal tradeoffs.

symbols.meaning: present-value resources; fixed at 180 in the linear-utility boundary illustration

assumptions: Increasing, concave differentiable period utility; β > 0.
Illustration U = ln(c₁) + 0.8ln(c₂), with strictly positive consumption.

derive.title: Write dated utility
derive.why: β weights future utility, not future goods themselves.

derive.title: Compute marginal utilities
derive.why: Diminishing marginal utility makes scarce consumption especially valuable.

derive.title: Hold utility constant
derive.why: The slope is the future consumption sacrificed for one current unit.

derive.title: Evaluate at equal consumption
derive.why: With β < 1, equal quantities do not imply equal dated marginal utilities.
derive.question: Is equal consumption inconsistent with β = 0.8?
derive.answer: No. At R = 1.25, the market tradeoff exactly matches this MRS.

graph.title: Draw one indifference curve
graph.why: Every point gives the same lifetime utility.

graph.title: Add the resource constraint
graph.why: The budget slope is −1.25.

graph.title: Find the highest feasible curve
graph.why: The illustrated tangency occurs at (100,100).
graph.question: Why do higher indifference curves represent preferred bundles?
graph.answer: Utility increases with each dated consumption good.

increase.title: Increase current consumption on one indifference curve
increase.why: Future consumption must fall to compensate.

increase.title: Compare marginal utilities
increase.why: As c₁ rises and c₂ falls, current marginal utility falls relative to future marginal utility.

increase.title: Read a flatter curve
increase.why: The household gives up fewer future goods for another current unit.
increase.question: Does convexity mean marginal utility is increasing?
increase.answer: No. Here diminishing marginal utility produces a declining willingness to substitute.

decrease.title: Reduce current consumption on the same curve
decrease.why: Future consumption must rise to preserve utility.

decrease.title: Make current goods scarcer
decrease.why: Current marginal utility rises while future marginal utility falls.

decrease.title: Read a steeper tradeoff
decrease.why: The household needs more future compensation for another current sacrifice.
decrease.question: Is the slope positive because future consumption rises?
decrease.answer: No. c₁ falls while c₂ rises, so the slope remains negative.

edge.title: Use linear period utility
edge.why: Switch explicitly to u(c) = c. The new graph plots lifetime utility along a fixed budget, not logarithmic indifference curves; strict concavity no longer holds.

edge.title: Substitute the budget
edge.why: Substitute c₂ = R(W − c₁). The plotted budget uses W = 180 and R = 1.25, while the three utility lines use β = 0.6, 0.8 and 1 to display all three regimes.

edge.title: Select a corner or indifference
edge.math: βR < 1: all current; βR > 1: all future; βR = 1: all feasible bundles tie
edge.why: A unique smooth tangency is unavailable.
edge.question: Why does the usual smoothing logic fail with linear utility?
edge.answer: There is no rising marginal cost from concentrating consumption in one date.

euler.goal: Derive the consumption Euler equation as a marginal reallocation test.
assumptions: Smooth strictly concave utility; both consumption dates positive; no binding borrowing constraint.
Illustration u = ln(c), β = 0.8, R = 1.25 and W = 180.

derive.title: Eliminate future consumption
derive.why: One extra current unit removes R future units.

derive.title: Differentiate lifetime utility
derive.why: The indirect future loss must be included.

derive.title: Balance marginal gains
derive.why: Otherwise moving a small amount across dates improves utility.

derive.title: Solve the log illustration
derive.why: The budget and the Euler condition jointly determine levels.
derive.question: Does the Euler equation alone determine both consumption levels?
derive.answer: No. It sets their marginal relationship; the budget supplies the resource total.

graph.title: Draw the current marginal benefit
graph.why: It falls as current consumption rises.

graph.title: Add the future marginal cost
graph.why: More current consumption leaves less future consumption and raises its marginal value.

graph.title: Locate the crossing
graph.why: The graph compares both terms in the same current-consumption margin.
graph.question: At c₁ = 80, which side is larger?
graph.answer: Current marginal benefit is 0.0125, exceeding future marginal cost 1/125 = 0.008.

increase.title: Raise present-value resources by eighteen
increase.why: At fixed c₁, more future consumption is affordable.

increase.title: Reduce future marginal cost
increase.math: βR u′(c₂) falls at each fixed c₁
increase.why: The current marginal-benefit curve is unchanged.

increase.title: Find the new crossing
increase.why: Both dates receive some of the resource increase.
increase.question: Why does current consumption rise even if the added income arrives next period?
increase.answer: The unconstrained household can reallocate lifetime resources across dates.

decrease.title: Reduce resources by eighteen
decrease.why: At any fixed c₁, less remains for next period.

decrease.title: Raise the marginal future cost
decrease.why: Scarcer future consumption makes another transfer toward today more costly.

decrease.title: Resolve the equality
decrease.why: Both dates absorb the resource loss.
decrease.question: Does the lower optimum require a shift in the current marginal-utility function?
decrease.answer: No. The function is unchanged; the budget changes the future marginal-cost curve.

edge.title: Impose a binding borrowing limit
edge.why: Use the separate example y₂ = 125, with the same unconstrained W = 180.

edge.title: Evaluate the forbidden adjustment
edge.why: The household would like more current consumption but cannot borrow.

edge.title: Replace equality with constrained optimality
edge.why: At the upper bound on c₁, a positive marginal gain need not be zero.
edge.question: Does failure of the Euler equality prove irrational behavior here?
edge.answer: No. The desired improvement is infeasible because the borrowing limit binds.
