profile.goal: Determine the direction of consumption growth from patience, returns and marginal utility.
assumptions: Strictly increasing, strictly concave identical period utility; interior unconstrained allocation.
β = 1/(1+ρ), with 1+ρ > 0 and R > 0.

derive.title: Start from the Euler condition
derive.why: The marginal-utility ratio equals the weighted return.

derive.title: Express patience as a rate
derive.why: Compare the market return with impatience.

derive.title: Use diminishing marginal utility
derive.why: Higher marginal utility identifies the smaller consumption level.

derive.title: Handle equality
derive.why: Equal consumption follows from identical strictly concave period utility.
derive.question: Does β < 1 by itself imply declining consumption?
derive.answer: No. A sufficiently high return can offset impatience.

graph.title: Start at a flat profile
graph.why: The equality of dated consumption is a property of the chosen parameters.

graph.title: Raise the return while keeping incomes fixed
graph.why: The new budget pivots through the same income bundle.

graph.title: Locate the rising profile
graph.why: For log utility c₂/c₁ = βR = 1.2.
graph.question: Does a rising profile mean the household saves from current income?
graph.answer: Not necessarily in general; compare c₁ with y₁. It does save in this illustration.

increase.title: Raise R to 1.5
increase.why: The reward to postponing consumption rises.

increase.title: Use the log Euler ratio
increase.why: Future consumption exceeds current consumption.

increase.title: Use the budget for levels
increase.why: The ratio alone would not determine the scale.
increase.question: Can the same ratio hold for a richer household?
increase.answer: Yes. With log utility the ratio stays 1.2, while both levels scale with wealth.

decrease.title: Lower R to 1
decrease.why: The return no longer offsets time preference.

decrease.title: Infer the declining profile
decrease.why: Current consumption exceeds future consumption.

decrease.title: Calculate the levels
decrease.why: The smaller future quantity has higher period marginal utility.
decrease.question: Why can the Euler condition still hold?
decrease.answer: Future marginal utility is discounted by β and multiplied by R.

edge.title: Let a borrowing limit bind
edge.why: The unrestricted Euler equality may fail.

edge.title: Re-evaluate the observed profile
edge.why: Current scarcity is enforced by inaccessible future income.

edge.title: Qualify the earlier inference
edge.why: The r-versus-ρ rule requires interior unconstrained intertemporal trade.
edge.question: Does unequal consumption at r = ρ necessarily contradict optimization?
edge.answer: No. A binding constraint can prevent the equal-consumption allocation.

income-shocks.goal: Compare current and future income shocks by present value and by saving timing.
assumptions: Unconstrained log utility, β = 0.8 and R = 1.25.
Baseline y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75, W = 180 and c₁ = c₂ = 100.

derive.title: Value the dated shock
derive.why: A future dollar is not a current dollar.

derive.title: Use the log allocation
derive.why: Each date receives a share of lifetime resources.

derive.title: Translate wealth into consumption
derive.why: These particular parameters make the two level changes equal.

derive.title: Recover saving separately
derive.why: Identical consumption shifts need not imply identical saving shifts.
derive.question: How can two shocks produce the same consumption but different saving?
derive.answer: They can have the same present value while arriving at different dates.

graph.title: Draw the original budget
graph.why: The baseline choice is (100,100).

graph.title: Add a resource increase of eighteen
graph.why: Either Δy₁ = 18 or Δy₂ = 22.5 produces this same parallel line.

graph.title: Locate the new tangency
graph.why: The pure wealth effect raises both normal goods.
graph.question: Would equal nominal increases at the two dates shift the budget equally?
graph.answer: No. The future increase is discounted by R.

increase.title: Raise current income by eighteen
increase.why: The household immediately receives the extra resources.

increase.title: Smooth the gain
increase.why: Current consumption rises by less than current income.

increase.title: Compute added saving
increase.why: Saving transfers part of the current income gain forward.
increase.question: If instead future income rose by 22.5, what is Δs₁?
increase.answer: −10: current consumption rises by ten without a current income increase.

decrease.title: Reduce future income by 22.5
decrease.why: The household anticipates fewer lifetime resources.

decrease.title: Reduce both dated consumptions
decrease.why: The loss is shared across dates.

decrease.title: Increase current saving
decrease.why: Lower consumption today prepares for lower income tomorrow.
decrease.question: Does worse expected future income necessarily reduce current saving?
decrease.answer: No. In this certainty-based example, the household reallocates consumption and increases current saving by ten to prepare for the known future income loss.

edge.title: Bind current borrowing
edge.why: The unconstrained response rule is no longer feasible.

edge.title: Raise future income by twenty-five
edge.why: If the constraint continues to bind, future resources cannot be borrowed into today.

edge.title: Compare income timing
edge.why: A current-income increase can relax the borrowing limit itself.
edge.question: Must equal-PV shocks still produce equal current consumption changes?
edge.answer: No. That equivalence relies on access to intertemporal trade.

interest-effects.goal: Separate intertemporal substitution from borrower or saver wealth effects.
assumptions: Same positive rate for borrowing and lending; no initial assets in this walk.
Illustration uses log utility, β = 0.8, y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75, initially R = 1.25. Qualitative ambiguity extends beyond this log example.

derive.title: Write the rotating budget
derive.why: The endowment bundle remains feasible at all R.

derive.title: Isolate substitution
derive.why: A higher R makes current consumption more expensive in future goods, reducing compensated c₁.

derive.title: Classify the wealth effect
derive.math: s₁ > 0: lender gains; s₁ < 0: borrower loses from a marginal R increase
derive.why: The sign depends on the initial net trade.

derive.title: Combine channels
derive.why: For a saver, current-consumption effects oppose; for a borrower, both lower c₁ under normality.
derive.question: Is saving guaranteed to increase for every saver when the rate rises?
derive.answer: No. With fixed y₁, the ambiguous c₁ response makes saving ambiguous too.

graph.title: Draw the old budget and utility curve
graph.why: The household initially saves twenty.

graph.title: Add the steeper budget
graph.why: The new rate is R = 1.5.

graph.title: Add the compensated tangent
graph.why: It has the new slope but preserves old utility.
graph.question: Which segment measures the saver's income effect?
graph.answer: The move from the compensated choice to the new actual optimum.

increase.title: Raise the gross return
increase.why: The saver gains purchasing opportunities but faces a higher relative price of current consumption.

increase.title: Apply the log formula
increase.why: Here substitution dominates the income effect on c₁.

increase.title: Recover saving and future consumption
increase.why: Saving rises in this illustration.
increase.question: May this numerical result be promoted to a universal saver theorem?
increase.answer: No. Other concave preferences can give a larger opposing income effect.

decrease.title: Lower the gross return
decrease.why: Current consumption becomes cheaper relative to future consumption.

decrease.title: Trace the opposing effects
decrease.why: Substitution raises current consumption; the saver's loss of resources tends to lower it.

decrease.title: Compute this log result
decrease.why: The substitution effect dominates for current consumption here.
decrease.question: Does a lower rate enrich this initial saver?
decrease.answer: No. The wealth effect is negative; the observed rise in c₁ comes despite it.

edge.title: Start at zero net saving
edge.why: Switch to this explicit zero-saving endowment. The initial optimum is exactly (100,100), rather than the original saver example's (120,75) income bundle.

edge.title: Retain the price change
edge.why: The no-trade bundle stays feasible, but the budget's slope changes. The first-order endowment wealth effect is zero initially; the substitution incentive remains.

edge.title: Avoid a false no-effect claim
edge.why: Solving the unchanged log preferences under the new rate gives positive saving and a different consumption allocation, despite the fixed endowment point.
edge.question: What fails in the statement 'the endowment is unchanged, so consumption is unchanged'?
edge.answer: It ignores the changed slope and thus the changed marginal tradeoff.

initial-wealth.goal: Distinguish beginning assets, end assets and saving under the lecture's timing convention.

symbols.meaning: assets entering period 1 before earning its return
wealth measured after the current return has already accrued

assumptions: Assets a₀ earn R before period-1 spending; no terminal assets.
Illustration a₀ = 8, y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75, R = 1.25 and log utility with β = 0.8, where β is the future utility weight.

derive.title: Bring opening assets to the spending date
derive.why: The eight units earn two units before current consumption.

derive.title: Write end assets
derive.why: Initial principal is available but is not itself new income.

derive.title: Define current saving
derive.math: s₁ = ra₀ + y₁ − c₁ = a₁ − a₀
derive.why: Saving is the change in asset holdings, excluding consumption of opening principal.

derive.title: Eliminate end assets
derive.why: The initial asset term follows its specified date.
derive.question: Why is adding a₀ instead of Ra₀ incorrect under this timing?
derive.answer: It omits the return earned before current spending.

graph.title: Show principal and its return
graph.why: Eight units become ten spendable current resources.

graph.title: Apply the consumption allocation
graph.why: End assets become about 24.444.

graph.title: Separate stock and flow
graph.why: The difference is the initial principal eight.
graph.question: How is future consumption financed?

increase.title: Raise a₀ by eight
increase.why: Under the convention, spendable lifetime resources rise by RΔa₀ = 10.

increase.title: Smooth the extra wealth
increase.why: Current consumption rises by less than the added current resources.

increase.title: Compare stocks and saving
increase.why: Greater initial wealth can raise end assets while reducing new saving.
increase.question: Why are these signs not contradictory?
increase.answer: End assets include inherited principal; saving measures only the change from that larger initial stock.

decrease.title: Remove the initial assets
decrease.why: Present-value resources fall from 190 to 180.

decrease.title: Resolve consumption
decrease.why: Both dates absorb the wealth loss.

decrease.title: Recompute assets and saving
decrease.why: They now coincide because initial assets are zero.
decrease.question: Does lower initial wealth necessarily reduce current saving in this example?
decrease.answer: No. Saving rises from about 16.444 to twenty while end assets fall.

edge.title: Change the definition of opening wealth
edge.why: If wealth is measured after the current return, denote it B₀ = Ra₀.

edge.title: Rewrite the budget consistently
edge.why: Do not earn the current return twice.

edge.title: Match symbols to dates
edge.why: The apparent difference between formulas can be a timing convention.
edge.question: May we replace a₀ by B₀ while retaining Ra₀ in the formula?
edge.answer: No. That would count an extra return on already accumulated current resources.

closed-form.goal: Solve log and square-root utility allocations rather than memorizing a single formula.

symbols.meaning: current and future disposable income in the numerical shock examples

assumptions: Positive resources and interior unconstrained choices.
Compare U = ln(c₁)+βln(c₂) with U = √c₁+β√c₂; these preferences have different marginal utilities.

derive.title: Solve the log Euler equation
derive.why: The consumption ratio follows from the derivative of log utility.

derive.title: Use the log budget
derive.why: Future consumption then equals βRW/(1+β).

derive.title: Cancel the common factor two
derive.why: These are the square-root marginal utilities in the Euler equation. Multiply both sides by two; β and R remain because they weight and convert the future benefit.

derive.title: Isolate the future square root
derive.why: Multiply by the positive √c₂, then by the positive √c₁. This isolates the future-consumption root without reversing any inequality or changing a sign.

derive.title: Square the positive sides
derive.why: Both sides of the previous equality are positive because β, R and consumption are positive. Squaring therefore gives the equivalent positive-consumption relation.

derive.title: Substitute future consumption into the budget
derive.math:
c₁ + c₂/R = W
⇒ c₁ + (β²R²c₁)/R = W
⇒ c₁ + β²Rc₁ = W
derive.why: The budget values future consumption in current units. Dividing by R removes one, but not both, of the two return factors in β²R².

derive.title: Collect the current-consumption terms
derive.why: Factor c₁ out of the sum and divide by the positive coefficient 1 + β²R. This is why the denominator differs from the log formula.

derive.title: Recover and check both consumption levels
derive.math:
c₁ = W/(1 + β²R)
c₂ = (βR)²W/(1 + β²R)
At β = 0.8, R = 1.25, W = 180: c₁ = c₂ = 100
derive.why: Recover c₂ from the squared Euler relation, then verify c₁ + c₂/R = W. The displayed budget is the numerical special case in which the log and square-root optima coincide; the derivation itself is general.
derive.question: Why does substituting c₂ into the budget produce β²R, rather than β²R², beside c₁?
derive.answer: The squared Euler relation gives c₂ = β²R²c₁, but the budget contains c₂/R. Dividing by R leaves β²Rc₁.

graph.title: Plot the common illustrative budget
graph.why: W = 180 and R = 1.25 determine feasibility.

graph.title: Add the log indifference curve
graph.why: The displayed curve specifically belongs to log utility.

graph.title: Locate the shared special-case optimum
graph.why: Both utility forms choose (100,100) at these particular parameters.
graph.question: Does a shared optimum mean the two utility functions always give the same choices?
graph.answer: No. Changing R or β generally separates their allocation formulas.

increase.title: Increase current income in the square-root case
increase.why: The numerical parameters now differ from the log plot and are explicitly stated.

increase.title: Allocate current consumption
increase.why: The denominator comes from the square-root Euler relation.

increase.title: Recover future consumption
increase.why: The future increase must be discounted before adding it to today's increase.
increase.question: What budget check confirms the result?

decrease.title: Reduce future income in that same case
decrease.why: Use square-root utility with β = 0.9 and R = 2. Start from y₁ = 262 and y₂ = 524, so c₁ = 200 and c₂ = 648. The future-income loss leaves y₂ = 262 and has present value −131.

decrease.title: Reduce current consumption
decrease.why: Lifetime resources, not raw future income, enter the numerator. The new levels are c₁ = 150 and c₂ = 486, both strictly positive.

decrease.title: Reduce future consumption
decrease.why: The two changes satisfy the dated resource loss.
decrease.question: Why should −50 and −162 not be added directly?
decrease.answer: They are goods at different dates; −50 + (−162)/2 = −131.

edge.title: Check the borrowing requirement
edge.why: Use a separate square-root illustration with the same β = 0.9 and R = 2, but incomes y₁ = 100 and y₂ = 500. The unrestricted c₁ ≈ 133.588 requires borrowing, so c₁ ≤ 100 binds.

edge.title: Apply the feasible set
edge.why: With no borrowing, compare the candidate against c₁ ≤ y₁.

edge.title: Replace the infeasible candidate
edge.math: c₁ = y₁; c₂ = y₂ when the no-borrowing constraint binds
edge.why: The formula is not an exemption from the constraint.
edge.question: What must be done before using any closed-form answer?
edge.answer: Check positive consumption, the timing convention, parameter domain and all borrowing or time constraints.

constraints.goal: Re-solve consumption when a borrowing boundary prevents the unrestricted optimum.
assumptions: Illustration log utility, β = 0.8, R = 1.25, y₁ = 80 and y₂ = 125.
No initial assets; no borrowing means s₁ ≥ 0, equivalently c₁ ≤ y₁.

derive.title: Solve without the extra restriction
derive.why: This supplies a candidate, not yet an admissible answer.

derive.title: Translate the borrowing rule
derive.why: The desired current consumption requires twenty of borrowing.

derive.title: Apply the binding boundary
derive.why: The household uses current income but cannot transfer future resources backward.

derive.title: Check the one-sided incentive
derive.why: The household would like to increase c₁, but that direction is infeasible.
derive.question: Why not lower c₁ to restore the Euler equality?
derive.answer: Lowering c₁ makes the current shortage worse and reduces utility; the desired equality lies beyond the cap.

graph.title: Draw the lifetime budget
graph.why: Its intercepts are the same as those of an unconstrained household with W = 180.

graph.title: Add the current-consumption cap
graph.why: The vertical line removes the borrowing portion.

graph.title: Compare desired and feasible choices
graph.why: The unrestricted optimum is right of the cap.
graph.question: Which point is chosen when the constraint binds?
graph.answer: (80,125), the best feasible point at the cap.

increase.title: Raise current income by twenty
increase.why: Both lifetime resources and the borrowing cap rise.

increase.title: Check the new unrestricted choice
increase.why: It still exceeds current income.

increase.title: Use the still-binding boundary
increase.why: Every extra current-income unit is consumed currently.
increase.question: What is the local MPC out of current income while this boundary remains binding?
increase.answer: One, with future consumption unchanged.

decrease.title: Reduce current income by twenty
decrease.why: The borrowing cap moves left as current resources shrink.

decrease.title: Test the unrestricted candidate
decrease.why: Borrowing would still be desired.

decrease.title: Respect the tighter cap
decrease.why: Current consumption absorbs the entire current-income loss.
decrease.question: Can the household use unchanged future income to preserve c₁ = 80?
decrease.answer: Not when borrowing is prohibited and no other assets exist.

edge.title: Lower future income until the boundary stops binding
edge.why: At this threshold the unrestricted optimum exactly equals current income.

edge.title: Reduce future income further
edge.why: Use an explicit lower-future-income case. The new unrestricted solution is c₁ = c₂ = 200/3, below the unchanged current-income cap of 80.

edge.title: Return to the interior Euler solution
edge.why: The household now voluntarily saves, so the borrowing inequality is slack and the interior Euler solution applies again.
edge.question: Is a no-borrowing rule always binding?
edge.answer: No. It is irrelevant when the household voluntarily saves.

dated-mpcs.goal: Calculate all four dated consumption responses and verify the discounted resource check.
assumptions: Square-root utility U = √c₁ + β√c₂, interior and unconstrained.
Numerical illustration β = 0.9, R = 2, so D = 2.62.
For the signed-loss experiment, the initial incomes are y₁ = 262 and y₂ = 524; the future-income loss of 262 therefore leaves positive income and positive consumption at both dates.

derive.title: Write the solved allocation
derive.why: The first subscript identifies the consumption date.

derive.title: Differentiate current consumption
derive.why: A future-income unit has a smaller present value.

derive.title: Differentiate future consumption
derive.why: Future consumption includes accumulation at R.

derive.title: Check dated adding-up
derive.why: Responses exhaust the added resources in common date units.
derive.question: Must every dated MPC be below one?
derive.answer: No. A future consumption response to current income can exceed one because saving earns a gross return.

graph.title: Plot current consumption's response
graph.why: The line's slope is MPC_11.

graph.title: Add future consumption's response
graph.why: This slope can exceed one because its output is dated tomorrow.

graph.title: Add the discounted future response
graph.why: Only this discounted value can be added to current consumption.
graph.question: At Δy₁ = 131, what adds up to the income increase?
graph.answer: 50 of current consumption plus 81 of discounted future consumption.

increase.title: Increase current income by 131
increase.why: Keep β and R fixed.

increase.title: Use both relevant derivatives
increase.why: The future consumption increase exceeds the original current-income increase.

increase.title: Account for investment across dates
increase.why: The response is feasible because the saved resources earn a return.
increase.question: Is MPC_21 > 1 evidence of a violated budget?
increase.answer: No. Discounting gives 50 + 162/2 = 131.

decrease.title: Reduce future income by 262
decrease.why: Use square-root utility with β = 0.9 and R = 2. Start from y₁ = 262 and y₂ = 524, so c₁ = 200 and c₂ = 648. The future-income loss leaves y₂ = 262 and has present value −131.

decrease.title: Use the future-income derivatives
decrease.why: MPC_12 and MPC_22 apply to this dated shock. The new levels are c₁ = 150 and c₂ = 486, both strictly positive.

decrease.title: Verify the loss in future units
decrease.why: Both dated reductions reconcile exactly.
decrease.question: Why is MPC_12 smaller than MPC_11 when R > 1?
decrease.answer: A unit of future income is worth only 1/R current units.

edge.title: Make the borrowing limit bind
edge.why: Use a separate square-root illustration with the same β = 0.9 and R = 2, but incomes y₁ = 100 and y₂ = 500. The unrestricted c₁ ≈ 133.588 requires borrowing, so c₁ ≤ 100 binds.

edge.title: Differentiate the binding solution
edge.why: While it stays binding, MPC_11 = 1, MPC_12 = 0, MPC_21 = 0 and MPC_22 = 1.

edge.title: Check the regime before differentiating
edge.why: At the threshold between regimes, one-sided derivatives can differ.
edge.question: May one apply the square-root interior MPCs mechanically at a binding cap?
edge.answer: No. First identify which constraints bind, then differentiate that regime's solution.

cw-income.goal: Recognize that wage income changes when leisure choices change.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Account for each time endowment
derive.math: n₁ = h − l₁; n₂ = h − l₂
derive.why: Work and leisure are choices in both periods.

derive.title: Value dated work
derive.math: y₁ = w₁(h − l₁); y₂ = w₂(h − l₂)
derive.why: Here y₁ and y₂ denote endogenous labor income.

derive.title: Separate income from full resources
derive.why: Full resources value all available time before purchasing leisure.

derive.title: Recognize the feedback
derive.why: Choosing more leisure reduces income; it cannot be treated as an independent income shock.
derive.question: Why cannot we solve consumption first using fixed labor incomes and then independently choose leisure?
derive.answer: The leisure decisions change those incomes, so all choices must satisfy the same joint budget.

graph.title: Reveal time allocations
graph.why: Each period has its own work–leisure split.

graph.title: Convert work to income
graph.why: The wage multiplies the chosen work hours.

graph.title: Connect income to saving and future spending
graph.why: The dated choices interact through the asset transfer.
graph.question: If l₁ rises by one at fixed w₁ = 2, what happens to current labor income?
graph.answer: It falls by two.

increase.title: Raise the current wage
increase.why: The price of current leisure and full resources both rise.

increase.title: Resolve all choices
increase.why: In this illustration, work also increases.

increase.title: Recompute actual earnings
increase.why: The income gain reflects both a higher wage and more work.
increase.question: Would w₁h be actual income here?
increase.answer: No. It is potential full-time income; actual income subtracts the value of chosen leisure.

decrease.title: Lower the current wage
decrease.why: Do not hold endogenous work fixed in the final solution.

decrease.title: Resolve current work
decrease.why: The joint log problem predicts less work at this wage.

decrease.title: Compute lower earnings
decrease.why: Both the wage and the hours adjustment reduce income here.
decrease.question: Can the sign of this hours response be assumed for all preferences?
decrease.answer: No. It is the result of this specified utility and endowment example.

edge.title: Reach no current work
edge.why: The time ceiling binds.

edge.title: Recompute current income
edge.why: A positive wage does not create income without work.

edge.title: Use intertemporal resources
edge.why: Current consumption can still be positive if future earnings can be borrowed against.
edge.question: Does zero current labor income force zero current consumption in this model?
edge.answer: No. Borrowing is allowed; imposing a borrowing limit would change the feasible set.

cw-budget.goal: Derive the full-income budget for four jointly chosen goods.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Write current saving
derive.why: Saving transfers current earned resources after consumption.

derive.title: Write future spending
derive.why: Future labor income and accumulated saving finance future consumption.

derive.title: Eliminate saving
derive.math: c₁ + c₂/R = w₁(h − l₁) + w₂(h − l₂)/R
derive.why: Both income terms still depend on leisure.

derive.title: Collect all choices on the left
derive.math: c₁ + w₁l₁ + (c₂ + w₂l₂)/R = w₁h + w₂h/R = W
derive.why: Leisure uses resources at its opportunity cost.
derive.question: Why is future leisure priced at w₂/R in current units?
derive.answer: Its lost future earnings must be discounted to the current date.

graph.title: Start with dated earnings
graph.why: Both leisure choices determine the income available.

graph.title: Connect through saving
graph.why: The return converts current transfers into future resources.

graph.title: Reveal the consolidated constraint
graph.why: The final node accounts for four goods in one common date unit.
graph.question: What is W for the numerical example?

increase.title: Raise the current wage
increase.why: Current leisure's price rises and full resources increase from 52 to 72.

increase.title: Inspect the fixed-expenditure slice
increase.math: Rw₁l₁ + w₂l₂ = fixed future-valued leisure expenditure
increase.why: The plotted slice isolates the changing relative price only.

increase.title: Restore the full budget for the final choice
increase.why: The actual wage shock also changes consumption and the expenditure available for leisure.
increase.question: May the plotted slice alone be used to read the final wage-shock optimum?
increase.answer: No. Full resources and spending allocations must also be re-solved.

decrease.title: Reduce the future wage
decrease.why: Both future leisure's price and future potential earnings fall.

decrease.title: Recompute full resources
decrease.why: The current value of the time endowment is smaller.

decrease.title: Keep both effects in the optimization
decrease.why: Treating the wage fall as a pure wealth change would omit its relative-price effect.
decrease.question: Does lower w₂ simply shift the full budget in parallel?
decrease.answer: No. It changes a price coefficient and the resource total.

edge.title: Add initial assets using the lecture's timing
edge.math: a₀ earns R before current spending
edge.why: The no-initial-assets assumption no longer holds.

edge.title: Extend full resources
edge.why: Here a₀ denotes the entering asset stock.

edge.title: Avoid double-counting labor earnings
edge.why: Full time values already include the labor resources before leisure is purchased.
edge.question: Should actual wage income be added again to W?
edge.answer: No. That would count the same time endowments twice.

cw-substitution.goal: Reduce the joint problem to independent choice variables before differentiating.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Choose independent controls
derive.why: Future consumption will be supplied by the budget.

derive.title: Solve the budget for c₂
derive.math: c₂ = Rw₁(h − l₁) + w₂(h − l₂) − Rc₁
derive.why: Every independent choice has a resource consequence.

derive.title: Substitute into lifetime utility
derive.why: The function u denotes utility from consumption and leisure in one period.

derive.title: Differentiate the indirect channels
derive.why: These derivatives carry the budget into all first-order conditions.
derive.question: Why is ∂c₂/∂l₁ equal to −Rw₁ rather than −w₁?
derive.answer: Lost current earnings would otherwise be carried forward at R.

graph.title: Show the primitive choices
graph.why: Current and future leisure determine dated earnings.

graph.title: Show the propagation through saving
graph.why: Current consumption and current leisure both reduce future resources.

graph.title: Close the dependence
graph.why: c₂ is determined, not a fourth independent choice after substitution.
graph.question: Would setting ∂U/∂c₂ = 0 after this substitution be a valid independent condition?
graph.answer: No. Increasing utility makes unrestricted c₂ desirable; the budget determines its feasible change.

increase.title: Increase current leisure slightly
increase.why: Hold c₁ and l₂ fixed for this partial derivative.

increase.title: Propagate the resource loss
increase.why: The indirect cost is borne in future consumption under this chosen coordinate system.

increase.title: Compare utility channels
increase.why: The same budget tradeoff must be counted once.
increase.question: Why should we not additionally subtract a separate current-consumption loss in this derivative?
increase.answer: c₁ is held fixed here; the full earnings loss has already entered through c₂.

decrease.title: Reduce future leisure slightly
decrease.why: Hold current consumption and current leisure fixed.

decrease.title: Increase future labor earnings
decrease.why: Extra future work directly funds future consumption.

decrease.title: Compare direct and indirect utility
decrease.why: The common β weights both future-period effects.
decrease.question: Does β change the future intratemporal wage equality after cancelling?
decrease.answer: No. It multiplies both benefits and costs within that date.

edge.title: Let the substituted c₂ reach zero
edge.why: Log utility and its derivative are undefined at zero consumption.

edge.title: Check the domain before differentiating
edge.why: Only choices satisfying this strict positivity condition belong to the log problem.

edge.title: Reject infeasible stationary candidates
edge.why: An algebraic solution outside the utility domain is not an optimum.
edge.question: Can we evaluate log derivatives at a negative c₂ and continue?
edge.answer: No. The candidate violates both the consumption domain and the economic feasibility requirement.

cw-euler.goal: Derive the Euler condition while recognizing that labor supply also adjusts.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Vary current consumption
derive.why: Hold both leisure choices fixed for this marginal comparison.

derive.title: Differentiate joint utility
derive.why: The same intertemporal tradeoff applies inside the larger problem.

derive.title: Use log consumption utility
derive.why: The consumption ratio is linked to prices and patience.

derive.title: Combine with both leisure conditions
derive.math: l₁ = c₁/w₁; l₂ = c₂/w₂ ⇒ c₁ = W/[2(1+β)]
derive.why: Each period allocates equal full expenditure to consumption and leisure in this log example.
derive.question: Why is the denominator not just 1+β?
derive.answer: Full resources also pay for leisure in both periods.

graph.title: Hold both leisure choices fixed
graph.why: These are the baseline joint optimum's leisure choices. Varying c₁ then traces the Euler margin only.

graph.title: Add the future marginal cost
graph.why: The current consumption increase removes 1.25 future units, whose marginal utility rises as future consumption shrinks.

graph.title: Locate the marginal balance
graph.why: Both curves meet at 9/130, confirming the Euler condition for the joint optimum.
graph.question: Does this marginal comparison alone choose the leisure levels?
graph.answer: No. They must also satisfy both intratemporal conditions and the full budget.

increase.title: Raise current wage from two to four
increase.why: Full resources rise from 52 to 72.

increase.title: Recompute consumption
increase.why: The Euler ratio stays one because β and R are unchanged.

increase.title: Recompute both leisure choices
increase.why: The labor decisions are jointly consistent with higher consumption.
increase.question: Why can the consumption ratio stay fixed while labor changes?
increase.answer: The unchanged Euler price ratio sets the ratio, while changed wage prices and wealth alter levels and leisure.

decrease.title: Reduce future wage from four to two
decrease.why: Full resources fall from 52 to 36.

decrease.title: Reduce both consumption levels
decrease.why: Lower full wealth reduces consumption at both dates.

decrease.title: Recompute leisure
decrease.why: The changed future leisure price also matters.
decrease.question: Does a fixed Euler ratio imply unchanged consumption levels?
decrease.answer: No. The budget determines their scale.

edge.title: Let current leisure hit its upper bound
edge.why: The interior four-good solution is infeasible.

edge.title: Keep the still-valid interior conditions
edge.why: The consumption Euler condition can remain valid even when current leisure is at a corner.

edge.title: Resolve the reduced budget
edge.why: Only the failed current-leisure equality must be replaced.
edge.question: Must every first-order equality fail when one constraint binds?
edge.answer: No. Retain conditions for feasible interior margins and replace only the constrained margin.

cw-intratemporal.goal: Derive the consumption–leisure tradeoff separately in each period.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Differentiate with respect to current leisure
derive.why: Its lost earnings would have supported future consumption.

derive.title: Use the Euler equation
derive.why: Substitute this equality into the current-leisure condition.

derive.title: Obtain current tangency
derive.why: The within-period tradeoff reduces to the current wage.

derive.title: Derive future tangency directly
derive.why: Both future utility terms carry β, which cancels.
derive.question: For log utility, what do these conditions imply?
derive.answer: c₁ = w₁l₁ and c₂ = w₂l₂ at an interior solution.

graph.title: Draw the current budget slice
graph.why: Optimal future choices are held fixed for this visual comparison.

graph.title: Add the current indifference curve
graph.why: Its slope is −c₁/l₁.

graph.title: Mark matching slopes
graph.why: The time ceiling is not binding.
graph.question: Why can this slice use an intercept different from current full-time earnings twenty?
graph.answer: Intertemporal borrowing and the fixed future allocation enter the remaining current resources.

increase.title: Raise the current wage to four
increase.why: The consumption cost of one current leisure hour rises.

increase.title: Solve the new joint optimum
increase.why: The MRS rises to match the higher wage.

increase.title: Verify the equality
increase.why: The changed levels satisfy the intratemporal rule.
increase.question: May we infer l₁ solely by dividing the old c₁ by the new wage?
increase.answer: No. Consumption also changes and must be solved jointly.

decrease.title: Lower the current wage to 1.5
decrease.why: Current leisure becomes cheaper in consumption units.

decrease.title: Resolve consumption and leisure
decrease.why: Their ratio equals 1.5.

decrease.title: Verify the tradeoff
decrease.why: The new solution remains within the ten-hour leisure ceiling.
decrease.question: What goes wrong if one predicts more than ten leisure hours from the formula?
decrease.answer: The interior condition has crossed its feasible boundary and must be replaced.

edge.title: Set w₁ = 1
edge.why: The unrestricted leisure choice would exceed ten.

edge.title: Use the constrained allocation
edge.why: The household does not work currently.

edge.title: Check the one-sided condition
edge.why: More leisure would be preferred at this tradeoff, but none is available.
edge.question: Why is MRS₁ > w₁ compatible with optimality?
edge.answer: The upper time bound prevents the otherwise desirable increase in leisure.

cw-relative-wage.goal: Derive the relative price of leisure across dates and separate it from the wealth effect.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Value current leisure in future goods
derive.why: Current foregone earnings also lose the interest they could earn.

derive.title: Value future leisure
derive.why: Its earnings cost already occurs at the future date.

derive.title: Form the relative price
derive.math: relative price of l₁ in l₂ units = Rw₁/w₂
derive.why: A fixed-expenditure leisure trade line has slope −Rw₁/w₂.

derive.title: Connect marginal utilities
derive.why: Use both leisure optimality conditions at an interior choice.
derive.question: For the baseline wages, what is the relative price?
derive.answer: 1.25(2)/4 = 0.625 future leisure hours per current leisure hour.

graph.title: Fix a leisure-expenditure slice
graph.why: This isolates a relative-price comparison in future-value units.

graph.title: Raise current wage in the slice
graph.why: Current leisure becomes more expensive; the line becomes steeper.

graph.title: Add a future-wage increase
graph.why: Future leisure becomes more expensive and the line becomes flatter.
graph.question: Are these fixed-expenditure lines the final full-budget responses to wage shocks?
graph.answer: No. The actual wage shock also changes full income and the chosen leisure expenditure.

increase.title: Increase the current relative wage
increase.why: Current leisure costs more relative to future leisure.

increase.title: Separate compensation from the slice
increase.why: For the specified log preferences, the compensated response shifts leisure away from the current period and toward the future period. This compensated quantity response is derived separately while preserving utility. The displayed fixed-expenditure lines show only the relative-price change; they are not utility-compensated budgets and their intercepts do not show the compensated quantities.

increase.title: Translate leisure into work
increase.why: The compensated channel favors current work relative to future work.
increase.question: Is this alone enough to determine each actual labor-supply change?
increase.answer: No. The wage change also creates wealth effects and changes consumption choices.

decrease.title: Reduce the current relative wage by raising w₂
decrease.why: Future leisure becomes relatively more costly.

decrease.title: Separate compensation from the slice
decrease.why: For the specified log preferences, the compensated response shifts leisure toward the current period and work toward the future period. This compensated quantity response is derived separately while preserving utility. The displayed fixed-expenditure lines show only the relative-price change; they are not utility-compensated budgets and their intercepts do not show the compensated quantities.

decrease.title: Restore the income channel
decrease.why: Higher future potential earnings also raise wealth and can increase both leisure demands.
decrease.question: Which component is identified by the ratio Rw₁/w₂ alone?
decrease.answer: The relative substitution incentive, not the complete uncompensated response.

edge.title: Bind current leisure at ten
edge.why: Further substitution toward current leisure may be infeasible.

edge.title: Replace the equality with the time constraint
edge.why: A marginal trade requiring l₁ > h is not available.

edge.title: Re-solve remaining choices
edge.why: The relative-price formula remains a price but no longer guarantees an interior leisure-ratio equality.
edge.question: Should every wage change still move both leisure quantities smoothly?
edge.answer: No. At a boundary one quantity can stay fixed while the remaining choices adjust.

cw-current-wage.goal: Trace a current wage change through present income, relative leisure prices and both labor choices.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Start from the joint log solution
derive.why: This uses the full budget and three interior optimality conditions.

derive.title: Recover current leisure
derive.why: The current wage appears in the relative future-income term.

derive.title: Differentiate current work
derive.why: This example's substitution effect dominates the income effect.

derive.title: Recover future leisure
derive.why: A higher current wage raises future leisure in this interior log example.
derive.question: Is the positive current-work response universal?
derive.answer: No. It follows from this utility specification; the general wage effect remains a balance of substitution and income effects.

graph.title: Draw current work against the current wage
graph.why: The baseline curve holds future wage at four.

graph.title: Mark the initial choice
graph.why: The horizontal coordinate is work, not leisure.

graph.title: Move along the unchanged schedule
graph.why: A current-wage change moves along this supply relationship.
graph.question: What would shift this curve instead?
graph.answer: A change in future wage, preferences, resources or another held-fixed determinant.

increase.title: Raise w₁ from two to four
increase.why: Potential current earnings and current leisure's price rise.

increase.title: Solve current choices
increase.why: The household works more now despite being wealthier.

increase.title: Solve future choices
increase.why: Higher lifetime resources allow more future leisure.
increase.question: Why can current work rise while future work falls?
increase.answer: The current relative wage favors working now, while the wealth gain supports leisure later.

decrease.title: Lower w₁ from two to 1.5
decrease.why: The household is poorer, but current leisure also becomes cheaper.

decrease.title: Solve the current response
decrease.why: Current work falls in the specified log case.

decrease.title: Solve the future response
decrease.why: Future work rises as future leisure falls.
decrease.question: Why does a lower current wage not force more current work here?
decrease.answer: The cheaper current leisure's substitution effect outweighs the opposing income effect in this example.

edge.title: Find the no-work threshold
edge.why: Below this wage, the unrestricted formula asks for too much leisure.

edge.title: Apply the time ceiling
edge.why: Do not extend labor supply into negative hours.

edge.title: Resolve the reduced problem
edge.why: With no current work, a small wage change within this corner earns no extra current income.
edge.question: Does the derivative from the interior formula remain valid below the threshold?
edge.answer: No. Current work stays zero locally.

cw-future-wage.goal: Explain how an anticipated wage change shifts current labor supply through lifetime resources and timing.

symbols.meaning: one-period utility from consumption and leisure
partial marginal utility of consumption and leisure
endogenous labor incomes w₁n₁ and w₂n₂
assets entering period 1 before its return, used only when that extension is stated
within-period marginal rates of substitution u_l/u_c
end-of-period-1 assets; equal to current saving when initial assets are zero

assumptions: Two-period consumer-worker with no initial assets, nonlabor income, taxes or terminal assets; same borrowing/lending return.
Illustration U = ln(c₁)+ln(l₁)+0.8[ln(c₂)+ln(l₂)], h = 10, R = 1.25, w₁ = 2 and w₂ = 4. Each interior formula requires 0 < l₁,l₂ < h and positive consumption.

derive.title: Start from current leisure
derive.why: Future earnings potential enters the current choice.

derive.title: Differentiate current work
derive.why: A higher future wage reduces current work in this interior example.

derive.title: Recover future leisure
derive.why: The future wage also changes the price of future leisure.

derive.title: Differentiate future work
derive.why: The example reallocates work toward the better-paid future date.
derive.question: Why does the future-wage change count as a current labor-supply shift?
derive.answer: At the same current wage, desired current work changes.

graph.title: Draw supply holding w₂ = 4
graph.why: This is the baseline current work–wage relationship.

graph.title: Add a higher future wage
graph.why: At each current wage, the model generally supplies less current labor, subject to the corner.

graph.title: Compare at w₁ = 2
graph.why: The same vertical wage coordinate identifies the shift.
graph.question: Why is this not movement along the baseline curve?
graph.answer: The held-fixed future wage changed from four to six.

increase.title: Raise future wage from four to six
increase.why: Anticipated future earning opportunities improve today.

increase.title: Solve current choices
increase.why: Current consumption rises while current work falls.

increase.title: Solve future choices
increase.why: Future work rises despite greater lifetime wealth.
increase.question: What enables higher current consumption before the wage gain arrives?
increase.answer: Borrowing against future income is allowed in this model.

decrease.title: Reduce future wage from four to two
decrease.why: The anticipated lifetime resource pool contracts.

decrease.title: Recompute current behavior
decrease.why: The household works more today and consumes less.

decrease.title: Recompute future behavior
decrease.why: Future leisure becomes cheaper, and the specified example reduces future work.
decrease.question: Must falling future earnings potential reduce current labor supply?
decrease.answer: No. Here the lower wealth raises current work.

edge.title: Raise future wage enough to exhaust current time adjustment
edge.why: The interior formula would set current leisure above ten. The added curve uses w₂ = 8 to illustrate the resulting corner at current wage two.

edge.title: Bind current leisure
edge.why: Current work cannot fall below zero.

edge.title: Re-solve at the corner
edge.why: Further future-wage gains raise consumption while current work remains zero.
edge.question: Does the interior negative derivative of current work apply beyond this threshold?
edge.answer: No. The constrained current-work response is zero while the same corner remains binding.

fiscal-budget.goal: Derive both-date financing and read deficits and surpluses.

symbols.meaning: Real government purchases now and later
Real lump-sum tax totals now and later
Current government borrowing; negative means saving
Real interest rate and gross return R=1+r

derive.title: Finance today

derive.title: Repay tomorrow

derive.title: Eliminate borrowing

derive.title: Discount both sides

graph.title: Plot the feasible tax paths
graph.why: Each point finances G₁=100, G₂=50 at r=.10. The slope −1.1 prices tax timing.

graph.title: Hold current taxes fixed
graph.why: The vertical reference selects T₁=80; it is a condition, not another behavioral curve.

graph.title: Read the intersection
graph.why: Borrowing 20 requires repayment 22 in addition to future purchases 50.

increase.title: Increase current purchases
increase.why: Hold T₁=80, G₂=50, r=.10 fixed.
increase.question: Which dated tax must cover the extra financing?

increase.title: Recompute debt

decrease.title: Recompute financing

decrease.title: Read the lower line

edge.title: Cross into surplus

Earnings-tax rate, real wage and work hours in the explicitly changed-tax edge case
Illustrative utility from consumption at both dates
Consumption in the separate consumption–leisure edge illustration

derive.title: Carry saving forward
derive.why: Saving earns R; borrowing would require repayment at R.

derive.title: Substitute and collect

graph.title: Locate an optimum

graph.title: Add the taxed budget
graph.why: The intercept falls while both lines retain slope −1.1.

increase.title: Raise a current head tax
increase.why: No future offset is supplied.
increase.question: What is the PV wealth loss?

increase.title: Move the intercept
increase.why: An unchanged slope identifies a wealth effect rather than a direct substitution effect.

increase.title: Solve consumption
increase.why: Both dates fall because log consumption is normal.

decrease.title: Cut a current head tax
decrease.why: There is no later compensating increase.

decrease.title: Expand feasible purchases

decrease.title: Allocate the gain
decrease.why: Equal PV spending shares put 10 extra goods into current consumption and 11 later.

edge.title: Change the tax base

edge.title: Redo the relevant price

fiscal-wealth.goal: Separate current-only, future-only and persistent government purchases.

symbols.meaning: Real government purchases now and later
Real lump-sum tax totals now and later
Current government borrowing; negative means saving
Real interest rate and gross return R=1+r
Income before tax now and later
Current consumption response per unit of PV wealth
Illustrative log utility U=ln(c₁)+ln(c₂), which gives m=1/2

assumptions: Fixed Y₁, Y₂, r; G has no direct utility or production benefit.
Representative household internalizes financing taxes and can borrow/save.
Illustration uses log utility, hence m=1/2.

derive.title: Finance the purchase path
derive.why: PV taxes must match the added real purchases.

derive.title: Translate to private resources
derive.why: The household bears the financing burden under the stated representative setup.

derive.title: Smooth the wealth change
derive.why: Only part of the lifetime loss is allocated to current consumption.
derive.question: Does future G enter current saving directly?
derive.answer: No. Current saving subtracts G₁ only.

derive.title: Keep dates separate
derive.why: Substitute consumption into the current resource identity.

graph.title: Start with lifetime resources
graph.why: This budget displays the consumption effect, not national saving itself.

graph.title: Add a purchase burden
graph.why: A current G increase of 20 or future-only increase of 22 both cost PV 20.
graph.question: Will the consumption reduction alone reveal the saving effect?
graph.answer: No. We must also identify whether G₁ changed.

graph.title: Read equal consumption effects
graph.why: Both paths move the log optimum to (90, 99); only the current-G path directly uses current output.

increase.title: Raise current G only
increase.why: Future purchases stay fixed.
increase.question: Can consumption fall by less than the purchase increase?

increase.title: Find the private response
increase.why: Half the PV loss is borne today.

increase.title: Subtract current purchases
increase.why: Released consumption resources cover only half the added G.

decrease.title: Cut current G only
decrease.why: Future purchases and output remain unchanged.
decrease.question: Do all released resources become saving?

decrease.title: Spend part of the gain
decrease.why: Wealth rises 20, so current consumption rises 10.

decrease.title: Save the remainder
decrease.why: The public resource release exceeds the extra private spending.

edge.title: Move the shock into the future
edge.why: Now ΔG₁=0 and ΔG₂=22; the current-only assumption fails.
edge.question: Does current national saving still fall?
edge.answer: No. Consumption falls while current G stays fixed.

edge.title: Redo the identity
edge.why: The same wealth loss reduces C₁ by 10, which is entirely additional current saving.

edge.title: Cut future purchases instead
edge.why: With current G unchanged, a future cut of 22 raises lifetime wealth by 20 and current consumption by 10. Current national saving falls by 10 because no current public resources were released.

edge.title: Check a persistent path
edge.why: At r=0 and m=.5, equal purchase rises of 20 on both dates reduce C₁ by 20 and leave S₁ unchanged.

fiscal-ricardian.goal: Derive tax-timing neutrality without confusing it with spending neutrality.

symbols.meaning: Real government purchases now and later
Real lump-sum tax totals now and later
Current government borrowing; negative means saving
Real interest rate and gross return R=1+r
Income before tax now and later

assumptions: G₁, G₂ fixed; same family internalizes future taxes.
Lump-sum taxes, common borrowing/lending rate, no binding limit.
Preferences and pretax income unchanged.

derive.title: Hold purchases fixed
derive.why: Only the dates of collection change, not the real public resource claim.

derive.title: Recover the future offset
derive.why: A current cut requires a future rise including interest.
derive.question: At R=1.1, what offsets a current cut of 20?
derive.answer: A future increase of 22.

derive.title: Apply the household constraint
derive.why: The same PV tax burden leaves household wealth unchanged.

derive.title: Keep the optimum
derive.why: The feasible set and preferences are the same, so both consumption choices remain the same.

graph.title: Draw the unchanged budget
graph.why: The experiment moves disposable income between dates, not the budget frontier.

graph.title: Move the endowment
graph.why: A current cut 20 and future tax rise 22 move income from (80,132) to (100,110).
graph.question: Is there a new outer budget line?
graph.answer: No. Both endowments have W=200.

graph.title: Retain consumption
graph.why: The optimum remains (100,110); saving/borrowing adjusts to the income timing.

increase.title: Increase current taxes
increase.why: Finance an equal-PV future tax cut.
increase.question: Does lifetime wealth fall?
increase.answer: No. The future relief has PV 20.

increase.title: Move income earlier to later
increase.why: The endowment becomes (60,154), still on the same budget.

increase.title: Use financial adjustment
increase.why: To preserve c₁=100, saving falls by 20; this requires borrowing to remain feasible.

decrease.title: Reduce current taxes
decrease.why: The later liability rises by principal plus interest.
decrease.question: How much extra private saving offsets the relief?
decrease.answer: 20, with consumption unchanged.

decrease.title: Move the endowment
decrease.why: Current income rises to 100 and future disposable income falls to 110.

decrease.title: Offset public dissaving
decrease.why: The current tax cut reduces public saving 20 while private saving rises 20.

edge.title: Impose a borrowing ban
edge.why: In a separate constrained illustration, set r=0 and total disposable resources to 240. The household wants c₁=120 but has current resources 80.
edge.question: Is the unrestricted budget set still available?
edge.answer: No. Only the truncated segment is feasible.

edge.title: Apply current relief
edge.why: A cut raises the ceiling to 100 even though total resources remain 240.

edge.title: Identify the failed premise
edge.why: Consumption rises 20 because the feasible set expands. Government accounting still holds; unconstrained timing neutrality does not.

fiscal-saving.goal: Add private and public saving before inferring the national result.

symbols.meaning: Current output, consumption, purchases and lump-sum taxes

assumptions: Closed-economy accounting; real flows for one period.
Comparisons hold Y, G fixed unless stated.

derive.title: Private resources after tax
derive.why: Consumption is subtracted from disposable income.

derive.title: Public balance
derive.why: Taxes left after purchases are government saving; deficits are negative.

derive.title: Add without double counting
derive.why: Taxes transfer resources between sectors and cancel algebraically.
derive.question: Does cancellation mean taxes cannot affect S?
derive.answer: No. They can change C.

derive.title: Evaluate an illustration
derive.why: A deficit can coexist with positive national saving.

graph.title: Build the private branch
graph.why: Follow the resources retained by the household.

graph.title: Add public saving
graph.why: Government dissaving enters with a negative sign, not as an additional positive flow.
graph.question: What joins the branches?
graph.answer: Their sum, national saving.

graph.title: Read the combined identity
graph.why: The cancellation explains why T acts through behavior rather than directly in the final expression.

increase.title: Increase current T by 20
increase.why: First hold consumption fixed to isolate the accounting transfer.
increase.question: Will the national total change?
increase.answer: No, if C and G remain fixed.

increase.title: Recompute both sectors
increase.why: Private saving falls while the public deficit shrinks.

increase.title: Add the new values
increase.why: The sectoral movements offset exactly.

decrease.title: Keep the signs
decrease.why: More disposable income increases private saving; the larger deficit reduces public saving.

decrease.title: Sum the components
decrease.why: The private gain exactly matches public dissaving.

edge.question: Can the old zero result still be used?

edge.title: Redo both definitions

edge.title: Locate the source of the fall
edge.why: The remaining 10 goes to extra consumption.

fiscal-constraints.goal: Identify when a tax-timing change relaxes a binding borrowing ceiling.

symbols.meaning: Income before tax now and later

assumptions: r=0, zero initial assets and no borrowing.
Disposable incomes initially 80 and 160.
Preferences seek equal consumption; total resources 240.

derive.title: Find the unconstrained target
derive.why: Equal consumption would spread total resources over both dates.

derive.title: Impose available financing
derive.why: Without borrowing, current consumption cannot exceed current disposable income.
derive.question: Is the preferred point feasible?
derive.answer: No. It requires borrowing 40.

derive.title: Locate the constrained optimum
derive.why: Consumption rises with available current resources until the preferred point is reached.

derive.title: Preserve lifetime accounting
derive.why: The constraint changes feasibility, not the total resource sum.

graph.title: Draw the unrestricted line
graph.why: It shows every allocation permitted by lifetime resources alone.

graph.title: Retain only the feasible segment
graph.why: The segment stops where current income is exhausted.
graph.question: Where must the constrained choice stop?
graph.answer: At c₁=80 before the desired c₁=120.

graph.title: Compare the choices
graph.why: The gap between E and the free target measures desired borrowing.

increase.title: Increase current relief by 20
increase.why: Future disposable income falls by 20, leaving wealth unchanged.
increase.question: Does this relax the binding constraint?
increase.answer: Yes. Current resources rise from 80 to 100.

increase.title: Extend the feasible segment
increase.why: The optimum can move further along the same lifetime line.

increase.title: Resolve current consumption
increase.why: The new ceiling is still below 120, so it remains binding.

decrease.title: Reduce current resources by 20
decrease.why: A current tax rise is paired with equal future relief.
decrease.question: Can the household borrow to preserve 80?
decrease.answer: No. The ceiling falls to 60.

decrease.title: Shorten the feasible segment
decrease.why: Future resources cannot be brought forward through prohibited borrowing.

decrease.title: Resolve the new boundary
decrease.why: Current consumption falls despite unchanged lifetime wealth.

edge.title: Reach the unconstrained target
edge.why: Suppose relief raises current income to 140 and future income becomes 100.
edge.question: Must current consumption rise to 140?
edge.answer: No. The desired c₁ remains 120.

edge.title: Test the constraint again
edge.why: The target is now affordable under the new c₁≤140 ceiling. The solid feasible segment includes c₁=120, and the household saves 20.

edge.title: Change the local conclusion
edge.why: Further small tax timing changes can be absorbed by saving. An existing legal ban alone does not prove non-neutrality.

fiscal-bequests.goal: Trace future tax incidence instead of assuming every PV offset belongs to the same person.

symbols.meaning: Gross real return 1.1 in the illustration
PV wealth of households A and B
Their current-consumption responses to PV wealth
Aggregate current consumption in the redistribution illustration

assumptions: Same-family neutrality requires operative transfers.
Redistribution illustration has unrelated households and no borrowing constraints.

derive.title: Identify the recipient
derive.why: A current tax cut initially gives one household more disposable resources.

derive.title: Identify the payer
derive.why: The balancing liability may fall on that household, descendants, or somebody unrelated.
derive.question: Does aggregate PV balance locate the individual tax burden?
derive.answer: No. Incidence must be specified.

derive.title: Trace an operative transfer
derive.why: A parent saves 100 and transfers the 110 future payoff to offset the child’s tax.

derive.title: Test consumption neutrality
derive.why: The family can preserve consumption only if preferences and transfer feasibility support that adjustment.

graph.title: Start with current relief
graph.why: The first node identifies who gains resources now.

graph.title: Add the later liability
graph.why: The future node records the person who actually loses resources.
graph.question: What connects the two generations?
graph.answer: An adjustable bequest.

graph.title: Reveal the offset
graph.why: Saving and its return create the needed transfer rather than free net wealth.

increase.title: Increase relief by 100
increase.why: Assign the required future tax to descendants who the parent fully internalizes.
increase.question: How much must the bequest rise?

increase.title: Save the current gain
increase.why: Keeping parent consumption fixed sends the full relief into saving.

increase.title: Pay the family liability
increase.why: The extra bequest covers the descendants’ future tax.

decrease.title: Reduce current family resources
decrease.why: A current tax rise of 100 is matched by a future tax cut of 110 for descendants.
decrease.question: Which transfer adjustment could preserve consumption?
decrease.answer: Reduce an existing bequest by 110.

decrease.title: Use an available transfer margin
decrease.why: If the intended bequest exceeds 110, the parent can consume more of its current resources instead of transferring them later.

decrease.title: Confirm both budgets
decrease.why: The smaller bequest is offset by descendants’ tax relief; this conclusion requires the transfer margin to be feasible.

edge.title: Hit the zero-bequest limit
edge.why: If the intended bequest was zero, the proposed reduction cannot be carried out.
edge.question: Which neutrality condition fails?
edge.answer: The feasible intergenerational transfer margin.

edge.title: Redo individual resources
edge.why: Without a compensating transfer, the parent loses resources even though descendants gain.

edge.title: Check unrelated taxpayers
edge.why: If A gains 100 and B loses PV 100 with m_A=.75, m_B=.25, aggregate current spending rises 50. Equal aggregate PV taxes do not alone ensure neutrality.

fiscal-evidence.goal: Connect a survey to a theoretical prediction without overclaiming what it measures.

symbols.meaning: Present value at a common date

assumptions: Historical survey shares are from the supplied lecture.
Respondent counts are not expenditure amounts.

derive.title: Classify the intervention
derive.why: The 1992 withholding reduction delayed payment until April 1993, rather than removing the later bill.

derive.title: State the benchmark
derive.why: Under strict Ricardian conditions, a pure timing shift does not increase consumption.
derive.question: What observation would challenge universal zero response?
derive.answer: Some households increasing consumption because of the delay.

derive.title: Read what was asked
derive.why: The survey measured intended actions: 43% said spend; 57% save, repay debt, or adjust withholding.

derive.title: Limit the inference
derive.why: Intended spending is evidence against universal planned neutrality, not proof of actual amounts or one particular mechanism.

graph.title: Reveal the policy
graph.why: Begin with the dated payment change before interpreting survey responses.

graph.title: Compare prediction and report
graph.why: The survey node describes stated plans, not a causal spending coefficient.
graph.question: Can 43% be used as an aggregate MPC?
graph.answer: No. It is a share of respondents, not the fraction of cash spent.

graph.title: Add mechanisms and limitations
graph.why: Constraints and myopia are alternatives; measured actual behavior is still needed.

increase.title: Imagine more planned spending
increase.why: In an illustrative new sample, more respondents report spending after the same timing policy.
increase.question: Does this strengthen or weaken universal neutrality?
increase.answer: It makes universal zero planned response harder to sustain.

increase.title: Keep the measurement fixed
increase.why: The comparison remains about reported intentions, not realized expenditure.

increase.title: Do not select a cause
increase.why: Greater reported response still fits more than one mechanism.

decrease.title: Imagine less planned spending

decrease.title: Interpret debt repayment

decrease.title: Preserve uncertainty
decrease.why: Actual expenditure and the response of the remaining households still matter.

edge.title: Change the policy definition

edge.question: What must be resolved first?
edge.answer: How the government budget is financed.

edge.title: Rebuild the comparison
edge.why: Specify spending cuts, future taxes or another financing source before applying tax-timing neutrality.

edge.title: Avoid an invalid test
edge.why: A response to changed lifetime resources does not by itself reject a theorem holding those resources fixed.

graph.title: Add inventory investment

graph.title: Sum the categories

increase.title: Increase production above sales

increase.title: Count the addition

edge.title: Separate new services

edge.title: Apply the same logic to shares

investment-pv.goal: Derive the investment condition by timing every cost and future receipt.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods

derive.why: Subtract wages and the investment payment made now.

derive.why: The firm sells remaining capital after production and depreciation.

derive.title: Isolate the product
derive.why: Multiply by R and subtract resale value.

graph.title: Draw the marginal payoff
graph.why: The illustration uses MPK=12/√K, which declines with capital.

graph.title: Add the opportunity cost
graph.why: At pₖ=10, r=.10, d=.20, cost is 3.
graph.question: Where is marginal PV profit zero?
graph.answer: At MPK=3, which occurs at K=16.

graph.title: Read the optimum
graph.why: Both sides are goods per extra capital unit; comparing total output with user cost would be invalid.

increase.title: Increase capital below the optimum
increase.why: At K=9, MPK=4 exceeds cost 3.
increase.question: Is the extra unit profitable in PV?
increase.answer: Yes. Its net future benefit exceeds the financing cost.

increase.title: Calculate the sign
increase.why: The derivative equals the marginal net surplus discounted.

increase.title: Approach the intersection
increase.why: More capital reduces MPK until the profitable margin closes.

decrease.title: Reduce capital above the optimum
decrease.why: At K=36, MPK=2 is below cost 3.
decrease.question: Can removing a unit increase profit?
decrease.answer: Yes. It avoids a cost exceeding the output benefit.

decrease.title: Calculate the saving
decrease.why: The marginal derivative is negative, so a small negative change in K raises Π.

decrease.title: Return toward the optimum
decrease.why: Removing capital raises remaining units’ MPK toward 3.

edge.title: Remove terminal resale
edge.why: The original salvage assumption fails; keep pₖ=10 and r=.10.
edge.question: What future output must cover the purchase?
edge.answer: The full gross cost 11.

edge.title: Redo the derivative
edge.why: There is no resale term to cancel principal.

edge.title: Resolve the smaller target
edge.why: With MPK=12/√K, the new target is (12/11)², about 1.1901, instead of 16.

investment-labour.goal: Differentiate the three independent choices without discounting only one side.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
A_t times the labor derivative of production
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: N₁, N₂, K₂ are independent controls after substitution.
Within-period labor plot conditions on capital and technology.

derive.title: Identify independent controls
derive.why: I₁ and K₂ are linked, so do not choose both independently.

derive.title: Differentiate current labor
derive.why: Only current production and current wage cost depend on N₁.

derive.title: Differentiate future labor
derive.why: Both future output and future wages carry 1/R.
derive.question: Does the future condition become MPN₂=Rw₂?
derive.answer: No. The common positive discount factor cancels.

derive.title: Keep capital separate
derive.why: Its condition includes current purchase and future salvage.

derive.title: Solve jointly when needed
derive.why: If capital and labor complement each other, the conditions must hold together; individual curve pictures are conditional.

graph.title: Draw labor productivity
graph.why: For output 24√N, the derivative is 12/√N.

graph.title: Add the real wage
graph.why: The competitive wage is horizontal in this conditional hiring diagram.
graph.question: What labor quantity equates both?
graph.answer: N=16 at wage 3.

graph.title: Read the solution
graph.why: Labor increases until marginal revenue in goods equals marginal wage cost.

increase.title: Raise the wage to 4
increase.why: Productivity and capital stay fixed.
increase.question: Will the old N=16 still satisfy the FOC?
increase.answer: No. Its marginal product 3 is below wage 4.

increase.title: Reduce hiring
increase.why: Fewer workers raise the marginal product of remaining labor.

increase.title: Read the higher wage line
increase.why: This changes cost, not the productivity curve.

decrease.title: Lower the wage to 2
decrease.why: The marginal product at the old employment remains 3.
decrease.question: Is another worker locally profitable?
decrease.answer: Yes. Its product exceeds the lower wage.

decrease.title: Expand hiring
decrease.why: Diminishing productivity closes the benefit-cost gap.

decrease.title: Read the lower wage line
decrease.why: The change is a movement along conditional labor demand.

edge.title: Consider a boundary solution
edge.why: To consider zero hiring, switch to a technology with finite marginal product at zero. The plotted square-root illustration instead has unbounded marginal product near zero and would not produce this corner at a finite positive wage.
edge.question: What if every feasible worker adds less than the wage?
edge.answer: The optimum can be N=0 instead.

edge.title: Use the inequality
edge.why: At the boundary, do not force an impossible positive solution.

edge.title: Keep joint curvature in view
edge.why: FOCs alone need not give a unique finite K, N pair for every production function; check concavity and feasible constraints.
