investment-usercost.goal: Derive interest plus depreciation cost from purchase and resale.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Real current purchase price and future resale price in the extension
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: Same real capital price at purchase and resale.
Plot: pₖ=10, d=.20, baseline r=.10; MPK=12/√K.

derive.title: Price today’s sacrifice
derive.why: An extra unit costs pₖ now instead of being lent at return R.

derive.title: Price surviving capital
derive.why: After use, fraction 1−d can be sold at the same price.

derive.title: Subtract the recovered principal
derive.why: Only the unrecovered opportunity cost needs production to cover it.
derive.question: Why does full pₖ not remain as the one-period cost?
derive.answer: Because undepreciated capital is resold.

derive.title: Simplify and preserve units
derive.why: Interest and physical depreciation multiply the real unit price.

graph.title: Start with MPK
graph.why: This technological schedule remains unchanged when only interest changes.

graph.title: Add baseline cost
graph.why: The horizontal line is (.10+.20)10=3.
graph.question: Why is cost horizontal against K?
graph.answer: The price-taking firm does not change r, d or pₖ by choosing K.

graph.title: Find capital demand
graph.why: Solve 12/√K=3 to obtain 16.

increase.title: Increase r to .20
increase.why: Hold d, pₖ and future technology fixed.
increase.question: Which curve changes?
increase.answer: The user-cost line rises; MPK does not shift.

increase.title: Compute the new hurdle
increase.why: The extra interest raises cost by 10(.10)=1.

increase.title: Resolve K
increase.why: The higher hurdle intersects diminishing MPK at a smaller stock.

decrease.title: Decrease r to zero
decrease.why: Depreciation remains .20.
decrease.question: Does user cost become zero?
decrease.answer: No. Physical depreciation still costs 2.

decrease.title: Compute remaining cost
decrease.why: Only the interest component disappears.

decrease.title: Resolve the larger stock
decrease.why: More units remain worthwhile at the lower hurdle.

edge.title: Allow capital gains
edge.why: Suppose future resale price q₂ differs from current q₁.
edge.question: Can (r+d)q₁ still be used unchanged?
edge.answer: No. Resale must be valued at q₂.

edge.title: Redo the subtraction
edge.why: Financing uses today’s price; survival uses tomorrow’s expected price.

edge.title: Check the boundary
edge.why: If uc≤0 and MPK remains positive for all finite K, this simple model may have no finite interior optimum; a negative K is not a solution.

investment-pricechanges.goal: Derive how an expected resale gain changes capital demand.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Current purchase and deterministic future resale prices
Tax rate on future output only
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: Explicit extension of the lecture’s common-price model.
q₁=10, r=.10, d=.20; resale is untaxed.

derive.title: Record the purchase
derive.why: The marginal current cash cost is q₁.

derive.title: Record future output and sale
derive.why: Only the surviving fraction receives the resale price.

derive.title: Discount and equate
derive.why: A zero marginal PV profit makes the unit just worthwhile.
derive.question: Which price belongs in the financing term?
derive.answer: The current purchase price q₁.

derive.title: Isolate the user cost
derive.why: An expected resale gain reduces unrecovered cost.

derive.title: Add a stated revenue tax
derive.why: Only retained output is taxed in this extension.

graph.title: Draw the unchanged return
graph.why: Future physical productivity stays 12/√K.

graph.title: Add common-price cost
graph.why: When q₂=q₁=10, the extension collapses to uc=3.
graph.question: Does a resale-price change shift physical MPK?
graph.answer: No. It changes the financial benefit of the remaining capital.

graph.title: Locate the reference
graph.why: The baseline target is 16 physical units.

increase.title: Increase expected q₂ to 12
increase.why: Purchase price and physical depreciation remain unchanged.
increase.question: Is the surviving asset now more valuable?
increase.answer: Yes. It resells for .8×12=9.6 per original unit.

increase.title: Recompute cost
increase.why: Subtract 9.6 from the gross purchase opportunity cost 11.

increase.title: Solve the higher target
increase.why: The lower hurdle permits more capital.

decrease.title: Decrease expected q₂ to 8
decrease.why: The unit’s physical survival is still .8.
decrease.question: Does expected capital loss raise or lower user cost?
decrease.answer: It raises user cost.

decrease.title: Recompute cost
decrease.why: Only 6.4 goods are recovered from resale.

decrease.title: Solve the lower target
decrease.why: A larger required marginal product selects fewer units.

edge.title: Set full depreciation
edge.why: Change d to 1; no unit survives for sale.
edge.question: Can any q₂ change still matter?
edge.answer: No. Its coefficient 1−d is zero.

edge.title: Rebuild the cost
edge.why: The whole gross financing cost must be covered by output.

edge.title: Resolve without a resale channel
edge.why: All q₂ values lead to the same K*=(12/11)² in this changed-d case.

investment-optimum.goal: Read an intersection as a marginal-profit test, not a memorized diagram.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: Diminishing conditional MPK=12/√K; fixed uc=3.
Positive interior K and suitable concavity.

derive.title: Compare like quantities
derive.why: Both marginal output and cost are goods per extra capital unit.

derive.title: Test an additional unit
derive.why: Net future surplus determines whether an increment helps.
derive.question: What sign encourages expansion?
derive.answer: A positive sign.

derive.title: Use diminishing returns
derive.why: Adding capital lowers its marginal product; removing capital raises it.

derive.title: Solve the zero surplus
derive.why: The interior maximum closes the gap.

graph.title: Draw marginal benefit
graph.why: MPK falls because each additional unit adds less output.

graph.title: Add constant marginal cost
graph.why: User cost is fixed with respect to the firm’s K.
graph.question: Is any positive MPK sufficient to justify investment?
graph.answer: No. It must cover cost.

graph.title: Read the intersection
graph.why: The optimum equates benefit and cost, not capital and cost.

increase.title: Start with too little K
increase.why: At K=9, MPK=4.
increase.question: Would increasing K improve profit?
increase.answer: Yes. The marginal return exceeds cost 3.

increase.title: Add profitable units
increase.why: The return gradually falls as capital increases.

increase.title: Stop at equality
increase.why: Continuing beyond 16 would admit units whose cost exceeds their product.

decrease.title: Start with excess K
decrease.why: At K=36, MPK=2.
decrease.question: Would reducing K improve profit?
decrease.answer: Yes. Avoiding cost 3 sacrifices product 2.

decrease.title: Remove loss-making marginal units
decrease.why: As K falls, the remaining marginal product increases.

decrease.title: Stop at the same target
decrease.why: The optimal stock does not depend on the direction of approach in this frictionless illustration.

edge.title: Remove diminishing curvature
edge.why: Equality by itself is only a first-order condition.
edge.question: Could an equality be a minimum or part of a flat set?
edge.answer: Yes, without the needed curvature.

edge.title: Check second-order behavior
edge.why: For this illustration dMPK/dK=−6/K^(3/2)<0, so surplus crosses downward.

edge.title: Check a physical bound
edge.why: If feasible K is capped below 16, the optimum can be at that cap with MPK>uc; equality is not required at the boundary.

investment-shifts.goal: Distinguish changed technology from movement along an investment schedule.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Desired saving and investment in the explicitly separate goods-market illustration
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: Inherited K, d and cost fixed for productivity comparisons.
All shocks concern future production unless explicitly stated.

derive.title: Write the target condition
derive.why: The firm compares future marginal productivity with cost.

derive.title: Solve for capital
derive.why: Square only after isolating the positive square root.

derive.title: Translate into additions
derive.why: At fixed inherited K and d, a larger target requires larger current investment.
derive.question: Does changing r shift technological MPK?
derive.answer: No. It changes user cost.

derive.title: Name the diagram correctly
derive.why: A future-A change shifts MPK against K and investment against r; changing the plotted r moves along investment demand.

graph.title: Draw baseline productivity
graph.why: Use A=12 and the same cost normalization as the earlier capital picture.

graph.title: Add the unchanged cost line
graph.why: It holds at 3 for all productivity cases.
graph.question: Which schedule must move if A rises?
graph.answer: The entire MPK schedule.

graph.title: Read the original target
graph.why: The baseline isK*=16.

increase.title: Increase future A to 15
increase.why: Every given K becomes more productive.
increase.question: At K=16, is marginal benefit now above cost?

increase.title: Shift marginal benefit up
increase.why: The cost line remains the reference.

increase.title: Resolve investment needs
increase.why: The target rises to 25, requiring 9 more additions with inherited capital fixed.

increase.title: Carry the shift into goods equilibrium
increase.why: In a separate illustrative market, hold S=80+200r fixed and raise the investment intercept from 140 to 160. This +20 shift illustrates stronger investment demand; it is not numerically derived from the earlier A change.

increase.title: Resolve the higher market rate
increase.why: At the old rate investment exceeds saving. The higher equilibrium rate encourages saving and partly restrains the new investment demand.

decrease.title: Decrease future A to 9
decrease.why: Marginal productivity falls at each K.
decrease.question: Is K=16 still worthwhile at the margin?

decrease.title: Shift marginal benefit down
decrease.why: There is no financing-cost change.

decrease.title: Reduce the target
decrease.why: K* becomes 9, so required additions fall 7.

decrease.title: Carry the weaker demand into equilibrium
decrease.why: In the separate market illustration, hold S=80+200r fixed and lower the investment intercept from 140 to 120. The assumed −20 shift is separate from the numerical capital calculation above.

decrease.title: Resolve the lower market rate
decrease.why: At the old rate saving exceeds desired investment. The lower equilibrium rate reduces saving and partly restores investment along the new schedule.

edge.title: Make productivity temporary today
edge.why: Future technology, wages, costs and inherited K are explicitly unchanged.
edge.question: Does today’s productivity alone move future MPK?
edge.answer: No. Persistence must be specified.

edge.title: Redo the correct date
edge.why: The investment payoff still uses the old future schedule.

edge.title: Separate another channel
edge.why: If future wages or output also change in equilibrium, analyze those changes explicitly rather than silently relabel a current shock as permanent.

investment-tax.goal: Derive the tax-adjusted return without taxing the wrong cash flows.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: Revenue tax only; investment costs and resale untaxed in this example.
uc=3, MPK=12/√K; baseline τ=.25.

derive.title: Keep only after-tax output
derive.why: The firm retains fraction 1−τ of the extra product.

derive.title: Keep the cost rule explicit
derive.why: The tax does not automatically apply to salvage or purchase costs.

derive.title: Equate net benefit and cost
derive.why: An interior unit must cover its full user cost after tax.
derive.question: Do we multiply or divide uc to obtain pre-tax MPK?
derive.answer: Divide by 1−τ.

derive.title: Solve the hurdle
derive.why: A smaller retained fraction demands a higher gross product.

derive.title: Recover desired capital
derive.why: For the illustration, capital responds nonlinearly.

graph.title: Draw pre-tax productivity
graph.why: Keep MPK on the vertical axis, so the tax appears in the hurdle.

graph.title: Add the baseline taxed hurdle
graph.why: τ=.25 raises required pre-tax MPK from 3 to 4.
graph.question: Where is the taxed target?
graph.answer: At K=9.

graph.title: Locate the tax wedge
graph.why: The untaxed cost 3 remains a reference; pre-tax output 4 leaves 3 after tax.

increase.title: Increase τ to .50
increase.why: The retained share falls from .75 to .50.
increase.question: Does required pre-tax MPK rise by only .25?
increase.answer: No. The denominator changes nonlinearly.

increase.title: Recalculate the hurdle
increase.why: The firm must produce 6 to keep 3.

increase.title: Reduce the capital target
increase.why: Diminishing MPK reaches 6 at only 4 units.

decrease.title: Decrease τ to zero
decrease.why: The full marginal product can now be retained.
decrease.question: What pre-tax hurdle remains?
decrease.answer: Only the unchanged user cost 3.

decrease.title: Remove the wedge
decrease.why: Cost and pre-tax product again meet directly.

decrease.title: Expand capital
decrease.why: The target rises from 9 to 16 without a technology shift.

edge.title: Approach a confiscatory tax
edge.why: As τ approaches 1 with uc>0, the denominator approaches zero.
edge.question: Can the old finite interior solution be retained?
edge.answer: No. The required pre-tax product diverges.

edge.title: Return to the original equation
edge.why: At τ=1, retained output is zero and cannot cover a positive cost.

edge.title: Change tax structure carefully
edge.why: A tax on fully measured economic profits is not this revenue tax. Specify deductions and salvage treatment before deriving its FOCs.

investment-incentives.goal: Calculate deductions and credits before translating them into investment incentives.

symbols.meaning: Profit-tax rate for the deduction example
Number of periods until a usable tax saving
Present value of the usable tax saving

assumptions: Tax benefits are usable unless a boundary explicitly changes that assumption.
Timing illustration values tax savings in current real goods.

derive.title: Start with a deduction
derive.why: An allowance reduces taxable profit before the rate is applied.

derive.title: Contrast a credit
derive.why: A usable credit is subtracted directly from tax due.
derive.question: At τ=.25, are a deduction 100 and credit 100 equivalent?
derive.answer: No. They save 25 and 100 respectively.

derive.title: Account for timing
derive.why: Later benefits must be discounted when comparing incentive values.

derive.title: Interpret the effective wedge
derive.why: The lecture’s effective rate is a hypothetical revenue-tax rate yielding the same K*, not necessarily the statutory rate.

graph.title: Build the deduction route
graph.why: The first node is taxable profit, not tax due.

graph.title: Apply the rate
graph.why: Only this step converts a deduction into a tax saving.
graph.question: Where does a credit enter?
graph.answer: Directly at the tax-bill stage.

graph.title: Compare effective incentives
graph.why: Both provisions may reduce the investment wedge, but by different amounts.

increase.title: Increase a usable allowance
increase.why: At τ=.25, raise D from 100 to 140.
increase.question: How much additional tax saving results?

increase.title: Apply the marginal tax rate
increase.why: Only a quarter of the larger deduction becomes cash tax relief.

increase.title: Translate the incentive
increase.why: With other provisions fixed, the lower effective burden can raise desired K.

decrease.title: Reduce a usable credit
decrease.why: Cut C_tax from 100 to 60.
decrease.question: How much tax relief is lost?
decrease.answer: 40 because a credit operates directly on the bill.

decrease.title: Recalculate after-tax cost
decrease.why: The firm now finances 40 more of the eligible expenditure itself.

decrease.title: Trace capital incentives
decrease.why: A less generous credit can raise the effective wedge and reduce K*, holding other rules fixed.

edge.title: Make the benefit unusable now
edge.why: Suppose no current tax is due and no refund or carryforward is available.
edge.question: Is the quoted deduction still an immediate cash saving?
edge.answer: No. The usability assumption fails.

edge.title: Redo the timing
edge.why: If a later carryforward instead exists, value its actual future tax saving at that date.

edge.title: Avoid a statutory shortcut
edge.why: Equal nominal allowances can produce different incentives because timing, tax rates and usability differ.

investment-gross.goal: Recover gross investment from a stock target and identify replacement.

symbols.meaning: Inherited capital, next-period capital, and desired stock
Physical additions; I₁ equals J₁ when capital price is 1
Real price of one capital unit
Extra future output per unit of capital
One-period user cost in output goods
Generic capital quantity in the illustrative MPK curve; interpreted as the chosen future stock

assumptions: K₁=100, d=.10, pₖ=1 in the graph.
No adjustment cost; unrestricted resale unless changed in edge track.

derive.title: Measure the desired stock change
derive.why: Net investment is a difference between dated stocks.

derive.title: Replace what wears out
derive.why: Replacement is an amount, not merely the depreciation rate.

derive.title: Add both components
derive.why: Gross investment can be positive even when net investment is negative.
derive.question: What if K*=95?
derive.answer: Net I=−5 but gross I=5.

derive.title: Simplify survivors
derive.why: This form directly subtracts capital already available next period.

graph.title: Draw net investment
graph.why: Zero net investment occurs where the desired stock equals 100.

graph.title: Add gross investment
graph.why: Replacement shifts the line upward by 10.
graph.question: Must positive gross I imply stock expansion?
graph.answer: No. The interval 90<K*<100 has positive gross I but negative net I.

graph.title: Read maintenance
graph.why: At K*=100, gross I is 10 and net I is 0.

increase.title: Raise the target to 110
increase.why: Inherited capital and depreciation do not change.
increase.question: How much additional gross investment is needed?
increase.answer: 10 more units.

increase.title: Calculate expansion plus replacement
increase.why: Net accumulation 10 plus replacement 10 gives 20.

increase.title: Move along the gross line
increase.why: The slope is 1 at fixed inherited capital and d.

decrease.title: Lower the target to 95
decrease.why: The firm wants a smaller stock than it inherited.
decrease.question: Does it need zero gross investment?
decrease.answer: No. Depreciation would otherwise shrink the stock to 90.

decrease.title: Offset part of depreciation
decrease.why: Five new units limit the stock decline to 5.

decrease.title: Separate signs
decrease.why: Gross I is positive while net I is −5.

edge.title: Prohibit disinvestment
edge.why: Suppose desired K*=80 but impose I≥0.
edge.question: Can the firm reach 80 next period?
edge.answer: No .90 inherited units survive and cannot be sold under this constraint.

edge.title: Apply the lower bound
edge.why: Unrestricted I would be −10; constrained I becomes 0.

edge.title: State the actual stock
edge.why: The feasible K₂ is 90, not the unconstrained target 80.

investment-equilibrium.goal: Derive saving–investment clearing and the rate adjustment on each side.

symbols.meaning: Fixed output, desired consumption and government purchases
Real rate expressed as a decimal
Short labels for desired saving and investment in the numerical schedules

assumptions: Closed economy, fixed Y.
Illustrative S=80+200r, I=140−400r.
Saving slopes upward as the maintained aggregate case.

derive.title: Start with desired goods demand
derive.why: Equilibrium requires planned private and public absorption to match output.

derive.title: Move consumption and G left
derive.why: The residual output is desired national saving.

derive.title: Identify loanable funds
derive.why: Saving supplies finance while investment demands it.
derive.question: Does actual accounting S=I prove desired plans match?
derive.answer: No. Actual investment can contain unintended inventories.

derive.title: Solve the illustrative rate
derive.why: Gather both rate terms before dividing.

derive.title: Recover the quantity
derive.why: Both functions must give the same equilibrium amount.

graph.title: Plot the saving supply
graph.why: Higher r raises desired saving in this maintained aggregate comparison.

graph.title: Add investment demand
graph.why: Higher r raises user cost and reduces desired investment.
graph.question: What is the common rate at their crossing?

graph.title: Mark both markets’ balance
graph.why: The intersection quantity is 100 real goods.

increase.title: Increase saving at every r
increase.why: Let the intercept rise from 80 to 100, for example after lower expected future income.
increase.question: At the old r, is saving now above investment?
increase.answer: Yes: 120 versus 100.

increase.title: Let the rate fall
increase.why: Lower r reduces desired saving along its new curve and encourages investment.

decrease.title: Decrease saving at every r
decrease.why: Let the intercept fall from 80 to 60, for example after greater expected future income.
decrease.question: At the old r, is investment now above saving?
decrease.answer: Yes: 100 versus 80.

decrease.title: Let the rate rise
decrease.why: Higher r restrains C and I while increasing S along the new schedule.

edge.title: Allow unintended inventories
edge.why: Suppose output is 1000 but desired absorption is 970.
edge.question: Can the accounting identity still hold?
edge.answer: Yes. Unsold 30 counts as unintended inventory investment.

edge.title: Distinguish desired from actual
edge.why: Actual I equals desired I plus 30; this does not establish intended goods clearing.

edge.title: Check the adjustment assumption
edge.why: This walk adjusts r at fixed Y. A model with fixed r and output responding to inventories is a different closure, not the same diagram.

investment-crowding.goal: Track a saving shift through the rate to equilibrium investment.
assumptions: Fixed Y; the illustrated G change reduces desired saving 20 at each r.
Baseline S=80+200r, I=140−400r; C response is embedded in the saving shift.

derive.title: Begin with the resource claim
derive.why: A temporary current G increase can absorb more than the reduction in C releases.

derive.title: Shift saving at each rate
derive.why: This is a left shift before the market rate adjusts.
derive.question: Does the investment schedule itself move?
derive.answer: No. The fiscal example moves along unchanged investment demand.

derive.title: Use the excess demand for funds
derive.why: At r=.10, saving 80 falls short of investment 100, putting upward pressure on r.

derive.title: Solve the new composition
derive.why: The higher rate lowers investment; equilibrium saving equals that lower I.

graph.title: Build the old equilibrium
graph.why: Draw saving and unchanged investment first.

graph.title: Add the shifted saving line
graph.why: Its intercept is lower at every rate.
graph.question: Will equilibrium saving be higher just because r rises?
graph.answer: No. The left shift dominates; new S must equal lower I.

graph.title: Mark crowding out
graph.why: The investment reduction is a movement along I, not an I shift.

increase.title: Increase the fiscal resource claim
increase.why: Use the stated saving reduction 20 at every r.
increase.question: Which adjustment closes the funds shortage?
increase.answer: A higher real rate.

increase.title: Raise the cost of investment
increase.why: The new r=2/15 is above .10; capital demand and investment decline.

increase.title: Measure displacement
increase.why: I falls from 100 to 86.6667 while S falls to the same amount.

decrease.title: Reduce the fiscal resource claim
decrease.why: A saving increase 20 at each r creates excess funds at the old rate.
decrease.question: Which direction does r move?
decrease.answer: Down.

decrease.title: Encourage private investment
decrease.why: Lower cost raises desired I along its unchanged curve.

decrease.title: Measure the gain
decrease.why: Investment and equilibrium national saving rise to 113.3333.

edge.title: Remove all C response
edge.why: In a separate edge model, Y and C stay fixed even after G changes.
edge.question: How much private I can a G rise 20 displace?
edge.answer: Exactly 20 in goods equilibrium.

edge.title: Use vertical saving
edge.why: S=Y−C−G does not respond to r; it shifts 100→80.

edge.title: Read complete displacement
edge.why: The new rate is .15 and I=80. This magnitude depends on the changed fixed-C assumption.

assets-functions.goal: Identify the economic task money performs in each situation.

symbols.meaning: Real purchasing power of that balance

assumptions: Money is widely accepted in payment.
A function need not perform perfectly to be useful.

derive.title: Start with barter
derive.why: Without money, each trader must want the other’s offered good.

derive.title: Introduce accepted payment
derive.why: The seller can accept money and spend it elsewhere, lowering exchange/search costs.
derive.question: Which function removes double coincidence?
derive.answer: The medium-of-exchange function.

derive.title: Separate denomination
derive.why: A contract quoted in dollars uses the unit of account even before payment occurs.

derive.title: Carry purchasing power
derive.why: Holding money for later purchases uses the store-of-value function.

graph.title: Reveal exchange
graph.why: This branch explains why specialization becomes easier.

graph.title: Add valuation and time
graph.why: Price quotation and transferring purchasing power are different jobs.
graph.question: Does a valuable asset automatically do all three?
graph.answer: No. It may store value without being widely accepted in payment.

graph.title: Add the inflation channel
graph.why: A fixed monetary amount can lose real value while still being used for transactions.

increase.title: Increase the price level
increase.why: Hold M=100 and raise P from 2 to 2.5.
increase.question: Does the balance buy more or fewer goods?
increase.answer: Fewer.

increase.title: Divide by the new price
increase.why: Nominal wealth in currency is unchanged, but real purchasing power falls.

increase.title: Identify the affected function
increase.why: This directly worsens store-of-value performance; it need not immediately end exchange use.

decrease.title: Decrease the price level
decrease.why: Hold M=100 and reduce P from 2 to 1.6.
decrease.question: Can zero-interest currency gain purchasing power?
decrease.answer: Yes, through falling prices.

decrease.title: Recalculate goods purchasable
decrease.why: The same 100 buys 62.5 rather than 50.

decrease.title: Separate yield from function
decrease.why: A positive real gain does not turn currency into productive capital; it still transfers purchasing power.

edge.title: Consider severe instability
edge.why: Prices change so fast that quotations and payment acceptance become unreliable.
edge.question: Is the damage limited to saving?
edge.answer: No. Unit-of-account and exchange functions can also deteriorate.

edge.title: Rebuild exchange arrangements
edge.why: People may use a more stable currency or costly barter.

edge.title: Keep classification conditional
edge.why: Money’s usefulness rests partly on expected acceptance, not intrinsic material value.

assets-liquidity.goal: Separate ease of payment from return, risk and intrinsic value.

symbols.meaning: Expected nominal return when comparing assets

assumptions: Comparisons hold other characteristics fixed unless stated.
Risk comparisons assume a risk-averse holder.

derive.title: Ask about transaction conversion
derive.why: Liquidity concerns speed and ease of turning an asset into a means of payment.

derive.title: Ask about expected payoff
derive.why: Expected return concerns payouts and price changes, not payment convenience.

derive.title: Ask about uncertainty
derive.why: Risk concerns uncertainty of realized value.
derive.question: Can an asset be liquid and risky?
derive.answer: Yes. These are separate attributes.

derive.title: Classify monetary substance
derive.why: Fiat money lacks commodity value; commodity money also has a nonmonetary use.

graph.title: Reveal the liquidity test
graph.why: An asset already usable for payment avoids conversion delays.

graph.title: Separate the other axes of choice
graph.why: The flow deliberately avoids a fake single-dimensional ranking.
graph.question: Does higher return imply higher liquidity?
graph.answer: No. Neither definition implies the other.

graph.title: Add fiat and commodity cases
graph.why: Both can provide liquidity despite different intrinsic-value properties.

increase.title: Increase an asset’s liquidity
increase.why: Make it easier to sell or transfer without changing expected return or risk.
increase.question: Why might demand rise?
increase.answer: It now provides payment flexibility at the same other attributes.

increase.title: Trace the saved friction
increase.why: The holder needs less time or fewer costly conversions to finance purchases.

increase.title: Compare at fixed wealth
increase.why: Its portfolio share may rise; total wealth does not have to rise.

decrease.title: Decrease payment convenience
decrease.why: Introduce an early withdrawal penalty or a transfer limit.
decrease.question: Can equal interest rates make this change irrelevant?
decrease.answer: No. Liquidity services changed even if return did not.

decrease.title: Trace the added friction
decrease.why: Emergency transactions now require waiting or paying a penalty.

decrease.title: Compare substitutes
decrease.why: At fixed return and risk, the asset becomes less attractive than a more liquid alternative.

edge.title: Change multiple attributes
edge.why: Suppose liquidity falls but expected return rises.
edge.question: Is the net demand change signed?
edge.answer: Not without preferences and the magnitudes of both changes.

edge.title: Redo the tradeoff
edge.why: The higher payoff compensates partly or fully for reduced convenience for some holders.

edge.title: Reject intrinsic-value shortcuts
edge.why: Gold can be commodity money without being more liquid than every fiat payment method.

assets-aggregates.goal: Build M1/M2 without mistaking classification changes for new money.

symbols.meaning: Narrow and broader aggregates using the lecture table

assumptions: Use the lecture’s December 2021 US table definitions.
Quantities in examples are hypothetical balances.

derive.title: Build M1
derive.why: Add currency and liquid deposits; the revised table includes checking and savings.

derive.title: Build M2
derive.why: Add qualifying small time deposits and retail noninstitutional MMMFs to M1.

derive.title: Avoid duplicate inclusion
derive.why: M2 already contains every M1 balance.
derive.question: If savings enters M1 after already being in M2, must M2 rise?
derive.answer: No. Its broad coverage can remain unchanged.

derive.title: Check component liquidity
derive.why: Fixed-term penalties and limited transaction services explain why broader components are less convenient.

graph.title: Add narrow components
graph.why: Both inputs feed M1 rather than separate M1 totals.

graph.title: Add broad-only balances
graph.why: Do not add the currency/deposit components again.
graph.question: For M1=200 and broad-only 40, what is M2?

graph.title: Read the containing total
graph.why: M2 is the inclusive total, not an alternative disjoint pile.

increase.title: Expand the narrow definition
increase.why: Move existing savings 40 from broad-only classification into M1.
increase.question: How much newly created purchasing power follows mechanically?
increase.answer: None from classification alone.

increase.title: Recompute both totals
increase.why: If old M1=160 and broad-only 80, new M1=200 and broad-only 40.

increase.title: Interpret the apparent jump
increase.why: A larger measured M1 need not represent an open-market purchase.

decrease.title: Move liquid funds into a time deposit
decrease.why: Transfer 20 from an M1 deposit to an included M2-only deposit.
decrease.question: Must broad money shrink?
decrease.answer: No. Both old and new balances are within M2.

decrease.title: Track the components
decrease.why: M1 falls 20 and broad-only holdings rise 20.

decrease.title: Preserve the broad total
decrease.why: This changes liquidity composition without reducing the aggregate M2.

edge.title: Read an older definition
edge.why: An older source may exclude savings from M1.
edge.question: Should differently defined M1 series be compared without adjustment?
edge.answer: No. Definitions and dates differ.

edge.title: Align measurement first
edge.why: Reclassify balances consistently before interpreting money growth.

edge.title: Keep the lecture table authoritative here
edge.why: The older final-page reading teaches stock/flow distinctions; it does not override the revised membership table.

assets-supply.goal: Trace a central-bank operation into nominal and real money supply.

symbols.meaning: Nominal money stock and price level
Nominal alternative-asset yield and real rate

assumptions: Exogenous M in the course model.
Money-graph comparison fixes P, Y and πᵉ.
Baseline real supply 100 and L=180−1000r.

derive.title: Identify the transaction partner
derive.why: An open-market purchase buys existing financial assets from the public.

derive.title: Track the payment
derive.why: New money paid out increases the public’s nominal monetary stock.

derive.title: Convert nominal to real
derive.why: The price level determines how much purchasing power the stock provides.
derive.question: If both M and P rise 10%, do real balances rise?
derive.answer: No. The ratio is unchanged.

derive.title: Read the supply graph
derive.why: At fixed M and P, the quantity supplied does not depend on r.

graph.title: Draw fixed real supply
graph.why: A vertical line records 100 regardless of the interest rate.

graph.title: Add desired holdings
graph.why: Downward demand lets the rate reconcile portfolios with supply.
graph.question: What is the baseline clearing r?

graph.title: Locate equilibrium
graph.why: At this rate, desired and supplied real money are both 100.

increase.title: Purchase assets and add money
increase.why: At fixed P, let real supply increase 100→120.
increase.question: At the old rate, will money be in excess supply?
increase.answer: Yes. Desired balances remain 100 initially.

increase.title: Shift the vertical line
increase.why: The demand function is unchanged in this comparison.

increase.title: Find the lower clearing rate
increase.why: Lower yield encourages holding the larger monetary stock.

decrease.title: Sell assets and withdraw money
decrease.why: At fixed P, real supply falls 100→80.
decrease.question: At the old rate, is there excess demand for money?
decrease.answer: Yes. Desired balances 100 exceed supply 80.

decrease.title: Shift the supply left
decrease.why: Public asset purchases from the central bank absorb monetary balances.

decrease.title: Find the higher rate
decrease.why: The higher alternative yield reduces desired balances to 80.

edge.title: Allow prices to change too
edge.why: A nominal expansion does not by itself fix the real expansion.
edge.question: What if M and P both double?
edge.answer: Real supply stays unchanged.

edge.title: Redo the ratio
edge.why: The original vertical real-supply line is still appropriate.

edge.title: Distinguish fiscal financing
edge.why: Buying newly issued government debt directly is the lecture’s monetary-financing case, not the existing-public-assets operation.

assets-portfolio.goal: Separate wealth accounting from portfolio preferences and realized returns.

symbols.meaning: Money and net nonmonetary positions in common value units
Purchase price, resale price and payout

assumptions: Liabilities are included in net positions.
Risk examples use risk aversion.

derive.title: Calculate net resources
derive.why: Subtract liabilities from gross assets.

derive.title: Allocate the stock
derive.why: All net wealth must appear somewhere in the portfolio.
derive.question: Can high annual income be simply added to today’s wealth?
derive.answer: No. Income is a flow whose spending/saving must be traced.

derive.title: Compute total return
derive.why: Payouts and price changes both affect realized performance.

derive.title: Choose before realization
derive.why: Expected return, risk and liquidity guide demand before the realized payoff is known.

graph.title: Build the balance sheet
graph.why: Assets and liabilities determine the available net stock.

graph.title: Add preferences and attributes
graph.why: Wealth alone does not fix the money share.
graph.question: Can shares change while total W stays constant?
graph.answer: Yes. Relative attractiveness can change.

graph.title: Read desired holdings
graph.why: The final node must respect the adding-up constraint.

increase.title: Increase wealth at a fixed share
increase.why: Let W rise 1000→1200 with desired money share 20%.
increase.question: Must money holdings rise in this fixed-share example?
increase.answer: Yes, from 200 to 240.

increase.title: Allocate the additional stock
increase.why: The unchanged share makes the wealth effect transparent.

increase.title: Keep income distinct
increase.why: This is a stock comparison; a higher income flow affects wealth only through saving and valuation changes.

decrease.title: Reduce wealth at the same share
decrease.why: Let W fall 1000→800.
decrease.question: Does money have to stay at 200?
decrease.answer: No. Fixed 20% implies 160.

decrease.title: Reduce all proportionate holdings
decrease.why: The lost wealth reduces the budget available for the same portfolio mix.

decrease.title: Separate share changes
decrease.why: If liquidity needs or risk also change, the money share need not remain 20%; re-solve preferences.

edge.title: Improve return but increase risk
edge.why: Keep total wealth and liquidity fixed.
edge.question: Is the net asset-demand response predetermined?
edge.answer: No. The benefits and costs oppose each other.

edge.title: Compare expected and realized
edge.why: A forecast of higher return is not a guaranteed later payoff.

edge.title: Check the arithmetic illustration
edge.why: Buying for 100, receiving 3 and selling for 102 gives 5%, not the 3% payout rate.

assets-demand.goal: Derive money demand’s signs from transactions and the return forgone.

symbols.meaning: Nominal money stock and price level
Nominal alternative-asset yield and real rate
Partial income derivative of real money demand, and desired nominal money holdings

assumptions: Baseline money pays iₘ=0.
L=100+Y−1000i is an illustration, not an estimated law.
Real-rate plot fixes πᵉ=.02 unless stated.

derive.title: Start with transaction needs
derive.why: Higher real income normally creates more purchases requiring liquidity.

derive.title: Compare nominal yields
derive.why: Holding zero-interest money sacrifices the alternative nominal return.

derive.title: Link to the real-rate graph
derive.why: At fixed expectations, higher r raises i approximately.
derive.question: Why does the curve slope down against r?
derive.answer: Higher r raises the nominal return forgone at fixed πᵉ.

derive.title: Distinguish monetary units
derive.why: Multiply real demand by the price level for nominal demand.

graph.title: Draw the initial schedule
graph.why: At Y=100, πᵉ=.02, the illustration becomes L=180−1000r.

graph.title: Add a fixed quantity reference
graph.why: The supply 100 helps compare demanded balances and a clearing rate.
graph.question: Does increasing Y change the supply line?
graph.answer: Not when M and P are fixed.

graph.title: Locate the baseline
graph.why: The curve’s downward slope is separate from its income shifts.

increase.title: Increase income to 120
increase.why: At each r, transactions demand rises by 20.
increase.question: At r=.08, is desired L still 100?
increase.answer: No. It becomes 120.

increase.title: Shift real demand right
increase.why: The intercept rises from 180 to 200 while its slope is unchanged.

increase.title: Clear fixed supply
increase.why: Higher r discourages enough holdings to return demand to 100.

decrease.title: Decrease income to 80
decrease.why: Transaction needs fall at every r.
decrease.question: Does this lower desired balances at the old rate?
decrease.answer: Yes, from 100 to 80.

decrease.title: Shift the demand left
decrease.why: The new intercept is 160.

decrease.title: Clear with a lower rate
decrease.why: A lower return forgone restores demand to the fixed supply 100.

edge.title: Let money pay interest
edge.why: The zero-money-return assumption fails.
edge.question: If i and iₘ each rise 2 points, does the return gap change?
edge.answer: No. Their difference is unchanged.

edge.title: Replace the argument
edge.why: Use the return gap rather than i alone.

edge.title: Keep magnitude assumptions separate
edge.why: L_Y>0 does not by itself prove income elasticity below 1; the lecture’s less-than-proportional response is an additional maintained restriction.

assets-fisher.goal: Obtain real returns from a ratio of goods rather than subtracting large rates.
assumptions: Positive price levels.
Nominal contract i=.10 for directional plots.

derive.title: Measure goods sacrificed
derive.why: Investing one dollar gives up the goods it buys today.

derive.title: Measure future goods received
derive.why: The investment pays 1+i dollars at the future price.

derive.title: Form a gross real return
derive.why: Divide goods received by goods sacrificed.
derive.question: Why is subtraction not yet justified?
derive.answer: Purchasing power is a ratio of gross returns.

derive.title: Recover the net rate
derive.why: Subtract 1 and combine the numerator.

derive.title: Identify the approximation
derive.why: Dropping the product rπ is justified only when sufficiently small.

graph.title: Plot the exact contract payoff
graph.why: With fixed i, the exact real return falls as inflation increases.

graph.title: Add the local subtraction rule
graph.why: The dashed line is an approximation, not another exact return.
graph.question: At π=.05, is r exactly .05?

graph.title: Mark the exact result
graph.why: Use the gross price factor rather than simply subtracting percentages.

increase.title: Increase inflation to .10
increase.why: The promised nominal payoff remains 1.10.
increase.question: What happens when prices also grow by 10%?
increase.answer: Purchasing power is unchanged.

increase.title: Divide equal gross factors
increase.why: The real return is zero despite positive nominal interest.

increase.title: Move along the same contract curve
increase.why: No nominal contract was repriced.

decrease.title: Decrease inflation to zero
decrease.why: The nominal contract still pays 10%.
decrease.question: Do any nominal gains get eroded by inflation now?
decrease.answer: No. The price factor is 1.

decrease.title: Recover the full real gain
decrease.why: All nominal growth becomes purchasing-power growth.

decrease.title: Locate the new point
decrease.why: The same contract now has a higher realized real return.

edge.title: Use large inflation
edge.why: At π=.20, the first-order shortcut is less reliable.
edge.question: Are exact r and i−π equal?
edge.answer: No. Exact r is −.083333 while subtraction gives−.10.

edge.title: Redo the gross ratio
edge.why: The denominator 1.20 cannot be replaced harmlessly by 1.

edge.title: Keep forecasts separate
edge.why: Realized returns use actual inflation. Under uncertainty, a ratio using mean inflation is not generally an exact expected return.

assets-expectations.goal: Choose the right fixed variables before interpreting higher expected inflation.

symbols.meaning: Nominal money stock and price level
Nominal alternative-asset yield and real rate

assumptions: Use the lecture approximation i≈r+πᵉ.
Fixed-r graph uses r=.08.
The separate fixed-M/P/Y case uses L=100+Y−1000i, Y=100, M/P=100.

derive.title: Write the return decomposition
derive.why: Expected inflation separates the nominal opportunity cost from the expected real rate.

derive.title: Specify a Fisher comparison
derive.why: Holding r fixed isolates how lenders price expected purchasing-power erosion.

derive.title: Specify a different equilibrium comparison
derive.why: With M/P and Y fixed, stable invertible money demand pins down i.
derive.question: In this second comparison, which rate can absorb a πᵉ change?
derive.answer: The real rate r.

derive.title: Recover real interest
derive.why: At the same nominal clearing rate, higher expected inflation lowers r.

graph.title: Plot fixed-r nominal rates
graph.why: This upward line is the Fisher comparison only.

graph.title: Add the original nominal rate
graph.why: The horizontal dashed reference marks .10, not a second market-clearing rule.
graph.question: At πᵉ=.04, what nominal rate preserves r=.08?
graph.answer: .12 approximately.

graph.title: Locate the initial state
graph.why: At πᵉ=.02, i=.10 gives r≈.08.

increase.title: Raise πᵉ to .04 at fixed r
increase.why: The expected real compensation remains .08.
increase.question: Which nominal rate is now required?
increase.answer: .12 approximately.

increase.title: Add the larger inflation component
increase.why: The nominal rate rises by 2 percentage points.

increase.title: Move along the Fisher line
increase.why: This result does not also hold M/P and Y fixed unless another variable adjusts.

decrease.title: Lower πᵉ to zero at fixed r
decrease.why: The expected real rate remains .08.
decrease.question: Does nominal interest become zero?
decrease.answer: No. The .08 real component remains.

decrease.title: Remove only the inflation component
decrease.why: The approximate nominal rate becomes .08.

decrease.title: Read the lower point
decrease.why: The expected purchasing-power compensation is unchanged.

edge.title: Hold M/P and Y fixed instead
edge.why: Now i must stay .10 when πᵉ rises .02→.04.
edge.question: Can r stay .08 in this closure?
edge.answer: No. It must fall to .06 approximately.

edge.title: Shift demand drawn against r
edge.why: Higher expectations reduce L at each r, but not at each unchanged i.

edge.title: Resolve the different equilibrium
edge.why: The same supply 100 meets demand at r=.06, leaving i≈.06+.04=.10.

assets-walras.goal: Use consistent portfolio values to infer the residual asset-market balance.

symbols.meaning: Wealth valued at current asset prices
Money and net nonmonetary holdings in common value units
Price and excess demand of market j

assumptions: Complete portfolio budget and consistent valuation.
Positive remaining-market price for the N-market inference.

derive.title: Write desired adding up
derive.why: All desired net holdings must fit wealth.

derive.title: Write supplied adding up
derive.why: The same wealth values the available portfolio.

derive.title: Subtract the equations
derive.why: The wealth terms cancel, linking the two imbalances.
derive.question: If money demand exceeds supply by 20, what happens to nonmoney?
derive.answer: Its supply exceeds demand by 20 in value.

derive.title: Impose one clearing condition
derive.why: Money excess demand zero leaves nonmoney excess demand zero.

graph.title: Start with valued wealth
graph.why: Both sides must refer to the same prices and available holdings.

graph.title: Reveal the two residuals
graph.why: Money and nonmoney excess demands are not freely independent.
graph.question: Can both excess demands be positive under this budget?
graph.answer: No. They must add to zero in value.

graph.title: Use the sum
graph.why: The final implication concerns the two asset groups in this abstraction.

increase.title: Increase desired money
increase.why: Let wealth 100, monetary supply 40, and desired money rise 40→60.
increase.question: What desired nonmoney holding remains?

increase.title: Apply the residual budget
increase.why: Supplied nonmoney is 60 while desired nonmoney is 40.

increase.title: Interpret proposed trades
increase.why: People try to sell nonmoney to obtain money; price adjustment reconciles holdings.

decrease.title: Decrease desired money
decrease.why: Keep the same supply but let desired money fall 40→30.
decrease.question: Where does the remaining wealth go?
decrease.answer: Desired nonmoney rises to 70.

decrease.title: Compute the imbalance
decrease.why: Money excess supply 10 offsets nonmoney excess demand 10.

decrease.title: Interpret asset pressure
decrease.why: People seek nonmoney assets with balances they do not wish to hold.

edge.title: Add other markets
edge.why: Money clearing alone no longer represents the full economy’s equilibrium.
edge.question: What does general Walras law actually require?
edge.answer: Consistent budgets and clearing of N−1 markets before inferring the last.

edge.title: Use the value equation
edge.why: The remaining positive price multiplies a zero residual when all other residuals vanish.

edge.title: Keep the scope precise
edge.why: The two-asset result does not establish full employment or goods-market clearing at arbitrary prices.

assets-adjustment.goal: Connect excess money balances to bond prices and yields.

symbols.meaning: Fixed nominal bond payoff and current bond price

assumptions: Fixed Y, P, πᵉ=.02 and zero interest on money.
Illustration L=180−1000r, initial real supply 100.
One-period bond pays F=110 with no intervening coupon.
The linked money–bond illustration uses the lecture approximation i≈r+πᵉ; the fixed-payoff bond yield formula itself is exact.

derive.title: Compute yield from a fixed payoff
derive.why: The return includes the difference between future payoff and purchase price.

derive.title: Differentiate the price effect
derive.why: A larger denominator lowers the return on the same payoff.

derive.title: Identify portfolio pressure
derive.why: Excess money supply prompts attempted bond purchases; a shortage of money relative to desired holdings prompts attempted bond sales.
derive.question: Do private bond purchases destroy aggregate M?
derive.answer: No. Sellers receive the money.

derive.title: Close through desired holdings
derive.why: Changing yields changes the opportunity cost until demand equals supplied money.

graph.title: Draw the yield schedule
graph.why: Every point uses the same nominal payoff 110.

graph.title: Add the initial yield reference
graph.why: The horizontal .10 line helps locate the initial price 100.
graph.question: If price rises, which way does yield move?
graph.answer: Down, with the payoff held fixed.

graph.title: Mark the starting bond
graph.why: Price 100 and payoff 110 imply 10% nominal return.

increase.title: Increase real money supply 100→120
increase.why: At the old rate, people hold more money than they desire.
increase.question: Which asset do they try to buy?
increase.answer: Bonds or other nonmonetary assets.

increase.title: Reconcile the two diagrams
increase.why: Money clearing gives r=.06; with πᵉ=.02, nominal i≈.08.

increase.title: Read the price increase
increase.why: Bond demand pushes price up and yield down; lower yield makes the larger money stock willingly held.

decrease.title: Decrease real money supply 100→80
decrease.why: At the old rate, people want more money than exists.
decrease.question: How do they try to obtain it?
decrease.answer: By selling nonmonetary assets.

decrease.title: Solve the higher return
decrease.why: Money clearing gives r=.10 and nominal i≈.12.

decrease.title: Read the price decline
decrease.why: Selling pressure lowers bond prices and raises yields, discouraging money holdings.

edge.title: Change the payoff assumption
edge.why: Suppose the bond has coupons or is sold before maturity.
edge.question: Can F/p_B−1 automatically describe the holding-period return?
edge.answer: Only if F includes every relevant payoff for that holding period.

edge.title: Redo total return

edge.title: Keep the equilibrium link
edge.why: A single model r must clear goods and assets simultaneously; separate partial diagrams do not authorize two incompatible equilibrium rates.

assets-longrun.goal: Solve the price level after solving the real side of the model.

symbols.meaning: Full-employment output, desired national saving and investment

assumptions: Classical long-run closure: labor determines Y*, goods determine r.
Nominal M is policy-given; L>0.
Baseline illustration L=100, M=200.

derive.title: Solve labor first
derive.why: Real production at full employment determines Y* before choosing the monetary price level.

derive.title: Solve desired saving and investment
derive.why: Their equality determines the real rate under this closure.

derive.title: Evaluate real money demand
derive.why: At given Y*, r and expectations, L is a real quantity.
derive.question: Which variable remains to clear the asset market?
derive.answer: The flexible price level P.

derive.title: Isolate prices
derive.why: Dividing the nominal stock by desired real holdings restores equilibrium.

graph.title: Build a proportional relation
graph.why: With L=100, every additional 100 nominal units requires 1 more price-index unit.

graph.title: Mark the chosen money stock
graph.why: The vertical reference holds current M at 200.
graph.question: What P yields real balances 100?

graph.title: Locate monetary equilibrium
graph.why: The reference point solves 200/P=100.

increase.title: Increase M=200→240
increase.why: Hold Y*, r, πᵉ and therefore L fixed.
increase.question: Does real supply stay permanently 20% higher?
increase.answer: No. P adjusts proportionately in this long-run comparison.

increase.title: Resolve P
increase.why: The new nominal stock is divided by the same 100 real demand.

increase.title: Preserve real balances
increase.why: The higher price level absorbs the nominal increase.

decrease.title: Decrease M=200→160
decrease.why: Keep the real side and expected inflation unchanged.
decrease.question: Can P stay 2 in long-run clearing?
decrease.answer: No. That would supply only 80 real balances.

decrease.title: Resolve the lower price
decrease.why: A lower P restores the desired real holdings.

decrease.title: Preserve the ratio
decrease.why: This is a20% level reduction, not a permanent −20% inflation rate.

edge.title: Let real demand change
edge.why: Suppose L rises 100→120 at fixed M=200.
edge.question: Does P remain proportional to an unchanged M alone?
edge.answer: No. The denominator changed.

edge.title: Recalculate the ratio
edge.why: More desired purchasing-power balances require lower prices.

edge.title: Read the shifted relation
edge.why: The new money–price ray is flatter; a once-only price change is not continuing inflation.

assets-growth.goal: Derive exact finite growth rules and their local approximations.

symbols.meaning: Positive quantities related by the stated equation
Growth of nominal money, real money demand and prices
Partial derivatives of f with respect to its two inputs
Differentiable function relating output quantity z to inputs x and y

assumptions: Positive levels and denominators.
Numerical money graph fixes baseline g_M=.10.

derive.title: Take logs of a product
derive.why: Multiplication of levels becomes addition of logs.

derive.title: Differentiate proportionally
derive.why: The derivative of ln x is dx/x.

derive.title: Check finite changes
derive.why: Expand the two new gross factors rather than silently deleting their product.
derive.question: For 10% and 20% growth, is total exactly 30%?
derive.answer: No. The 2% cross term makes 32%.

derive.title: Expose the approximation
derive.why: The product of small growth rates is the neglected term.

derive.title: Use a quotient
derive.why: Log subtraction gives the derivative rule; finite changes require division.

derive.title: Use a general function
derive.why: Total differentiation weights each input’s change by its marginal contribution.

derive.title: Normalize to elasticities
derive.why: Multiply/divide each term by its input to produce dimensionless weights.

graph.title: Plot exact ratio growth
graph.why: For P=M/L, the curve divides gross growth factors.

graph.title: Add the approximation
graph.why: The dashed difference formula is a local simplification.
graph.question: At g_L=.05, is price growth exactly .05?

graph.title: Mark the exact point
graph.why: The approximation is nearby but should not replace exact arithmetic when asked.

increase.title: Increase money growth to 20%
increase.why: Keep real money-demand growth 5%.
increase.question: Can demand growth be ignored?
increase.answer: No. It remains in the denominator.

increase.title: Use the gross factors
increase.why: Faster numerator growth raises price growth.

increase.title: Shift the exact relationship
increase.why: The old curve remains as the comparison.

decrease.title: Decrease money growth to zero
decrease.why: Real demand still grows 5%.
decrease.question: Can the price level fall despite a constant M?
decrease.answer: Yes. More desired real balances require a lower P.

decrease.title: Compute the exact decline
decrease.why: The denominator grows while the numerator does not.

decrease.title: Read the lower curve
decrease.why: This is deflation in the stated comparison.

edge.title: Let demand shrink 10%
edge.why: Keep money growth 10%; the two changes have opposite signs.
edge.question: Is the exact price increase 20%?

edge.title: Redo the denominator
edge.why: A smaller denominator amplifies the numerator’s increase.

edge.title: Check a zero baseline
edge.why: If a quantity initially equals zero, its percentage growth and log are undefined. Use level changes or the original equation instead.

assets-elasticity.goal: Turn level derivatives into point elasticities and money-growth contributions.

symbols.meaning: Point income and interest elasticities of L
Finite proportional growth of M, Y, i
Partial level derivatives of real demand

assumptions: Stable L=300+.8Y−1000i>0 in the illustration.
Baseline Y=1000, i=.10, P=2.
Finite elasticity growth formula is first-order unless direct evaluation is used.

derive.title: Differentiate the levels
derive.why: The coefficients tell how many balance units change per input unit.

derive.title: Normalize by current demand
derive.why: Proportional demand change divides the level response by L.

derive.title: Expose the elasticities
derive.why: Multiplying and dividing by the input produces a proportional response coefficient.
derive.question: Is −1000 itself the interest elasticity?
derive.answer: No. Multiply it by i/L.

derive.title: Evaluate the starting point
derive.why: At Y=1000 and i=.10, L=1000 gives elasticities .8 and −.1.

derive.title: Combine with the price ratio
derive.why: Subtract both demand-growth contributions from nominal money growth.

derive.title: Track the negative sign
derive.why: A higher nominal rate reduces demand, so its contribution raises implied price growth at fixed g_M.

graph.title: Draw demand against income
graph.why: At fixed i=.10, the level slope is .8.

graph.title: Add a rate comparison
graph.why: Raising i to .12 shifts the line down 20 without changing its income slope.
graph.question: Does the unchanged slope mean the elasticity is constant everywhere?
graph.answer: No. η_Y=.8Y/L varies with Y and L.

graph.title: Mark the baseline point
graph.why: The normalization Y/L happens to equal 1 here.

increase.title: Increase Y by 5%
increase.why: Hold i and target P fixed.
increase.question: Must required M also rise 5%?
increase.answer: No. Income elasticity is .8 at the initial point.

increase.title: Recompute demand exactly
increase.why: The linear function adds .8×50=40.

increase.title: Accommodate transactions
increase.why: At P=2, the central bank requires M=2080, up 4% from 2000.

decrease.title: Decrease Y by 5%
decrease.why: Keep i=.10 and target P=2.
decrease.question: How much does L fall?
decrease.answer: 40 real units.

decrease.title: Recompute the level
decrease.why: Use the original function rather than guessing a unit elasticity.

decrease.title: Reduce money consistently
decrease.why: M must fall to 1920 to maintain both P and i.

edge.title: Start interest at zero
edge.why: At Y=1000, i=0, L=1100, the point interest elasticity is zero.
edge.question: Does this imply a rate rise cannot change L?
edge.answer: No. Percentage rate growth is undefined at zero; the level derivative remains −1000.

edge.title: Use the level change
edge.why: Raising i from 0 to .01 lowers demand 10.

edge.title: Read the valid comparison
edge.why: The new demand 1090 is lower despite the initial zero elasticity.

assets-hyperinflation.goal: Compound monthly rates and connect monetary stabilization to fiscal financing.
assumptions: Constant monthly rates are numerical illustrations.
The lecture threshold is at least 50% per month, not per year.

derive.title: Identify the time unit
derive.why: A monthly 50% rate is not an annual 50% rate.

derive.title: Apply one gross factor per month
derive.why: Each month’s increase applies to the already higher price level.

derive.title: Compound rather than add
derive.why: At 50% monthly, the annual multiplier is about 129.746.
derive.question: Is annual inflation 12×50%=600%?
derive.answer: No. Compounding gives about 12,874.6%.

derive.title: Trace fiscal pressure
derive.why: When taxes and borrowing cannot finance spending, money creation may cover the gap; stopping it leaves financing to replace.

graph.title: Draw stable prices first
graph.why: This reference separates a constant level from growing prices.

graph.title: Add monthly compounding
graph.why: The curvature reflects applying each percentage to a larger base.
graph.question: What does a fixed nominal balance buy after prices multiply 129.746?
graph.answer: About 1/129.746 of its former purchasing power.

graph.title: Mark the annual price factor
graph.why: The plotted point is a multiplier, not the net percentage rate.

increase.title: Increase monthly inflation to 60%
increase.why: Keep the initial price level identical.
increase.question: Can an extra 10 points create a small annual difference only?
increase.answer: No. It compounds over 12 months.

increase.title: Calculate the new factor
increase.why: Repeated multiplication magnifies the higher monthly rate.

increase.title: Compare common starting values
increase.why: The higher path ends far above the 50% path.

decrease.title: Decrease monthly inflation to 40%
decrease.why: This is below the lecture’s monthly hyperinflation threshold, but still very high.
decrease.question: Does the price level now fall?
decrease.answer: No. Inflation remains positive.

decrease.title: Recompute price growth
decrease.why: The annual level still multiplies about 56.694.

decrease.title: Name the change correctly
decrease.why: This is disinflation, not deflation.

edge.title: Stop monetary financing
edge.why: Suppose government spending still exceeds nonmonetary finance.
edge.question: Has the fiscal shortfall disappeared?
edge.answer: No. Removing one financing source does not erase expenditure.

edge.title: Close the budget another way
edge.why: Lower G, higher T or feasible borrowing must replace the lost monetary revenue.

edge.title: Trace monetary functions
edge.why: Severe instability can impair saving, price quotation and payment acceptance, leading to stable-currency use or barter.

assets-institutions.goal: Separate the textbook closure from the policy institution described in the lecture.

symbols.meaning: Domestic-currency cost of one unit of foreign currency in the illustration
A stated nominal policy-rate target in the changed-closure example

assumptions: Institutional statements are from supplied course slides, not a current policy update.
Import-price illustration holds foreign prices fixed and abstracts from incomplete pass-through.

derive.title: Identify monetary versus fiscal authority
derive.why: The lecture assigns US monetary policy to the Fed and fiscal policy to the Treasury.

derive.title: Read the Fed instrument
derive.why: The nominal federal funds target concerns overnight interbank reserves; price stability and full employment are its stated dual objectives.

derive.title: Read the MAS framework
derive.why: The supplied lecture emphasizes a trade-weighted exchange-rate basket and Singapore’s import exposure.
derive.question: Does that make the formal course model an open-economy model?
derive.answer: No. The institution overview does not supply a full exchange-rate model.

derive.title: Use the given exercise closure
derive.why: When a problem fixes exogenous M, solve that specified model rather than silently replacing its instrument.

graph.title: Reveal the model assumption
graph.why: Exogenous nominal M is the textbook closure.

graph.title: Separate US authorities
graph.why: The Fed and Treasury perform different policy functions.
graph.question: Which authority is responsible for the fiscal tax/spending budget?
graph.answer: The Treasury/fiscal government, not the money-market equation itself.

graph.title: Add Singapore’s channel
graph.why: Trade exposure explains why import prices matter for the exchange-rate framework.

increase.title: Increase the domestic-currency cost of imports
increase.why: Let e rise while P* stays fixed.
increase.question: What happens to the direct domestic-currency import price?
increase.answer: It rises under the stated pass-through illustration.

increase.title: Apply the unit conversion
increase.why: More domestic currency is needed for the same foreign-currency good.

increase.title: Connect the institutional intuition
increase.why: High import content makes this channel economically relevant; it does not specify exact aggregate inflation.

decrease.title: Decrease e at fixed P*
decrease.why: The domestic currency buys foreign currency more cheaply.
decrease.question: Can this lower the direct import cost?
decrease.answer: Yes, in the stated simple comparison.

decrease.title: Redo the conversion
decrease.why: The same foreign price is multiplied by a smaller e.

decrease.title: Keep the causal claim limited
decrease.why: Domestic inflation also depends on other prices, pass-through and policy responses.

edge.title: Replace the instrument assumption
edge.why: A problem targets an interest rate rather than fixing M.
edge.question: Can money supply still be imposed independently without another rule?
edge.answer: Not generally. The policy closure must be specified consistently.

edge.title: Identify the accommodating variable
edge.why: At fixed P, Y, maintaining a target i may require adjusting M to money demand.

edge.title: Respect source scope
edge.why: Detailed modern operating tools, independence and the open-economy trilemma are not derivable from this short institutional overview alone.

assets-anticipation.goal: Separate news about future money from an actual current shipment.
assumptions: Conditional flexible-price comparison with r, Y, current M fixed.
Illustration M=200, r=.02, L=150−1000i.
Specified news changes πᵉ; this is not a complete dynamic expectations model.

derive.title: Distinguish dates
derive.why: An actual shipment changes current M; news about a future shipment does not itself add money today.

derive.title: Specify the expectations response
derive.why: Anticipated future supply can increase expected erosion of cigarette money.

derive.title: Find the nominal opportunity cost
derive.why: At fixed r, expected inflation changes i approximately.
derive.question: Can current demand change before current M changes?
derive.answer: Yes, through expectations.

derive.title: Solve current prices
derive.why: With current M fixed, lower desired real holdings require a higher P.

graph.title: Draw the initial balance relationship
graph.why: At πᵉ=.03, i≈.05, L=100, current M=200 implies P=2.

graph.title: Add a lower-demand relationship
graph.why: A shift to L=80 makes each nominal stock support a higher P.
graph.question: Did current M need to rise?
graph.answer: No. The comparison stays at M=200.

graph.title: Read the price response
graph.why: P rises to 2.5 because people want fewer real balances.

increase.title: Increase expected inflation .03→.05
increase.why: Keep r=.02 and current M=200.
increase.question: What nominal opportunity cost follows?

increase.title: Recompute desired balances
increase.why: Higher i makes monetary holdings less attractive.

increase.title: Recompute current P
increase.why: The announcement affects price through demand, not a current shipment.

decrease.title: Decrease expected inflation .03→.01

decrease.title: Recompute greater real demand

decrease.title: Resolve the lower current price
