cycles-turning.goal: Locate a phase and a turning point without confusing the level with its direction.

symbols.meaning: Observation date, with the frequency stated separately
Real aggregate activity at date t
Chosen trend level at date t
Proportional growth from the preceding observation
Proportional deviation from the chosen trend

assumptions: Use the lecture’s activity-direction convention: rising activity is expansion and falling activity is contraction.
The invented observations illustrate definitions, not an official chronology.

derive.title: Choose the activity measure
derive.why: Use real aggregate activity through time. A price index or unemployment rate has a different interpretation; do not label its own peak an output peak.
derive.math: Y_t is measured in real units.

derive.title: Compare adjacent dates
derive.why: Subtract the previous activity observation. A positive difference means activity increased during that interval; a negative difference means it declined.

derive.title: Find a reversal
derive.why: A peak has rising activity before it and falling activity after it. In the illustration activity rises 104→109 then falls 109→106.
derive.question: Is the point with activity 109 an entire contraction?
derive.answer: No. It is the local peak. The declining intervals after it form the contraction.

derive.title: Locate the trough
derive.why: Activity falls to 102 and then rises to 105. The trough separates a contraction from the following expansion.

derive.title: Join complete phases
derive.why: From the peak at t=2 to the next peak at t=6, activity passes through the trough at t=4. The interval contains both contraction and expansion.
derive.math: Cycle length in this illustration: 6−2=4 observations.

graph.title: Draw real activity
graph.why: Place date on the horizontal axis and the actual activity index on the vertical axis. Read movements along the curve, not its distance from the chart bottom.

graph.title: Mark the peak
graph.why: Reveal the change from a positive slope before t=2 to a negative slope afterward. The local maximum is defined by its neighboring observations.
graph.question: Does the later value 111 prevent 109 from being an earlier peak?
graph.answer: No. A cyclical peak is local, not necessarily the highest value ever observed.

graph.title: Add the trough and next peak
graph.why: The trough at 4 ends the first contraction; the next peak at 6 ends the following expansion. The chart now displays a complete local cycle.

increase.title: Start at the trough
increase.why: Activity is 102 at t=4. Compare the next observation with this starting level rather than with an arbitrary benchmark.

increase.title: Compute the increase
increase.why: The move to 105 is a rise of 3, or about 2.94%. That interval is expansion under the stated convention.
increase.question: Would remaining below trend turn this rise into a contraction?
increase.answer: No. Rising activity and a negative trend gap can occur together.

increase.title: Keep the phase local
increase.why: Further rising activity reaches 111 at t=6. This continues the expansion until a subsequent reversal, without requiring a return to every earlier benchmark.

decrease.title: Start at the peak
decrease.why: At t=2 activity is 109. The level is high, but the next interval can still be a contraction.

decrease.title: Compute the decline
decrease.why: Activity falls to 106: a decrease of 3, or about 2.75%. The sign of the change identifies contraction.
decrease.question: Does the positive gap at t=3 rule out contraction?
decrease.answer: No. Activity is falling while its level remains above the stated trend.

decrease.title: End the contraction at its turning point
decrease.why: The decline continues to 102 at t=4. Once subsequent observations rise, 4 is identified as the trough, not another whole recession.

edge.title: Identify the uncertain condition
edge.why: The clean local pattern assumes the observations accurately reflect sustained aggregate activity. A single temporary or revised observation can break that assumption.

edge.title: Redo the classification with more evidence
edge.why: If a reported fall is later revised to a rise, the candidate peak may disappear. Wait for corroborating observations rather than mechanically calling every one-point wiggle a business-cycle turn.
edge.question: Does a delayed announcement imply that the actual trough occurs on the announcement date?
edge.answer: No. The turning date can be earlier than the later date when evidence establishes it.

edge.title: Keep severity separate
edge.why: A depression is a particularly severe recession in the lecture. A numerical threshold for severity is not supplied; do not invent one from this illustrative chart.

cycles-trend.goal: Compute growth and trend gaps independently, then apply a clearly stated convention.

symbols.meaning: Observation date, with the frequency stated separately
Real aggregate activity at date t
Chosen trend level at date t
Proportional growth from the preceding observation
Proportional deviation from the chosen trend

assumptions: Real activity and its trend are positive when logs or proportional changes are used.
Trend is supplied or estimated separately; it is not automatically constant.
The lecture quotes several textbook conventions, so labels must identify which one is used.

derive.title: Define growth from the preceding date
derive.why: The denominator is previous actual activity, because the question is how much actual activity changed over time.

derive.title: Define the gap at the same date
derive.why: The denominator is the current trend level. A positive gap means activity is above trend; it says nothing alone about its change from yesterday.

derive.title: Relate logs to proportional gaps
derive.why: Divide actual activity by its trend and take natural logs. The log gap is exact as a log difference but only approximately the proportional gap.
derive.math: ℓ_t=ln Y_t−ln Ytrend_t=ln(1+gap_t)≈gap_t for small gaps.

derive.title: Work one point fully
derive.why: At t=3, actual activity falls from 109 to 106 while trend equals 104.5. Growth is negative and the gap is positive.
derive.question: Which number tells you that activity is falling?
derive.answer: The growth rate −2.752%. The positive gap only compares activity with the current trend.

derive.title: Apply the stated definition
derive.why: The lecture’s activity-direction convention calls the falling interval contraction. The quoted Williamson language concerns sequences of trend deviations; the quoted Blanchard convention concerns negative GDP growth, usually two quarters. These are not interchangeable rules.

graph.title: Draw actual activity
graph.why: Start with the dated activity observations. The slope between observations answers the growth-direction question.

graph.title: Add the chosen trend
graph.why: Draw 100+1.5t on the same level axes. At any date, the vertical difference measures Y minus trend, not yet a percentage gap.
graph.question: What must divide the vertical difference to obtain the proportional gap?
graph.answer: The trend level at that same date.

graph.title: Compare the two counterexamples
graph.why: At t=3, activity falls above trend. At t=5 it rises below trend. These points separate movement over time from position relative to a reference.

increase.title: Observe the actual increase
increase.why: From t=4 to t=5, activity rises from 102 to 105. Growth is positive regardless of trend.

increase.title: Recompute the gap at the new date
increase.why: Trend at t=5 is 107.5. Activity is therefore 2.5 below trend even after rising.
increase.question: Is positive growth sufficient for a positive output gap?
increase.answer: No. The increase can leave the activity level below its current trend.

increase.title: Allow trend to rise faster
increase.why: In a separate numerical illustration, actual activity rises 100→102 while trend rises 100→104. Growth is +2%, but the gap falls from zero to about −1.923%.

decrease.title: Observe the actual decrease
decrease.why: From t=2 to t=3, activity falls from 109 to 106. This is negative growth.

decrease.title: Recompute the gap independently
decrease.why: With trend 104.5, activity at 106 still exceeds trend. A positive gap does not erase the fall in activity.
decrease.question: Can the gap increase while actual activity falls?
decrease.answer: Yes, if the trend level falls sufficiently faster than actual activity.

decrease.title: Check that edge numerically
decrease.why: In a separate illustration, activity falls 100→98 while trend falls 100→96. Actual growth is −2%, but the gap rises from zero to about +2.083%.

edge.title: Identify the chosen-reference assumption
edge.why: A reported gap presumes a particular trend estimate. Changing that estimate changes the gap even if measured output is unchanged.

edge.title: Replace the trend, not the output
edge.why: At t=3, the higher alternative trend is 107.5, so output 106 now has a negative gap. The activity path and its negative growth are unchanged.
edge.question: Did revising the trend itself change measured growth from 109 to 106?
edge.answer: No. Growth uses the actual observations; only the trend-based comparison changed.

edge.title: Retain exact meanings
edge.why: A large proportional gap need not equal the log gap: if output is 120 and trend 100, the gap is 20% but the log gap is about 18.232%. Two negative quarters is a quoted textbook convention, not a universal automatic institutional rule.

cycles-recurrence.goal: Recognize recurring and persistent phases without imposing a fixed timetable.

symbols.meaning: Observation date, with the frequency stated separately
Real aggregate activity at date t
Chosen trend level at date t
Proportional growth from the preceding observation
Proportional deviation from the chosen trend

assumptions: The illustrated series is invented and observed at equally spaced dates.
Persistence describes a tendency, not a deterministic forecast.

derive.title: Identify more than one phase
derive.why: A single rise and fall shows a fluctuation. Recurrence requires the contraction–trough–expansion–peak sequence to appear again.

derive.title: Measure intervals between comparable turns
derive.why: The illustrative peaks occur at dates 2, 7 and 13. Compare peak to peak rather than mixing a peak-to-trough interval with a full-cycle interval.

derive.title: Separate recurrence from periodicity
derive.why: Both intervals are full cycles, but they differ in length. The pattern recurs without repeating at one fixed predictable interval.
derive.question: Does observing two complete cycles establish a six-observation clock?
derive.answer: No. The observed lengths are already unequal, and history alone does not fix the next length.

derive.title: Define persistence locally
derive.why: Between t=4 and t=7 activity rises at each observation; between 7 and 10 it falls repeatedly. Such continuation illustrates persistence, without excluding the eventual reversal.

graph.title: Draw the irregular activity path
graph.why: Place the illustrative observations on time and level axes. Add a trend reference only as context, not as a timing rule.

graph.title: Reveal comparable peaks
graph.why: The three peaks show intervals of 5 and 6 observations. Their spacing is visibly unequal.
graph.question: Which feature disproves exact periodicity in this illustration?
graph.answer: The unequal distances between successive comparable peaks.

graph.title: Reveal intervening troughs
graph.why: The troughs connect the local contraction and expansion phases. Rising or falling sequences can persist for a while before they reverse.

increase.title: Follow an expansion sequence
increase.why: From t=4, activity rises 101→103→107→110. Multiple successive positive changes illustrate continuing growth.

increase.title: State what persistence suggests
increase.why: If recent growth tends to be followed by growth, the current direction is informative. It does not tell us the exact remaining length.
increase.question: Can persistent growth terminate at the peak at t=7?
increase.answer: Yes. Persistence is compatible with a subsequent reversal.

increase.title: Keep the prediction conditional
increase.why: The next observation is 106, a fall. A rule that extrapolated every positive sequence forever would fail here.

decrease.title: Follow a contraction sequence
decrease.why: After t=7, activity falls 110→106→103→99. Repeated negative changes illustrate persistent decline.

decrease.title: Do not confuse duration with permanence
decrease.why: A sequence of falls can continue for several observations yet eventually stop. The observed trough at 10 is followed by rising activity.
decrease.question: Does persistence require activity to keep falling without a lower turning point?
decrease.answer: No. A persistent phase is not an everlasting phase.

decrease.title: Check the observed reversal
decrease.why: The move 99→100 after t=10 begins the next expansion in this illustration. It does not establish that all future contractions last exactly three intervals.

edge.title: Identify the invalid assumption
edge.why: Forecasting the next peak by adding the last cycle length assumes periodicity. That condition is absent from the lecture’s business-cycle description.

edge.title: Redo the forecast as uncertainty
edge.why: The last observed interval is 6, but the previous was 5. Neither number is a guaranteed interval to the next peak.
edge.question: Can the next peak occur earlier or later than six observations after t=13?
edge.answer: Yes. Recurrent irregular cycles allow either outcome.

edge.title: Separate event and recognition
edge.why: Real-time dating also faces data revisions and the need to distinguish a durable turn from a temporary movement. A later announcement is evidence assessment, not a newly occurring historical turn.

cycles-direction.goal: Classify the sign of comovement separately from how much a variable fluctuates.

symbols.meaning: Output deviation from its trend in percentage points, on the horizontal axis
The other variable’s deviation from trend in percentage points, on the vertical axis
Slope linking x with y in the illustrative linear relation

assumptions: Compare like-for-like measurements over several observations.
The straight-line examples make definitions transparent; empirical relationships are not required to be exact lines.

For the directional numerical exercise, trend levels are held fixed; a rising or falling gap then corresponds to rising or falling activity. A positive gap alone still does not establish positive growth.

derive.title: Select a common reference
derive.why: Use aggregate activity as the reference series. Express both measurements consistently, such as deviations from their own trends; comparing nominal levels with real growth rates can mislead.

derive.title: Check the high-activity side
derive.why: In the illustration x=0.5y, output gap +4 is paired with variable gap +2. Both are above their own trends. This is a level comparison, not by itself a claim that either series is currently rising.

derive.title: Compare the low-activity side
derive.why: Output gap −4 is paired with variable gap −2. Moving between low and high output gaps moves x in the same direction, so the example describes procyclical comovement.
derive.question: Would one unusual observation alone overturn a broad procyclical pattern?
derive.answer: No. Classification concerns a systematic pattern across observations, not an exception-free identity. A positive gap by itself is not a growth rate.

derive.title: Reverse the slope for countercyclicality
derive.why: With x=−0.6y, high output is paired with low x and low output with high x. This is opposite comovement. Acyclical means no clear systematic cycle-related pattern, rather than a special required value.
derive.math: b>0: procyclical; b<0: countercyclical in this linear illustration.

graph.title: Build the procyclical relation
graph.why: Put output gap on the horizontal axis and variable gap on the vertical. Draw x=0.5y with a zero-deviation reference.

graph.title: Reveal both sides
graph.why: At y=+4, x=+2; at y=−4, x=−2. The upward slope summarizes same-direction comovement.
graph.question: Which slope would represent opposite comovement?
graph.answer: A negative slope: high output gap paired with low variable gap and the reverse.

graph.title: Add the countercyclical comparison
graph.why: The line x=−0.6y passes through opposite-signed pairs. It has a different direction, not merely a different amplitude.

increase.title: Raise the output gap
increase.why: Move the illustrative output gap from 0 to +4. Hold the relation being studied fixed; this is movement along a relation, not a shift in it.

increase.title: Compute both responses
increase.why: For the procyclical relation, x rises to +2. For the countercyclical relation, x falls to −2.4.
increase.question: Does a fall in the second variable during expansion make it lagging?
increase.answer: No. It suggests countercyclical direction; timing needs a separate comparison of turning dates.

increase.title: Separate sign from strength
increase.why: The steeper positive line x=1.2y gives +4.8 at the same output gap. It remains procyclical but varies more in this exact illustration.

decrease.title: Lower the output gap
decrease.why: Move the output gap from 0 to −4 while retaining the same illustrative relations.

decrease.title: Compute the distinct responses
decrease.why: The procyclical variable falls to −2; the countercyclical variable rises to +2.4. The negative coefficient is why the second moves upward.
decrease.question: Can a countercyclical variable rise during contraction?
decrease.answer: Yes. That is the opposite-direction movement the definition describes.

decrease.title: Avoid a causal leap
decrease.why: These signed pairs classify a relationship. They do not establish that output directly causes the other variable or identify the underlying shock.

edge.title: Identify the failed line assumption
edge.why: A real series may fluctuate without any clear stable relation to output. Then forcing a positive or negative straight line misstates the evidence.

edge.title: Redo the classification from the pattern
edge.why: If high and low output observations are accompanied by mixed variable movements without a systematic pattern, call the series acyclical under the lecture definition.
edge.question: Must such an acyclical variable stay at zero or remain constant?
edge.answer: No. It can vary substantially while lacking systematic cycle-related comovement.

edge.title: Keep volatility independent
edge.why: A very noisy variable can be acyclical; a small but consistently same-direction variation can be procyclical. Zero linear correlation alone can also miss a more complex pattern, so inspect the plotted observations and the stated definition.

cycles-timing.goal: Read lead, lag and coincidence without confusing their dates with the direction of movement.

symbols.meaning: Output deviation from trend in percentage points
Other variable deviation from trend in percentage points
Mathematical constant in the illustrative waves, not inflation

assumptions: Dates are aligned on the same time scale.
The regular waves are used only to isolate phase differences; actual business cycles are irregular.
For a countercyclical series, compare its peak with the corresponding output trough, or its trough with the corresponding output peak.
The illustrative reference trend is constant, so turning dates of the output gap and activity coincide in this phase exercise.

derive.title: Locate output turns first
derive.why: The illustrative output wave reaches a trough at t=4 and a peak at t=8. These dates are the reference, irrespective of the other variable.

derive.title: Move the other pattern earlier
derive.why: Using t+1 inside the same wave shifts its turns one date earlier: trough 3 and peak 7. That series is leading and procyclical in this comparison.

derive.title: Move the pattern later
derive.why: Using t−1 shifts turns one date later: trough 5 and peak 9. That series is lagging and procyclical. Coincident turns would occur with the output turns.
derive.question: Does a lagging variable necessarily move opposite to output?
derive.answer: No. Lagging concerns dates; this lagging example remains procyclical.

derive.title: Reverse direction without changing the lead
derive.why: Multiplying the leading wave by −1 produces a peak at 3 before the output trough at 4, and a trough at 7 before the output peak at 8. This is countercyclical and leading.

graph.title: Draw the output reference
graph.why: Use dates horizontally and percentage-point deviations vertically. Mark the output trough at 4 and peak at 8.

graph.title: Add the earlier series
graph.why: The leading series trough and peak each occur one date before their output counterparts. Read horizontal distances, not height differences.
graph.question: What feature establishes the lead in this graph?
graph.answer: The same-direction turning points occur one date before the corresponding output turns.

graph.title: Add the later series
graph.why: Its trough is at 5 and peak at 9, both after output. The common amplitude does not determine timing; the horizontal displacement does.

increase.title: Start around output recovery
increase.why: Output starts rising after its trough at t=4. The leading procyclical variable already began rising after its trough at t=3.

increase.title: Measure the date difference
increase.why: The leading trough precedes the output trough by one observation. It is a timing statement, not a guarantee that a rise in this variable will always predict recovery.
increase.question: Would the same numerical lead prove that the variable caused output to rise?
increase.answer: No. A common cause, anticipation or reverse-response mechanism can also produce a lead.

increase.title: Compare a lagging recovery
increase.why: The lagging procyclical series turns upward only after its trough at t=5. It moves in the same broad direction, with a later turn.

decrease.title: Start around output contraction
decrease.why: Output turns down after its peak at t=8. The leading procyclical series turned down after its peak at t=7.

decrease.title: Check the opposite-direction indicator
decrease.why: The countercyclical leading series reaches its trough at t=7 and begins rising before output starts falling at t=8.
decrease.question: Which pair of words describes the rising indicator before output’s downturn?
decrease.answer: Countercyclical and leading: its direction is opposite and its corresponding turn is earlier.

decrease.title: Use the correct corresponding turns
decrease.why: Comparing a countercyclical peak with an output peak can create a false timing label. Pair opposite turns when direction is opposite, and report the direction with the timing.

edge.title: Identify the exact-wave assumption
edge.why: The illustrated dates assume a stable phase shift and clear turns. Real observations may contain noise, revisions, variable leads or false signals.

edge.title: Redo inference with repeated episodes
edge.why: If an indicator turns early once but late in other episodes, an exact one-period leading rule is unsupported. Compare corresponding turns across observations and acknowledge the unstable timing.
edge.question: Does an observed leading pattern provide a perfectly reliable forecast?
edge.answer: No. Leading associations can be imperfect and may change across episodes.

edge.title: Keep definitions distinct from equations
edge.why: The trigonometric form is a teaching device for horizontal shifts. The lecture does not claim that actual business cycles are periodic or that the displayed lead is a structural causal parameter.

cycles-evidence.goal: Use the lecture’s observed patterns to test explanations while keeping measurement and causal claims separate.

symbols.meaning: Real output level when the graph’s axis states a level
Average labor productivity, real output per unit of labor input
Real wage, nominal wage divided by price level
Growth rate of nominal money, distinct from the stock’s trend deviation

assumptions: The lecture’s historical plots provide examples; they are not universal identities.
The lecture explicitly emphasizes knowing definitions rather than memorizing every variable’s classification.
Interpret the measurement actually named on each figure’s axis.

derive.title: Read the measurement before the pattern
derive.why: The opening figures show output, unemployment and consumer prices using different units. A rise in a price level is not itself an expansion; an unemployment peak is not automatically an output peak.

derive.title: Separate the three descriptions
derive.why: Direction describes comovement, timing compares turns, and variability compares amplitude. A series can be procyclical and coincident yet less variable than output.

derive.title: Apply the examples carefully
derive.why: The lecture highlights procyclical average labor productivity, slightly procyclical real wages, and procyclical leading nominal money growth. The productivity figure is described as coincident and less variable than GDP.

derive.title: Keep the money measurements distinct
derive.why: Page 21 names nominal money growth; page 24’s figure is labeled percentage deviations from trend in the money supply. A stock gap and a stock’s growth rate are distinct transformations.
derive.question: Can a money stock above trend have negative current growth?
derive.answer: Yes. Position relative to trend and the change from the preceding observation are different measurements.

derive.title: Ask a theory to explain several facts
derive.why: One successful comovement is not unique confirmation. A useful model should account for multiple patterns under stated mechanisms and be checked against alternatives.

graph.title: Reveal the measurement stage
graph.why: Start with what the horizontal and vertical axes measure. This prevents a change in units from being mistaken for a change in economics.

graph.title: Add the descriptive stage
graph.why: Describe direction, timing and variability separately before introducing a causal theory.
graph.question: Which step would justify replacing “moves before” with “causes”?
graph.answer: None of these descriptive steps alone. Causal claims require additional identifying evidence or assumptions.

graph.title: Reveal competing explanations
graph.why: An early money movement may affect later output, respond to expected output, or share a common driver. Add the testing and revision nodes to show what further work is needed.

increase.title: Consider stronger observed comovement
increase.why: Suppose additional observations show productivity rising more consistently when activity rises. This makes the procyclical description more stable in that sample.

increase.title: Check what strengthens and what does not
increase.why: The descriptive pattern becomes clearer. The direction of causation still does not follow from correlation alone.
increase.question: Does stronger correlation eliminate every common-shock explanation?
increase.answer: No. A common disturbance can create even very strong comovement.

increase.title: Add independent implications
increase.why: Check whether a proposed mechanism also explains timing, real-wage behavior and other variables. A richer set of successful implications is more informative than repeating one correlation.

decrease.title: Consider weaker observed comovement
decrease.why: Suppose new episodes include falling real wages during some expansions. That need not contradict the lecture’s weakly procyclical description, which allows dispersion.

decrease.title: Test the strength of the theory’s claim
decrease.why: A theory predicting a perfect positive relation faces a sharper problem than a theory predicting only weak average comovement.
decrease.question: Does one real-wage fall in an expansion prove that real wages are always countercyclical?
decrease.answer: No. The pattern must be evaluated across observations and against the claim’s stated strength.

decrease.title: Revise the conclusion proportionately
decrease.why: An unstable pattern may weaken a theory’s fit or limit its domain. It does not by itself select a unique replacement cause.

edge.title: Identify the real-time data assumption
edge.why: A turning-point inference may use an initial release that is later revised, or a short movement that does not persist. That undermines a mechanical immediate classification.

edge.title: Redo dating after confirmation
edge.why: The lecture’s examples show substantial delays between an actual peak or trough and its announcement. Revisions and confirming durability can change confidence about a historical date.
edge.question: Does a later announcement move the economy’s historical turning point to that announcement date?
edge.answer: No. It records when the turn was recognized with sufficient confidence, not when it occurred.

edge.title: Avoid invented universality
edge.why: These historical examples motivate definitions and theory checks. They do not guarantee that every country, period, real wage, or monetary measure has the same relationship.

cycles-international.goal: Compare countries’ cycle timing and amplitude while separating shared patterns from causal transmission.

symbols.meaning: Country A output deviation from its own trend, in percentage points
Country B output deviation from its own trend, in percentage points
Mathematical constant in illustrative waves, not inflation
Illustrative common vertical shift measured in percentage points

assumptions: Compare normalized domestic deviations rather than treating different countries’ raw output levels as directly comparable.
Invented waves illustrate comovement only; they are not fitted to the lecture’s country figures.
The course’s closed-economy framework does not by itself identify cross-border transmission.
The invented country trends are held fixed for the phase comparisons, so a curve’s increase or decline also indicates the direction of activity in that illustration.

derive.title: Put countries on comparable measurements
derive.why: Countries can have different output levels and trend growth. Comparing their deviations from their own trends helps separate cycle movements from scale.

derive.title: Compare direction over a broad phase
derive.why: In the illustration both countries decline toward nearby troughs, then rise toward nearby peaks. Related direction can coexist with imperfect alignment.

derive.title: Measure timing and amplitude separately
derive.why: Country A’s trough is at 4 with gap −4; B’s is at 4.5 with gap −3. The half-observation timing difference and smaller amplitude are distinct features.
derive.question: Do related international cycles require identical trough dates or depths?
derive.answer: No. They can be synchronized broadly while differing in timing and amplitude.

derive.title: List mechanisms without selecting one from correlation
derive.why: A shared disturbance can move both economies; trade or financial connections can transmit a disturbance; unrelated domestic events can also partly coincide. The picture alone does not identify which explanation is correct.

derive.title: Connect to the source evidence
derive.why: The lecture’s industrial-production panels and Euro-area/Germany example illustrate related historical cycles. They do not prove perfect worldwide synchronization or a required common currency.

graph.title: Draw one country with its own reference
graph.why: Plot A’s gap against date with a zero-gap line. The vertical axis is a domestic percentage-point deviation, not an absolute amount of GDP.

graph.title: Add the other country
graph.why: B has a smaller amplitude and turns half a date later. Comparing both curves shows a related broad pattern without identical observations.
graph.question: Which difference measures amplitude rather than timing?
graph.answer: The trough depth −4 versus −3. The horizontal difference 4 versus 4.5 measures timing.

graph.title: Retain the reference while reading the pattern
graph.why: A zero gap means activity equals that country’s trend, not zero output. Common signs and nearby turning dates are descriptive evidence, not a causal arrow.

increase.title: Observe simultaneous expansion directions
increase.why: After B’s trough at 4.5, both illustrative curves rise toward their next peaks. Their levels can still be below trend during part of this expansion.

increase.title: Illustrate a positive common disturbance
increase.why: For a transparent graphical exercise, add s=+1 percentage point to each gap at every displayed date. Both curves shift upward, keeping their original curves as references.
increase.question: Does this equal illustrative shift establish that real countries respond by exactly the same amount?
increase.answer: No. It only demonstrates a possible shared movement; actual responses depend on each economy and mechanism.

increase.title: Keep level shifts separate from growth
increase.why: The added constant raises gaps without changing the slopes of these illustrative paths. A higher gap at a date is not automatically faster growth over every interval.

decrease.title: Observe simultaneous contraction directions
decrease.why: From a date shortly after both peaks at 8 and 8.5, both illustrative curves fall. Shared contraction need not have exactly the same start date or depth.

decrease.title: Illustrate a negative common disturbance
decrease.why: Subtract one percentage point from each curve. Both gaps decline relative to their original paths, while their relative phase difference remains.
decrease.question: Would the joint deterioration prove A transmitted its shock to B?
decrease.answer: No. A common shock could lower both, and the figure contains no evidence selecting the causal route.

decrease.title: State the conditional mechanism
decrease.why: A global oil disruption is one possible common disturbance. To establish transmission from A to B instead, one would need evidence about timing, exposures and channels beyond shared declines.

edge.title: Identify the perfect-synchronization assumption
edge.why: A claim that all countries must turn at the same instant is stronger than the lecture’s evidence of frequent related phases. The illustrative curves already violate exact alignment.

edge.title: Redo the comparison using direction and dates
edge.why: Compare broad phases, specific turns and amplitudes separately. A domestic shock can offset a common disturbance, so one country may expand while another contracts over a particular interval.
edge.question: Would one divergent episode prove that international comovement never occurs?
edge.answer: No. It limits a claim of perfect synchronization, not the possibility of recurrent shared patterns.

edge.title: Do not infer an omitted mechanism
edge.why: The source figures do not establish a necessary currency arrangement or a unique direction of causality. A closed-economy model must be extended before it can fully explain international transmission.

market-clearing.goal: Distinguish two-market equilibrium from a consistent three-market allocation.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Competitive agents take prices as given; all sector budget constraints hold.
The labor closure determines Y* independently of r.

derive.title: Start with choices
derive.why: Household and firm labor choices must be mutually consistent before assigning potential output.

derive.title: Use goods consistency
derive.why: At that output, the real rate reconciles desired saving with desired investment.

derive.title: Determine the price level
derive.why: Prices reconcile the nominal stock with desired real holdings.
derive.question: If Y*=100 and r=5, what does L=Y−10 r imply for P when M=100?

derive.title: Check all markets
derive.why: Only the joint solution is full equilibrium. The other asset market clears by budget consistency in the two-asset closure.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw goods-equilibrium pairs with Y horizontal and r vertical.
graph.question: Does an IS–LM intersection automatically clear labor?
graph.answer: No; it must also lie on FE.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add asset-equilibrium pairs at the given price level.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The intersection is on FE at Y=100, so the labor restriction also holds.

increase.title: Raise demand, not capacity
increase.why: A larger spending intercept increases desired expenditure at old prices.
increase.question: Which market condition fails at the new intersection?
increase.answer: The full-employment condition Y=Y*, while goods and assets clear.

increase.title: Clear goods and assets
increase.why: These equations give Y=110, r=6 while FE remains 100.

increase.title: Diagnose the missing condition
increase.why: The positive gap motivates upward price adjustment in the sticky-price transition.

decrease.title: Reduce demand
decrease.why: Lower desired spending changes the goods-market locus.
decrease.question: Does the output fall prove capacity fell?
decrease.answer: No; Y*=100 is fixed and the gap is −10.

decrease.title: Reconcile the fast markets
decrease.why: At the preset price the intersection lies below unchanged capacity.

decrease.title: Identify adjustment pressure
decrease.why: Falling P raises real balances and can restore output toward FE.

edge.title: Find the failed inference
edge.why: Actual saving equals actual investment by accounting; desired equality adds an equilibrium requirement.
edge.question: Can an accounting identity establish general equilibrium by itself?
edge.answer: No; desired choices and all market conditions must be consistent.

edge.title: Recheck labor assumptions
edge.why: Efficiency-wage potential can include involuntary unemployment; the appropriate closure matters.

edge.title: State the zero-gap case
edge.why: At a consistent triple intersection there is no output-gap pressure to change P, but unemployment need not be zero.

fe.goal: Build FE from the labor outcome and distinguish its shifters.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
alternative plain-text notation for labor demanded

assumptions: Y*=AF(K, N*) within the competitive labor closure.
That labor solution has no direct r argument.

derive.title: Solve employment
derive.why: Labor demand and supply determine N*, including the wage adjustment.

derive.title: Convert labor to output
derive.why: Potential output is production at the equilibrium labor input.

derive.title: Vary only the plotted rate
derive.why: No term in this labor solution changes simply because the plotted r changes.
derive.question: If Y*=100 at r=2 and r=8, what joins those points?
derive.answer: A vertical line at Y=100.

derive.title: Draw the locus
derive.why: Every pair satisfying the labor condition has the same horizontal coordinate.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Determine potential output before putting it on the horizontal axis.
graph.question: Must Y* rise when the plotted r rises?
graph.answer: Not in the maintained labor closure.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Place two different rates at the same Y.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Joining the points produces FE; it is not an investment-demand curve.

increase.title: Improve production
increase.why: Higher A directly raises output and can raise MPN, labor demand and N*.
increase.question: Does rightward FE always imply a higher real wage?
increase.answer: No; a labor-supply expansion can lower the wage.

increase.title: Consider other channels
increase.why: More capital can raise output and MPN. More labor supply instead raises N* while lowering the clearing wage.

increase.title: Rebuild the entire locus
increase.why: Once new capacity is 110, every r is paired with 110.

decrease.title: Trace a productive loss
decrease.why: Lower A or capital destruction reduces attainable output; lower MPN can also reduce hiring.
decrease.question: Can capacity fall while the real wage rises?
decrease.answer: Yes, after a competitive labor-supply contraction.

decrease.title: Distinguish labor contraction
decrease.why: Fewer willing workers can lower N* while raising the competitive wage.

decrease.title: Move every rate pair
decrease.why: The curve shifts left rather than rotating.

edge.title: Change the closure
edge.why: A fixed efficiency wage replaces the competitive wage-clearing adjustment.
edge.question: Which step of the usual Ns→FE argument fails?
edge.answer: Wage adjustment no longer expands hiring; excess supply remains.

edge.title: Redo hiring
edge.why: Available workers rise from 100 to 120, but labor demand still calls for 80 jobs.

edge.title: Keep capacity fixed
edge.why: With effort and technology unchanged, the same employment gives the same Y*.

is-derivation.goal: Derive IS by changing output in the saving–investment market.

symbols.meaning: total interest sensitivity of consumption plus investment
goods-equilibrium leakage coefficient, 0.5 in the illustrated boundary
autonomous total expenditure, 75 in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration C=25+0.5 Y−3 r, I=40−2 r, G=10.
0<MPC<1 and investment has no direct current-Y effect.

derive.title: Write national saving
derive.why: Income not used for consumption or public purchases is available for investment.

derive.title: Substitute behavior
derive.why: Extra output raises saving because consumption rises by less than income.

derive.title: Impose desired equality
derive.why: One rate must reconcile both plans.
derive.question: What equation remains after collecting rate terms?

derive.title: Solve the locus
derive.why: Higher Y permits a lower rate, which raises investment and discourages saving.

graph.title: Draw desired investment
graph.why: Use the saving/investment quantity horizontally and r vertically. Hold output fixed for each saving curve.
graph.question: Which underlying curve moves when current Y alone rises?
graph.answer: Saving shifts while desired investment stays fixed.

graph.title: Solve at Y=100
graph.why: Add saving S=15+3r. Its intersection with I=40−2r gives a funds quantity of 30 and r=5.

graph.title: Repeat at higher output
graph.why: At Y=110, saving is five higher at every r. The new intersection is funds quantity 32 and r=4; the output associated with that rate is 110.

graph.title: Repeat independently at lower output
graph.why: At Y=90, saving is five lower at every r. Its intersection gives funds quantity 28 and r=6.

graph.title: Transfer output–rate pairs
graph.why: Change the horizontal axis from saving/investment quantity to output Y. Transfer (90,6), (100,5) and (110,4); do not transfer the funds quantities 28,30,32.
graph.question: Does the point with r=4 have horizontal coordinate 32 or 110 on IS?
graph.answer: 110. The funds quantity 32 belongs to the original saving–investment diagram.

graph.title: Connect the goods-equilibrium locus
graph.why: Repeating the calculation for every Y gives r=15−0.1Y. Join the transferred pairs on that derived relation; changing Y traced one IS rather than shifting it.

increase.title: Raise current income
increase.why: Saving rises by five at each rate.
increase.question: Why is IS itself unchanged?
increase.answer: Y is being varied to trace the locus; autonomous demand determinants stayed fixed.

increase.title: Clear the funds market
increase.why: The clearing rate falls to four and desired investment rises to 32.

increase.title: Transfer to the unchanged IS
increase.why: Replace the funds-quantity horizontal coordinate with the output used to derive this equilibrium. The pair moves down and right on the same goods-equilibrium curve.

decrease.title: Lower current income
decrease.why: Saving falls by five at each rate.
decrease.question: How does a higher rate help goods balance after Y falls?
decrease.answer: It reduces desired C and I, matching spending to lower output.

decrease.title: Find the higher rate
decrease.why: The clearing rate rises to six and investment falls to 28.

decrease.title: Transfer to the unchanged IS
decrease.why: Replace the funds-quantity horizontal coordinate with the output used to derive this equilibrium. The pair moves up and left on the same goods-equilibrium curve.

edge.title: Remove interest sensitivity
edge.why: Neither consumption nor investment responds to r; dividing by H is invalid.
edge.question: Does vertical IS mean fiscal demand is ineffective?
edge.answer: No; it fixes Y at the current demand intercept, which fiscal policy can change.

edge.title: Solve goods balance directly
edge.why: Output must equal 150, independently of r.

edge.title: Change the geometry
edge.why: IS is vertical; an autonomous spending change can still move that vertical line.

is-algebra.goal: Collect taxes, income and interest sensitivity correctly.
assumptions: C=c₀+c(Y−T)−a_c r; I=i₀−b_i r; T=T₀+t Y.
Normal case: 0<c<1,0≤t<1, H>0. Plot uses c=0.5, A₀=75, H=5.

derive.title: Insert the tax rule
derive.why: Only the untaxed share of an income increase enters disposable income.

derive.title: Expand consumption
derive.why: Apply the MPC to both disposable-income terms.

derive.title: Add goods demand
derive.why: Include investment and purchases before collecting terms.

derive.title: Collect coefficients
derive.why: The leftover income coefficient is leakage.
derive.question: What is D for c=0.5 and t=0.2?

derive.title: Read slope and intercept
derive.why: The vertical intercept is A₀/H and the slope is −D/H.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start with r=15−0.10 Y.
graph.question: Does this tax-rate change necessarily change the intercept?
graph.answer: No; with T₀ fixed it changes the income coefficient.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Raising t to 0.2 leaves the intercept at 15 but changes the slope to −0.12.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Against the same LM, the new intersection has lower output.

increase.title: Raise the tax rate
increase.why: Less extra income reaches consumption.
increase.question: Does a larger t flatten this IS?
increase.answer: No; it increases leakage and the absolute r-versus-Y slope.

increase.title: Recompute leakage
increase.why: The slope changes from −0.12 to −0.14.

increase.title: Reconcile markets
increase.why: The steeper curve intersects unchanged LM at lower Y and r.

decrease.title: Lower the tax rate
decrease.why: More additional income becomes disposable.
decrease.question: Why does lower t change the slope rather than cause a movement along IS?
decrease.answer: The behavioral tax rule used to construct the curve changed.

decrease.title: Recalculate induced demand
decrease.why: A larger consumption feedback reduces leakage.

decrease.title: Resolve the intersection
decrease.why: IS becomes flatter and equilibrium Y and r rise.

edge.title: Find the failed division
edge.why: Setting H=0 removes the interest response of spending. Do not divide goods balance by H.
edge.question: Why must the unsolved goods equation be used at H=0?
edge.answer: The formula solved for r divides by zero and no longer represents a valid algebraic operation.

edge.title: Solve the vertical boundary
edge.why: Now 0.5Y=75 fixes Y=150. The unchanged regular LM then gives r=10.

edge.title: Switch to the horizontal boundary
edge.why: This is a separate limit: set D=0 while retaining H=5 and A₀=75. Goods balance fixes r=15; the same regular LM then gives Y=200. D=0 requires a different limiting consumption/tax specification, such as c=1 and t=0, outside the maintained interior c<1 case.

edge.title: Check the double-zero degeneracy
edge.why: When both coefficients vanish, there is no goods solution if A₀ is nonzero. If A₀=0 too, goods balance becomes an identity; it contributes no additional restriction, and LM alone leaves a continuum of pairs.

is-shifts.goal: Separate autonomous spending changes from movements along IS.

symbols.meaning: expected future marginal product of capital

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
For a direct IS shift, hold current capacity and money-market determinants fixed.

derive.title: Freeze the coordinates
derive.why: A shifter changes spending before output or rates respond.

derive.title: Translate consumption or purchases
derive.why: Higher C or G lowers saving at the same Y and r.

derive.title: Translate investment incentives
derive.why: Higher future MPK or a lower effective capital tax raises desired investment.
derive.question: If I exceeds S at the old rate, which rate direction restores goods balance?
derive.answer: A higher rate reduces I and C, raising saving relative to investment.

derive.title: Map every output level
derive.why: A higher clearing rate at every Y means IS shifts up/right; a lower clearing rate shifts it down/left.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Hold Y=100 and draw the original plans.
graph.question: Is raising G the same experiment as raising current Y?
graph.answer: No; G changes an exogenous demand determinant while Y is held fixed.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Raise G by ten: saving at each r falls ten.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: At unchanged Y, the clearing r rises from five to seven, demonstrating an IS shift.

increase.title: Raise desired demand
increase.why: Higher future income, wealth or autonomous C raises consumption; higher G raises purchases; higher future MPK or lower capital tax raises investment.
increase.question: If wealth also raises money demand, may we stop after shifting IS?
increase.answer: No; the full wealth experiment must also consider LM.

increase.title: Restore balance at each Y
increase.why: The higher rate needed at each Y shifts the curve up.

increase.title: Clear both markets
increase.why: With regular unchanged LM, output and the rate both rise.

decrease.title: Reduce desired demand
decrease.why: Lower future income, wealth or autonomous C lowers consumption; lower G frees saving; lower future MPK or higher capital tax lowers investment.
decrease.question: Does a fall in future MPK automatically shift current FE?
decrease.answer: No; a future return change does not itself establish a current capacity change.

decrease.title: Find the lower clearing rate
decrease.why: A lower rate supports expenditure and discourages saving.

decrease.title: Read the intersection
decrease.why: The same LM converts the leftward IS shift into lower output and rate.

edge.title: Change tax timing only
edge.why: A current lump-sum cut is exactly offset by future taxes in present value; the spending path is unchanged.
edge.question: Which usual tax-stimulus link fails here?
edge.answer: The claim that the current tax cut raises desired consumption.

edge.title: Recompute lifetime resources
edge.why: Under Ricardian equivalence, after-tax wealth and desired consumption are unchanged.

edge.title: Retain IS
edge.why: Private saving offsets the public-saving fall, leaving national saving unchanged.

bond-adjustment.goal: Connect cash imbalances to bond prices and yields.

symbols.meaning: certain total payoff one year ahead
decimal nominal yield in the formula

assumptions: One-period fixed payoff; risk and payoff do not change.
The course approximation i≈r+πᵉ links yields and real rates when expectations are fixed.

derive.title: Measure the return
derive.why: Divide the gain by the price paid, not the payoff.

derive.title: Multiply through
derive.why: Move price terms to the same side.

derive.title: Factor the price
derive.why: The investment compounds into the fixed payoff.
derive.question: For F=110 and i=5%, what is P_b?

derive.title: Solve and interpret
derive.why: A lower yield requires a higher price for the same future payment.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Put current bond price horizontally and nominal yield vertically.
graph.question: Can price rise from 100 while the yield stays 10% if F remains 110?
graph.answer: No; a larger purchase cost reduces the return on that cost.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: The zero-yield line locates price equal to payoff.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: All points lie on the same fixed-payoff relation.

increase.title: Create excess cash holdings
increase.why: At the prevailing rate people hold more money than desired.
increase.question: Can all buyers collectively reduce aggregate M merely by buying bonds?
increase.answer: No; they transfer it to sellers.

increase.title: Buy other assets
increase.why: Bond buying raises prices; the seller receives the cash, so private trading does not destroy aggregate M.

increase.title: Lower opportunity cost
increase.why: Money becomes more attractive relative to bonds; at fixed expected inflation real r also falls.

decrease.title: Create excess desired cash
decrease.why: At the prevailing rate people want more money than the available stock.
decrease.question: What happens to the yield when a fixed-payoff bond is sold at a lower price?
decrease.answer: It rises because the same payoff is bought more cheaply.

decrease.title: Sell bonds
decrease.why: Selling pressure lowers bond prices as people seek cash.

decrease.title: Raise opportunity cost
decrease.why: The higher yield discourages money holding until desired and supplied balances match.

edge.title: Reach the simplified boundary
edge.why: Money and short bonds can become equal-return alternatives.
edge.question: Does the inverse formula isolate the cause of every observed price change?
edge.answer: No; payoff and risk must be held fixed for that interpretation.

edge.title: Redo the cash adjustment
edge.why: On a liquidity-trap branch, additional cash may be willingly held without further yield decline.

edge.title: Check the fixed-payoff premise
edge.why: If F or risk changes, a different payoff relation must be evaluated rather than attributing everything to rates.

lm-derivation.goal: Trace LM while keeping real money supply fixed.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
interest sensitivity of desired real money balances; written l_r in Lecture 6

assumptions: Illustration L=Y−10 r and R=50, with expected inflation fixed at zero.
Money demand rises with Y and falls with nominal opportunity cost.

derive.title: Choose one output
derive.why: Hold M, P and money-demand parameters fixed.

derive.title: Impose asset equilibrium
derive.why: The desired stock must equal available real balances.

derive.title: Find the clearing rate
derive.why: At this rate the portfolio choices match the stock.
derive.question: At Y=110 and the old r=5, is desired money above or below 50?

derive.title: Repeat over output levels
derive.why: Higher transactions demand requires a higher rate, producing upward LM.

graph.title: Draw money demand at Y=100
graph.why: Use desired real balances horizontally and r vertically. Expected inflation and the nominal stock/price ratio are held fixed.
graph.question: Can final demanded balances rise if supply stays exactly 50?
graph.answer: No. The rate adjusts until final demand equals the same real stock.

graph.title: Add the fixed real stock
graph.why: At supply 50, the Y=100 demand schedule clears at r=5.

graph.title: Repeat at higher output
graph.why: At Y=110, transactions demand is higher at every given r. The rate rises to 6 so desired balances still equal 50.

graph.title: Repeat independently at lower output
graph.why: At Y=90, money demand is lower at each given rate. The rate falls to 4, restoring desired holdings to the unchanged supply of 50.

graph.title: Transfer output–rate pairs
graph.why: Replace the horizontal money-stock axis with output Y. Transfer (90,4), (100,5) and (110,6); the equal stock of 50 is a maintained parameter, not their new horizontal coordinate.
graph.question: Why do these LM points have different Y even though each source equilibrium has 50 real balances?
graph.answer: The new horizontal axis measures the output level used to construct each demand schedule, not the resulting money stock.

graph.title: Connect the money-equilibrium locus
graph.why: Solving 50=Y−10r for every output gives r=0.1Y−5. This upward LM contains all transferred pairs with M/P and money-demand behavior unchanged.

increase.title: Increase transactions
increase.why: Desired money rises by ten at every given rate.
increase.question: Which rises: demand at each given r, or final equilibrium balances?
increase.answer: The demand schedule rises; final balances remain 50.

increase.title: Observe the initial shortage
increase.why: People sell bonds to obtain cash; lower bond prices raise yields.

increase.title: Clear the asset market
increase.why: Higher opportunity cost offsets the transaction effect; final L remains 50.

increase.title: Transfer to the unchanged LM
increase.why: Use output 110 as the horizontal coordinate and the newly computed rate 6 as the vertical coordinate. Higher Y traces the original LM; it does not change the fixed real stock.

decrease.title: Reduce transactions
decrease.why: Desired money falls by ten at each fixed rate.
decrease.question: Why must r fall rather than remain at five?
decrease.answer: At five, desired holdings are too small; a lower return on bonds restores demand for cash.

decrease.title: Identify unwanted holdings
decrease.why: Bond purchases raise their prices and lower yields.

decrease.title: Restore willingness to hold cash
decrease.why: The lower opportunity cost increases desired holdings back to 50.

decrease.title: Transfer to the unchanged LM
decrease.why: Use output 90 as the horizontal coordinate and the newly computed rate 4 as the vertical coordinate. Lower Y traces the original LM; it does not change the fixed real stock.

edge.title: Remove rate sensitivity at fixed supply
edge.why: Keep R=50 and the same goods relation, but set h=0 in L=Y−hr. The rate can no longer offset income-driven demand for money.
edge.question: Which adjustment mechanism fails when h becomes zero?
edge.answer: Changing r no longer changes desired money balances.

edge.title: Redo money balance without division
edge.why: Money equilibrium directly fixes Y=50. This keeps the same real stock used in the regular LM derivation.

edge.title: Use goods balance to find the rate
edge.why: At Y=50, unchanged IS gives r=10. The new LM is vertical at 50, while the original h=10 intersection was Y=100 and r=5.

lm-algebra.goal: Keep nominal opportunity cost in a real-rate diagram.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
income sensitivity of money demand; written l_Y in Lecture 6
interest sensitivity of money demand; written l_r in Lecture 6
expected inflation in the same units as r

assumptions: L=l₀+k Y−h(r+πᵉ), k>0, h>0; i≈r+πᵉ is the course approximation.
The linear line applies only where the resulting rate is feasible.

derive.title: Use nominal opportunity cost
derive.why: The financial return forgone by holding money is nominal.

derive.title: Equate real stocks
derive.why: Use M/P rather than M in a real-demand equation.

derive.title: Collect r
derive.why: Expected inflation enters with a negative sign.
derive.question: What coefficient remains on πᵉ after dividing by h?
derive.answer: −1; h cancels.

derive.title: Read the line
derive.why: The slope is k/h; higher expected inflation lowers the fixed-Y real clearing rate.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: With l₀=0, k=1, h=10, πᵉ=0, R=50, draw r=0.1 Y−5.
graph.question: Must a one-point πᵉ rise lower the joint-equilibrium r exactly one point?
graph.answer: No; the induced output change affects money demand too.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add IS only when solving the joint equilibrium.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: A change at fixed Y differs from the final change after Y adjusts.

increase.title: Raise expected inflation
increase.why: At fixed Y, r, nominal opportunity cost rises and desired money falls ten.
increase.question: At fixed Y alone, how far does clearing r fall?
increase.answer: Exactly one point under the stated linear approximation.

increase.title: Shift the real-rate intercept
increase.why: At each output, the real rate required for money-market clearing is one point lower; actual real balances remain 50.

increase.title: Resolve both markets
increase.why: Higher Y offsets part of the direct one-point real-rate reduction.

decrease.title: Lower expected inflation
decrease.why: At fixed r, nominal return falls and desired money rises.
decrease.question: Did M/P mechanically fall in this expectation experiment?
decrease.answer: No; the demand side changed through i.

decrease.title: Raise the intercept
decrease.why: At every Y, a higher real rate restores the nominal opportunity cost.

decrease.title: Reconcile expenditure
decrease.why: The joint rate increase is half a point because output also falls.

edge.title: Impose the bound
edge.why: Switch explicitly to the separate trap calibration: IS r=8−0.1Y, initial R=100 and πᵉ=0. The unconstrained line cannot be extended below the maintained floor.
edge.question: At i=0 with expected deflation of two percent, what is approximate r?
edge.answer: Positive two percent, because r≈i−πᵉ.

edge.title: Recompute the floor
edge.why: A nominal zero bound allows a negative real rate.

edge.title: Select the feasible branch
edge.why: Use the flat branch only when balances are sufficient; otherwise use the upward segment.

lm-shifts.goal: Separate real-supply changes from money-demand shifts.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
For each fixed Y, diagnose the imbalance before allowing r to move.

derive.title: Compute the real stock
derive.why: Prices can offset a nominal money change; compute the ratio.

derive.title: Freeze the old coordinates
derive.why: Compare available balances with desired money at the old Y, r.

derive.title: Find the corrective rate
derive.why: Excess supply needs a lower rate; excess demand needs a higher one.
derive.question: At Y=100, which r clears L=Y−10 r when R rises to 60?

derive.title: Move every fixed-Y pair
derive.why: A lower clearing rate at every Y shifts LM down/right; an income change alone would trace LM.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Hold Y=100 and its demand curve fixed.
graph.question: Is the change caused by moving along LM as Y rises?
graph.answer: No; real supply, an exogenous determinant, changed.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Raise real supply from 50 to 60.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The lower clearing rate represents LM shifting at a common output.

increase.title: Increase supply or reduce demand
increase.why: Higher M or lower P raises R. Higher πᵉ, lower l₀ or lower wealth-related cash demand reduces desired balances.
increase.question: Do all downward LM shifts mean real supply increased?
increase.answer: No; money demand can fall while supply stays fixed.

increase.title: Keep channels distinct
increase.why: Only the first two directly change M/P; the remaining changes shift demand.

increase.title: Resolve a supply example
increase.why: The unchanged IS turns lower rates into higher expenditure.

decrease.title: Reduce supply or raise demand
decrease.why: Lower M or higher P lowers R. Lower πᵉ, higher l₀ or higher wealth-related cash demand raises demand.
decrease.question: Does wealth necessarily raise Y through its portfolio channel?
decrease.answer: No; higher money demand shifts LM up and lowers Y at unchanged IS.

decrease.title: Trace the shortage
decrease.why: Asset selling raises yields until holding money becomes less attractive.

decrease.title: Read the supply example
decrease.why: The higher rate lowers interest-sensitive spending on IS.

edge.title: Scale both nominal variables
edge.why: Both change by the same factor 1.2.
edge.question: Do two twenty-percent changes add into forty-percent real growth?
edge.answer: No; M/P is a ratio and stays unchanged.

edge.title: Recalculate the ratio
edge.why: Equal proportional changes cancel exactly in real balances.

edge.title: Keep the curve fixed
edge.why: With all demand determinants unchanged, LM has the same intercept and slope.

equilibrium-algebra.goal: Solve labor, goods and money in sequence, then verify their common solution.
assumptions: This walk uses Tutorial 9: F(N)=15 N−0.5 N², Ns=−5+3 w, C=10+0.7 Y, I=30−200 r, L=10+Y−200 r.
Prices and wages are perfectly flexible; the illustration is distinct from the other walks’ rate units.

derive.title: Clear the labor market
derive.why: Substitute the firm’s MPN condition into labor supply: N=40−3 N, giving N=10, w=5.

derive.title: Produce potential output
derive.why: Use the actual production function, not the marginal product, to obtain total output.

derive.title: Derive goods equilibrium
derive.why: Collect terms to obtain r=0.2−0.0015 Y.

derive.title: Derive asset equilibrium
derive.why: Solve r=(10+Y−M/P)/200; P remains an unknown in full equilibrium.

derive.title: Determine the real allocation
derive.why: Then C=80 and I=20, which sum to Y with G=0.
derive.question: At this Y and r, how many real balances are desired?

derive.title: Solve the price level
derive.why: The nominal stock divided by desired real balances determines P.

derive.title: Derive the matching AD curve
derive.why: Substituting IS into money demand gives P=M/(1.3 Y−30), confirming the same equilibrium.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Use decimal r vertically; draw the derived IS.
graph.question: Why should FE be computed independently before checking this intersection?
graph.answer: It comes from labor and production, not from assuming the goods–asset output is potential.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: At P=2, M/P=100 gives the plotted LM.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Both intersect at Y=100, r=0.05, exactly on the independently calculated FE.

increase.title: Double nominal money
increase.why: Labor and goods equations are unchanged, so Y=100 and r=0.05 remain fixed.
increase.question: Does doubling M double the real balance people want at full equilibrium?
increase.answer: No; desired L stays 100, so P doubles instead.

increase.title: Recompute desired real balances
increase.why: No real determinant or expectation changes.

increase.title: Scale the price level
increase.why: Flexible prices adjust immediately; C, I, N and w stay at their previous real values.

decrease.title: Halve nominal money
decrease.why: The real labor and spending problems are unchanged.
decrease.question: What would go wrong with keeping P=2 after this contraction?
decrease.answer: Real balances would be 50 rather than the 100 required by the unchanged real equilibrium.

decrease.title: Keep the real requirement
decrease.why: The same real allocation needs the same desired balances.

decrease.title: Find the lower nominal price
decrease.why: A lower price level restores real money supply to 100 without reducing capacity.

edge.title: Check existence before accepting algebra
edge.why: With positive M, full equilibrium needs positive desired L.
edge.question: Does an IS–FE intersection guarantee a positive-price full equilibrium?
edge.answer: No; the money-market condition and its domain must also hold.

edge.title: Reject an inadmissible candidate
edge.why: A negative general price level lies outside the model’s economic domain.
edge.math: If L=−20 and M=100, formal P=−5

edge.title: Revisit assumptions or parameters
edge.why: Do not repair the result by taking an absolute value; that changes the model. Check the specification and feasible rates.

ad-derivation.goal: Construct AD from a sequence of price-indexed IS–LM equilibria.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
income sensitivity of money demand; written l_Y in Lecture 6
rate sensitivity of money demand; written l_r in Lecture 6

assumptions: General IS r=a−b Y and L=l₀+k Y−h(r+πᵉ), with k+hb>0.
Numerical plots use a 15, b 0.1, k 1, h 10, l₀ 0, πᵉ 0, M 100.

derive.title: Choose a price level
derive.why: This fixes real money supply for one IS–LM diagram.

derive.title: Substitute the goods rate
derive.why: Use IS to remove r while preserving both equilibrium conditions.

derive.title: Collect the output terms
derive.why: The money-demand income effect and the goods-induced rate effect both enter the coefficient.
derive.question: For the numerical calibration, what is the equation in Y and P?

derive.title: Plot the price–output pairs
derive.why: Each point clears goods and assets at that P; the denominator must be positive.

derive.title: Explain the slope
derive.why: Higher P reduces real balances, raises r and lowers interest-sensitive spending.

graph.title: Start from the unchanged goods locus
graph.why: In the source diagram use Y horizontally and r vertically. Hold IS, nominal M=100 and money-demand behavior fixed throughout the price experiments.
graph.question: Does choosing another price level shift IS in this derivation?
graph.answer: No. It changes real money supply and LM; the goods-expenditure relation remains fixed.

graph.title: Solve the first price experiment
graph.why: Choose P=2, giving R=100/2=50. Add the corresponding LM and solve both markets: Y=100, r=5. Record the price–output pair (100,2).

graph.title: Solve a higher-price experiment
graph.why: Choose P=2.5. Real balances fall to 40, shifting LM up. The new goods–money intersection is Y=95 and r=5.5, so record (95,2.5).

graph.title: Solve a lower-price experiment
graph.why: Choose P=10/7. Real balances rise to 70, shifting LM down. Both markets now clear at Y=110 and r=4, so record (110,10/7).

graph.title: Transfer the price–output pairs
graph.why: Change the vertical axis from r to P. Plot the price chosen for each experiment against the output that its IS–LM intersection produced. The three points are (95,2.5), (100,2) and (110,10/7).
graph.question: For the higher-price experiment, is the new vertical coordinate 5.5 or 2.5?
graph.answer: 2.5. The rate 5.5 belongs to the source IS–LM diagram; AD plots the price level.

graph.title: Connect the derived AD locus
graph.why: Repeating the experiment for every feasible positive P gives M/P=2Y−150. Join the transferred pairs using P=100/(2Y−150), rather than drawing a new AD for each price.

increase.title: Raise only the price level
increase.why: With M 100, real balances fall 50→40.
increase.question: Should a new AD curve be drawn for this price change alone?
increase.answer: No; the new point belongs on the original curve.

increase.title: Resolve IS–LM
increase.why: The higher rate reduces desired private expenditure.

increase.title: Move along the existing curve
increase.why: The point moves up/left to Y 95, P 2.5; autonomous demand is unchanged.

decrease.title: Lower only P
decrease.why: Real supply rises 50→70 with unchanged M.
decrease.question: Why does the fall in P support demand without changing M?
decrease.answer: It increases the purchasing power M/P of the existing nominal stock.

decrease.title: Resolve both markets
decrease.why: The lower opportunity cost supports consumption and investment.

decrease.title: Locate the new point
decrease.why: The economy moves down/right along AD to Y 110, P 10/7.

edge.title: Find the transmission failure
edge.why: Switch explicitly to the separate trap calibration: IS r=8−0.1Y, initial R=100 and πᵉ=0. On the flat branch, additional real balances are willingly held without lowering the nominal rate.
edge.question: Which link in the standard downward-AD story can fail in a trap?
edge.answer: More real balances need not lower the rate further.

edge.title: Redo the price experiment
edge.why: Hold nominal M=100 fixed in this separate trap experiment. Lowering P from 1 to 5/6 raises real balances from 100 to 120; both flat branches still intersect the same IS at Y=80 and r=0.

edge.title: Limit the normal slope argument
edge.why: The ordinary AD derivation assumed a finite money-demand rate sensitivity and an unconstrained clearing rate; use the piecewise model instead.

ad-shifts.goal: Ask what changes equilibrium output at a common price.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
money-demand rate sensitivity; written l_r in Lecture 6
money-demand income sensitivity; written l_Y in Lecture 6

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
Hold P fixed when determining the direction of an AD shift.

derive.title: Freeze the vertical coordinate
derive.why: A shift compares quantities at the same price, unlike moving along AD.

derive.title: Find the underlying market shift
derive.why: IS may change through spending; LM may change through real supply or desired money.

derive.title: Solve the new intersection
derive.why: Positive changes in the numerator raise output at that price.
derive.question: What happens if a rises while the remaining terms stay fixed?
derive.answer: Y rises at every P, so AD shifts right.

derive.title: Repeat for every price
derive.why: A consistently larger quantity at common prices defines a rightward shift, not an isolated movement.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: First show baseline AD.
graph.question: Why compare the two AD curves on a horizontal price line?
graph.answer: It holds the curve’s vertical coordinate fixed and isolates an exogenous demand change.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Hold P=2 as the common comparison line.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The IS-intercept increase from 15 to 17 raises output 100→110 at that P.

increase.title: Increase autonomous demand or liquidity
increase.why: Higher G, C, future income or MPK, lower capital tax, or a non-Ricardian tax cut can shift IS right; more M or lower money demand can shift LM right.
increase.question: Are a fiscal increase and a money increase identical in their rate effects?
increase.answer: No; fiscal expansion raises r while money expansion lowers r in the regular model.

increase.title: Check at the old price
increase.why: An a increase to 17 gives Y 110; M rising to 120 gives Y 105 in the separate scenarios.

increase.title: Move the entire AD relation
increase.why: Each experiment raises quantity at every feasible fixed P, so AD shifts right.

decrease.title: Reduce demand or liquidity
decrease.why: Lower autonomous spending/future returns, higher capital tax, a contractionary tax change, less M or higher money demand can reduce desired output.
decrease.question: Can higher P itself be listed as an AD shifter here?
decrease.answer: No; it is the coordinate used to trace AD.

decrease.title: Compare at P=2
decrease.why: Each is a separate fixed-price experiment against the same baseline.

decrease.title: Shift AD left
decrease.why: The reduced quantity is present at every common price, rather than being caused by a rise in P.

edge.title: Allow both wealth channels
edge.why: More wealth raises consumption and can also raise desired money holdings.
edge.question: If h=10, Δ a=2 and Δ l₀=20, what is Δ Y?
edge.answer: Zero. Both curves move upward enough to raise r at unchanged Y.

edge.title: Compute the net output effect
edge.why: The IS contribution is positive; the portfolio-demand contribution is negative.

edge.title: Include the zero case
edge.why: Output rises if h Δ a>Δ l₀, falls if smaller and stays fixed at equality. Do not assume an unambiguous AD shift.

sras-lras.goal: Choose a supply curve by its price-adjustment assumption.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
price level preset for the horizontal short-run illustration
expected price level in the alternative misperceptions supply relation
positive output response to an unexpected price-level change in the alternative supply relation

assumptions: The Lecture 6 short run holds P fixed and lets firms meet demand locally.
Full adjustment returns output to a fixed Y* unless a separate supply shock changes it.

derive.title: State the short-run restriction
derive.why: Fixing price leaves quantity to respond to demand; it does not fix output.

derive.title: Construct short-run supply
derive.why: At that one price, the illustrative firms meet feasible orders, producing horizontal SRAS.

derive.title: State the long-run restriction
derive.why: Labor and production determine the profit-maximizing capacity under full adjustment.
derive.question: Does vertical LRAS mean Y* can never change?
derive.answer: No; technology, capital or labor conditions can shift it.

derive.title: Select the intersection
derive.why: Short-run output comes from AD–SRAS; the full-adjustment allocation comes from AD–LRAS.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw horizontal SRAS at P 2, separating price rigidity from capacity.
graph.question: Which curve determines the long-run quantity?
graph.answer: Vertical LRAS at the independently determined potential.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add vertical LRAS at Y 100, which comes from the real side.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: With baseline AD all three meet; this coincidence need not survive a demand shock.

increase.title: Raise demand with P preset
increase.why: The monetary AD shift raises quantity to 105 on the original SRAS.
increase.question: Must the short-run quantity gain be permanent?
increase.answer: No; with fixed capacity the eventual change is in P.

increase.title: Read the gap
increase.why: Output exceeds the fixed full-employment benchmark, creating upward price pressure.

increase.title: Let prices adjust
increase.why: SRAS moves upward until AD meets LRAS at Y 100.

decrease.title: Reduce demand at the preset price
decrease.why: The lower AD curve gives Y 95 while P stays 2.
decrease.question: Why does price decline help output recover?
decrease.answer: It raises M/P and supports spending through the asset market.

decrease.title: Identify excess capacity
decrease.why: The negative output gap exerts downward price pressure.

decrease.title: Restore the full-employment quantity
decrease.why: Lower prices raise real balances until AD again supports Y 100.

edge.title: Change the rigidity assumption
edge.why: The misperceptions model has flexible prices but imperfect aggregate-price information.
edge.question: Can one use horizontal SRAS and the misperceptions equation as the same short-run assumption?
edge.answer: No; they represent different mechanisms.

edge.title: Redo short-run supply
edge.why: Output responds to a price surprise, producing upward rather than horizontal SRAS.

edge.title: Keep model boundaries explicit
edge.why: Full-information Classical flexibility gives immediate real equilibrium; neither alternative should be imposed on the fixed-price diagram silently.
