money-path.goal: Follow a money-level change from bond portfolios through output to final prices.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
Start in full equilibrium at Y*=100; real determinants and expected inflation remain fixed.
The initial price is sticky, then fully adjusts; a liquidity trap is treated separately.

derive.title: Implement the operation
derive.why: An open-market purchase creates money while buying existing government bonds; a sale withdraws money.

derive.title: Change real balances at preset P
derive.why: With P fixed, nominal money changes the real stock one-for-one.

derive.title: Rebalance portfolios
derive.why: Excess balances induce bond buying and lower rates; insufficient balances induce selling and higher rates.
derive.question: Before prices move, does M↑ shift IS or LM directly?
derive.answer: LM; it changes asset-market equilibrium.

derive.title: Change desired expenditure
derive.why: Lower r stimulates C and I; higher r restrains them, moving actual Y off fixed potential.

derive.title: Adjust prices until the gap closes
derive.why: Prices rise when output exceeds potential and fall when output is below potential, reversing the initial real-balance change.

derive.title: Check neutrality
derive.why: With the same final real allocation and money-demand determinants, desired real balances return to their original level.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw unchanged IS and FE before introducing the monetary side.
graph.question: Which curve must eventually move to restore FE if M stays higher?
graph.answer: LM moves back as P rises and real balances fall.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: At P 2, baseline LM gives the full-equilibrium point.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Higher M shifts LM down; the short-run intersection is right of FE.

increase.title: Add money before prices adjust
increase.why: The regular IS–LM equilibrium becomes Y 105, r 4.5; C=64 and I=31.
increase.question: Does the final real money stock remain 60?
increase.answer: No; the price adjustment returns it to 50.

increase.title: Recognize excess demand
increase.why: Production temporarily exceeds the fixed capacity benchmark.

increase.title: Complete the adjustment
increase.why: Real balances return to 50 and Y 100, r 5, C 60, I 30. Nominal W rises 20% if real w is unchanged.

decrease.title: Withdraw money at old P
decrease.why: The short-run rate rises to 5.5 and Y falls to 95; C=56, I=29.
decrease.question: Is a 20% price fall the inverse of a previous 20% rise?
decrease.answer: No; a rise then fall by 20% multiplies the level by 1.2×0.8=0.96.

decrease.title: Diagnose the demand shortfall
decrease.why: There is excess capacity at the preset price.

decrease.title: Let prices fall
decrease.why: Restored real balances bring all stated real variables back to their original values.

edge.title: Remove the rate-response link
edge.why: Switch explicitly to the separate trap calibration: IS r=8−0.1Y, initial R=100 and πᵉ=0. On the flat LM branch, additional balances are voluntarily held.
edge.question: Which step of the normal monetary chain fails in this boundary case?
edge.answer: More real balances no longer lower the nominal rate.

edge.title: Redo the short-run result
edge.why: Without a rate decrease, ordinary interest-sensitive spending need not rise.

edge.title: Limit the original claim
edge.why: The standard transition requires an operative rate channel; the trap can persist until another determinant moves or balances leave its feasible region.

fiscal-path.goal: Trace fiscal demand at fixed capacity and distinguish composition from total output.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
Here FE is fixed and the new G remains in place during price adjustment.
Illustration C=25+0.5 Y−3 r, I=40−2 r, G=10 initially; the fiscal experiment is a separate G±10 change.

derive.title: Change purchases at fixed coordinates
derive.why: Higher G lowers saving before Y or r changes; lower G raises saving.

derive.title: Derive the new goods locus
derive.why: Total spending rate sensitivity is five in this calibration.

derive.title: Solve against unchanged LM
derive.why: The first response uses the old P and fixed real supply.
derive.question: For G 10→20, which IS intercept results?
derive.answer: a rises from 15 to 17.

derive.title: Compare with FE
derive.why: Above-capacity output raises P, reducing real balances; below-capacity output lowers P.

derive.title: Use the final resource identity
derive.why: Full crowding out concerns total private spending, not investment alone.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start from goods and asset equilibrium at Y 100, r 5.
graph.question: Can a rise in r itself shift IS back?
graph.answer: No; r changes location along the new IS.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Shift IS up for higher G while initial LM stays fixed.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The short-run point is above FE; the final higher-P LM meets new IS on FE.

increase.title: Raise government demand
increase.why: At fixed P, Y rises 100→110 and r rises 5→6.
increase.question: Must short-run consumption fall after G rises?
increase.answer: No; its income and interest effects oppose. Here it rises by 2.

increase.title: Separate consumption and investment
increase.why: The income effect raises C here despite the rate restraint. Total private spending happens to remain 90 in this calibration.

increase.title: Complete fixed-FE adjustment
increase.why: Final C 54, I 26 sum to 80, exactly 10 less than before.

decrease.title: Reduce purchases
decrease.why: At preset P, Y 90 and r 4 give C 58 and I 32.
decrease.question: At fixed final Y, can C+I remain unchanged when G falls ten?
decrease.answer: No; it must rise ten to satisfy the resource identity.

decrease.title: Identify the negative gap
decrease.why: Lower P raises real balances and supports output recovery.

decrease.title: Find the full-adjustment composition
decrease.why: C 66 and I 34 replace the 10 units of purchases withdrawn.

edge.title: Relax fixed FE
edge.why: Tax-financed G can reduce private wealth and normal leisure in the competitive Classical labor model.
edge.question: Which premise of one-for-one long-run crowding out failed?
edge.answer: Potential output was no longer fixed.

edge.title: Redo labor equilibrium
edge.why: Labor supply rises, employment rises and potential output can rise as well.

edge.title: Use the correct identity
edge.why: If output rises 4 after G rises 10, private spending falls 6, not 10.

lm-slope.goal: Derive policy multipliers before comparing flatter and steeper LM.

symbols.meaning: intercept of the solved goods equation Y=A−Br
positive goods spending sensitivity to r
money-demand income sensitivity; written l_Y in Lecture 6
money-demand interest sensitivity; written l_r in Lecture 6

assumptions: Goods equilibrium Y=A−Br, money equilibrium R=k Y−hr, B, k, h>0.
All comparisons hold price and the other stated behavioral coefficients fixed; changing A is not necessarily a unit change in G.

derive.title: Read the LM slope
derive.why: More interest sensitivity means a smaller rate increase offsets added transactions demand.

derive.title: Remove r using goods equilibrium
derive.why: The units of B depend on the plotted rate units.

derive.title: Substitute into money equilibrium
derive.why: Multiply by B before collecting Y.

derive.title: Collect feedbacks
derive.why: Both the goods and money responses determine the denominator.
derive.question: What are the two output multipliers?
derive.answer: ∂Y/∂A=h/(h+k B), and ∂Y/∂R=B/(h+k B).

derive.title: Interpret the derivatives
derive.why: Higher h increases the demand-intercept multiplier but reduces the real-balance multiplier.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Compare money equations with h 5 and h 20, holding k 1, R 50 fixed.
graph.question: Does a flatter curve by itself identify which parameter changed?
graph.answer: No; k or h could have changed, with different policy implications.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: The h 20 curve is flatter; its baseline intersection also differs because only h changed.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Compare policy changes within each economy, rather than comparing their raw output levels.

increase.title: Increase h in the comparison
increase.why: Money demand responds more to rates, so less rate movement is needed for each transactions change.
increase.question: Which economy has the larger output change for the identical intercept increase?
increase.answer: The h 20 economy, comparing its own before and after equilibria.

increase.title: Apply the same fiscal-type shift
increase.why: Output rises 6⅔ with h 5 and 13⅓ with h 20.

increase.title: Explain greater fiscal effectiveness
increase.why: The higher-h economy has less rate crowding out for the same autonomous-demand shock.

decrease.title: Reduce h in the comparison
decrease.why: Desired money becomes less responsive to interest.
decrease.question: Does smaller h weaken the output response to money in this model?
decrease.answer: No; B/(h+k B) increases as h falls.

decrease.title: Inject the same real balances
decrease.why: Output rises 3⅓ with h 20 but 6⅔ with h 5.

decrease.title: Explain stronger money transmission
decrease.why: A given balance injection needs a larger rate adjustment when money demand is less interest-sensitive.

edge.title: Change a different parameter
edge.why: LM also becomes flatter because k/h falls.
edge.question: Why is “flatter LM means weaker money policy” incomplete?
edge.answer: It only holds for a flatter LM caused by higher h with other parameters fixed.

edge.title: Redo the multiplier
edge.why: With B=10 and h=20, lowering k from 1 to 0.5 raises the monetary multiplier from 10/30 to 10/25. Solving Y=150−10 r with 50=0.5 Y−20 r gives Y=140 and r=1.

edge.title: Reject a slope-only rule
edge.why: Raising h flattens LM but lowers that multiplier; lowering k flattens it but raises it.

vertical-lm.goal: Solve the zero-interest-sensitivity case without dividing by zero.

symbols.meaning: positive income sensitivity; written l_Y in Lecture 6
interest sensitivity, set to zero; written l_r in Lecture 6
leakage coefficient in the separate goods-boundary example
total interest sensitivity of spending in the separate goods-boundary example
autonomous total spending in the separate goods-boundary example

assumptions: L=l₀+k Y, k>0, fixed price; plotted case l₀ 0, k 1, R 100.
IS slopes down and its clearing rate is feasible.

derive.title: Set the behavioral boundary
derive.why: Interest no longer changes desired money holdings.

derive.title: Use the original equilibrium
derive.why: Do not insert h 0 into a formula that divides by h.

derive.title: Solve output directly
derive.why: Money equilibrium fixes output rather than a rate schedule.
derive.question: With R 100, l₀ 0, k 1, can Y 110 clear money at any r?
derive.answer: No; money demand would be 110 regardless of r.

derive.title: Find r from IS
derive.why: The goods market chooses the compatible rate at the fixed output.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw LM vertically at Y 100 because r is absent from money demand.
graph.question: Is this vertical line FE simply because it is vertical?
graph.answer: No; it is an asset-market restriction, not a labor-capacity restriction.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add downward IS r=15−0.1 Y.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: At the common output the goods rate is 5.

increase.title: Increase goods demand
increase.why: Higher G shifts IS up while real money supply stays fixed.
increase.question: Can fiscal expansion raise Y at fixed R in this limit?
increase.answer: No; it raises r and completely crowds out total private expenditure.

increase.title: Keep money equilibrium
increase.why: No rate change can support a different money-clearing output.

increase.title: Clear goods at that output
increase.why: Private spending falls enough in total to offset the added G.

decrease.title: Reduce real balances
decrease.why: A smaller stock supports a smaller transactions level.
decrease.question: Is monetary policy ineffective just because money demand ignores r?
decrease.answer: No; R directly determines Y in this limit.

decrease.title: Recompute the vertical line
decrease.why: LM shifts left instead of becoming horizontal.

decrease.title: Use the unchanged IS
decrease.why: Output falls and the rate rises after the monetary contraction.

edge.title: Make goods demand rate-insensitive too
edge.why: In this separate double-boundary example, money balance fixes Y=100 while goods balance fixes Y=150. Both restrictions are vertical.
edge.question: Can any interest rate reconcile these two different fixed output requirements?
edge.answer: No. Parallel vertical restrictions at different output levels have no common point.

edge.title: Check existence before solving a rate
edge.why: Every point on the goods locus violates money balance, and every point on the money locus violates goods balance. There is no fixed-price equilibrium in the stated equations.

edge.title: Compare a coincident case separately
edge.why: In the separate coincident case, set the goods intercept to A₀=50 with D=0.5 and H=0. Both restrictions then fix Y=100. Rates 3 and 8 are examples of the multiple compatible rates; neither is uniquely selected by these equations.

liquidity-trap.goal: Construct the flat branch and determine when an economy leaves it.

symbols.meaning: lowest real rate implied by the maintained nominal bound

assumptions: Simplified nominal bound i≥0 and Fisher approximation i≈r+πᵉ.
Illustration IS r=8−0.1 Y; LM r=max(−πᵉ, (Y−R)/10−πᵉ), baseline R 100, πᵉ 0.

derive.title: Find the return boundary
derive.why: Money and short bonds have the same financial return in the simplified exercise.

derive.title: Translate to the real rate
derive.why: The zero restriction applies to nominal, not necessarily real, interest.

derive.title: Specify sufficient liquidity
derive.why: On the flat branch, people willingly hold balances beyond the transaction component.
derive.question: With πᵉ 0 and IS r=8−0.1 Y, what Y is consistent with the floor?
derive.answer: Y 80 at r 0; R 100 is sufficient to keep that point on the flat branch.

derive.title: Join the normal region
derive.why: Once transactions absorb the available stock, LM becomes upward sloping; the floor is not a global solution for every supply.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw the horizontal branch to Y 100 and then the upward branch.
graph.question: Would a point to the right of Y 100 still have r 0 on this LM?
graph.answer: No; it lies on the upward branch.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add the demand relation with its rate response.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The intersection Y 80, r 0 lies on the flat segment, not beyond the kink.

increase.title: Increase money while trapped
increase.why: The flat branch extends but its rate remains zero, so the original IS still selects Y 80.
increase.question: Why can fiscal expansion work when extra money alone does not?
increase.answer: It shifts expenditure directly rather than relying on a further rate decline.

increase.title: Increase goods demand instead
increase.why: The IS shift raises output to 100 at the unchanged rate.

increase.title: Check the stopping condition
increase.why: Further demand growth can reach or leave the kink, after which the usual rate crowding out resumes.

decrease.title: Lower demand along the flat branch
decrease.why: Output falls 80→60 while the nominal rate remains zero.
decrease.question: Does every money cut leave Y unchanged in a trap?
decrease.answer: No; a large enough cut can exhaust the excess balances and move to the upward segment.

decrease.title: Withdraw a small amount of money
decrease.why: Y 80 is still on the flat branch, so this cut need not change output.

decrease.title: Withdraw enough to leave the trap
decrease.why: The joint solution becomes Y 70, r 1; the contraction now raises rates and lowers demand.

edge.title: Change expected inflation
edge.why: The nominal floor stays zero but the real floor falls to −2.
edge.question: At i 0, is negative expected inflation expansionary through the real-rate channel?
edge.answer: No; it raises r=i−πᵉ.

edge.title: Redo goods demand at the floor
edge.why: The lower real rate supports Y 100, which is still feasible at the new kink.

edge.title: Check the deflation case separately
edge.why: Expected deflation raises the real borrowing cost even though i=0. At the higher floor, unchanged goods demand supports only Y=60, independently recomputed from the same IS.

rbc-shocks.goal: Identify a real shock and specify how the model transmits it.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: RBC benchmark: competitive optimization, flexible wages/prices and market clearing.
The simple productivity comparison holds future income/MPK effects on IS aside and assumes upward labor supply.

derive.title: Name the disturbance
derive.why: A theory needs both a source of shocks and a propagation mechanism; “output fell” is an outcome, not a shock.

derive.title: Classify the direct market
derive.why: Technology, energy, management, labor-force or spending/saving changes can affect real production, FE or IS.

derive.title: Specify adjustment
derive.why: Flexible markets let the labor/production equilibrium change with the real opportunity.
derive.question: Can a recession occur in this model without output falling below potential?
derive.answer: Yes; potential itself can fall after an adverse productivity shock.

derive.title: Separate nominal disturbances
derive.why: A pure money-supply or money-demand disturbance starts in the asset market; it need not change productive capacity.

graph.title: Identify a real shock
graph.why: Begin with a named real disturbance rather than an observed output movement.
graph.question: Does naming a shock tell us the entire response without a propagation model?
graph.answer: No; market assumptions and behavioral equations determine transmission.

graph.title: Trace labor and capacity
graph.why: Follow labor and production to the new capacity.

graph.title: Complete the market response
graph.why: Only then use the goods and asset equations to complete the equilibrium.

increase.title: Improve current production
increase.why: A beneficial temporary productivity shock raises output directly and can raise MPN and hiring.
increase.question: Why is the higher Y not necessarily an above-potential boom?
increase.answer: It can equal the newly higher potential Y*=110.

increase.title: Recompute capacity
increase.why: The new FE lies to the right; the exact size is an assumed teaching scenario.

increase.title: Clear remaining markets
increase.why: With IS and M unchanged, higher Y and lower r raise desired balances and lower the clearing price.

decrease.title: Reduce productive opportunity
decrease.why: An energy disruption lowers attainable output and, in the lecture case, MPN.
decrease.question: Does lower Y prove that households simply stopped buying enough at unchanged capacity?
decrease.answer: No; that is a different demand-shock explanation.

decrease.title: Find the lower capacity
decrease.why: Lower employment and productivity can both contribute.

decrease.title: Complete equilibrium
decrease.why: The output decline is compatible with full market clearing at the new capacity.

edge.title: Change the scope of the shock
edge.why: A permanent productivity change may alter expected future income and future MPK.
edge.question: Which maintained assumption fails when future MPK changes?
edge.answer: That IS remains unchanged after the shock.

edge.title: Redo the goods-market step
edge.why: Consumption and investment can now shift IS as well as FE.

edge.title: Limit the simple sign chain
edge.why: The fixed-IS temporary-shock result is no longer sufficient; solve all affected markets.

rbc-transmission.goal: Carry a temporary productivity disturbance through every market.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
marginal physical production from one additional unit of labor before multiplying by A

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
Current productivity changes, with capital, future spending/return determinants and expected inflation fixed.
Higher A raises MPN; labor supply has its standard positive slope.

derive.title: Shift labor demand
derive.why: At the old employment, a higher MPN raises marginal hiring profit; lower MPN reduces it.

derive.title: Clear labor and produce
derive.why: The real wage and employment change, and production converts the new labor input into Y*.

derive.title: Use unchanged goods equilibrium
derive.why: A capacity change is a movement along IS, not an assumed direct IS shift.
derive.question: If Y* falls 100→90, which r clears goods?
derive.answer: r rises from 5 to 6.

derive.title: Calculate desired balances
derive.why: Income and rate changes reinforce one another in the temporary productivity experiment.

derive.title: Find the clearing price
derive.why: A smaller desired real stock needs a higher P for fixed nominal M.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Locate original capacity and the goods rate first.
graph.question: Does the adverse shock directly shift LM before P changes?
graph.answer: Not in this isolated exercise; the eventual P response shifts LM.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Use baseline LM to confirm the initial full equilibrium.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: A lower FE picks a higher point on IS; the final endogenous-price LM must pass through it.

increase.title: Raise A and MPN
increase.why: Labor demand shifts right; the competitive w and N* rise.
increase.question: Which money-demand effects reinforce each other after beneficial productivity?
increase.answer: Higher Y raises transaction demand, and lower r raises desired money holding.

increase.title: Use higher potential
increase.why: Higher income supports C and lower r supports both C and I.

increase.title: Clear money
increase.why: Both higher transactions and lower opportunity cost raise desired real balances.

decrease.title: Lower A and MPN
decrease.why: Labor demand shifts left; the competitive real wage and employment fall.
decrease.question: Does a one-time higher price level require permanently higher inflation?
decrease.answer: No; the transition can create temporary inflation without a permanent change in its rate.

decrease.title: Use the reduced potential
decrease.why: Lower income and higher rates reduce desired consumption; higher rates reduce investment.

decrease.title: Restore asset balance
decrease.why: The fixed nominal stock is reconciled with less desired real money by a higher price level.

edge.title: Allow a future-income response
edge.why: If expectations of future output change, consumption can shift today.
edge.question: Why is copying the fixed-IS r result unsafe for a permanent productivity shock?
edge.answer: The shock can change future-income and return determinants of IS.

edge.title: Allow an investment-return response
edge.why: Changed future MPK shifts desired investment at each rate.

edge.title: Redo the full intersection
edge.why: The two alternative IS curves show possible demand directions; they are not simultaneous shifts or solved endpoints. With FE=90 after the current adverse shock, the direction and size of the future-income/return response determine which new IS applies. Then recompute r and the clearing P.

classical-fiscal.goal: Include the wealth-driven labor response before predicting fiscal prices and rates.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration
money-demand income sensitivity; written l_Y in Lecture 6
money-demand rate sensitivity; written l_r in Lecture 6

assumptions: Competitive labor clearing and normal leisure; G is financed by present or future taxes.
Plot uses the common economy, with G↑ represented by a 15→17 and illustrative Y*100→104.
The lecture higher-P outcome assumes the new IS–old LM intersection is right of the new FE.

derive.title: Trace the financing
derive.why: Households have fewer private lifetime resources, even when the tax arrives later.

derive.title: Apply normal leisure
derive.why: Lower wealth reduces desired leisure and raises labor supplied at each wage.

derive.title: Clear labor
derive.why: Against unchanged labor demand, higher supply lowers w and raises employment; higher employment raises Y*.

derive.title: Shift the goods locus
derive.why: Government purchases also lower national saving at given Y, r, shifting IS up.
derive.question: Must the new IS intersection with old LM lie right of the new FE solely because both shift right?
derive.answer: No; compare their magnitudes. That relative position is an extra condition.

derive.title: Use the relative position
derive.why: Right of new FE means excess demand and P↑; left means the opposite pressure; equality needs no price change.

derive.title: Solve the sign algebra
derive.why: At fixed M, P moves oppositely to L. These formulas show why shift directions alone are insufficient.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start from the original triple intersection.
graph.question: Which comparison determines the sign of price adjustment?
graph.answer: The new IS–old LM output compared with the new potential, not the old potential.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: New IS meets old LM at Y 110, to the right of assumed new FE 104.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Higher P lowers real balances 50→38, moving LM up to the new full equilibrium.

increase.title: Raise purchases and taxes
increase.why: Wealth falls, normal leisure falls, labor supply rises; w falls and N* rises.
increase.question: Does higher output alone tell us whether P rises?
increase.answer: No; higher output raises L while higher r lowers it. Compare both.

increase.title: Shift IS and FE
increase.why: The goods rate becomes r=17−10.4=6.6.

increase.title: Calculate the price
increase.why: Y and r rise, but the rate effect dominates money demand in this particular configuration.

decrease.title: Reduce purchases and taxes
decrease.why: Greater lifetime private resources raise normal leisure and reduce labor supply; competitive w rises and employment falls.
decrease.question: Why is the lower-G FE response different from the fixed-FE Keynesian comparison?
decrease.answer: The competitive wage adjustment lets the wealth-induced labor-supply shift alter employment.

decrease.title: Move both real loci
decrease.why: The new goods rate is r=3.4.

decrease.title: Reconcile money
decrease.why: The lower rate raises money demand enough to dominate the smaller transactions need.

edge.title: Increase the capacity response
edge.why: Keep the same IS intercept increase, but allow a stronger labor/output response.
edge.question: Can G↑ and IS↑ coexist with unchanged or lower P in this comparative-static framework?
edge.answer: Yes, if the FE/output response offsets or outweighs the rate-driven decline in money demand.

edge.title: Recompute instead of assuming
edge.why: At potential 110, P stays 2; at 115, P falls to 100/60 despite higher G.

edge.title: State the conditional conclusion
edge.why: The lecture’s price rise is one configuration. Full crowding-out claims also change because Δ(C+I)=Δ Y−Δ G.

classical-money.goal: Show why flexible prices absorb a pure money-level change immediately.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
Full information, perfectly flexible wages/prices, unchanged real determinants and expected inflation.
This is a one-off money-level experiment, not a permanent money-growth change.

derive.title: Solve the real side first
derive.why: Labor and goods determine the real allocation without using nominal M.

derive.title: Evaluate money demand
derive.why: With the same real allocation and expectations, desired real balances are unchanged.

derive.title: Choose the compatible price
derive.why: P scales with M to preserve that stock.
derive.question: If M rises 20% while L is fixed, by what percentage does P rise?
derive.answer: Exactly 20%.

derive.title: Scale nominal wages too
derive.why: An unchanged real wage requires W to change proportionately with P.

derive.title: Separate timing from the result
derive.why: Full flexibility makes the adjustment immediate; there is no sustained horizontal-SRAS output detour.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw the supply-determined quantity first.
graph.question: Should the rigid-price point Y 105 be treated as an actual sustained Classical equilibrium?
graph.answer: No; price flexibility immediately selects Y 100 at the new price.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Find the baseline price at its AD intersection.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The monetary AD shift changes the vertical intersection on unchanged LRAS.

increase.title: Increase nominal money
increase.why: The real labor and goods solutions remain Y 100, r 5.
increase.question: Does the larger nominal stock imply a larger final real stock?
increase.answer: No; higher P offsets it exactly.

increase.title: Keep desired real balances
increase.why: No real resource or portfolio parameter changes.

increase.title: Adjust nominal units
increase.why: Output, employment, real wage, real rate and real spending are unchanged.

decrease.title: Contract nominal money
decrease.why: The same real allocation still solves labor and goods.
decrease.question: Is real wage unchanged if W is held fixed while P falls 20%?
decrease.answer: No; W must also fall 20% to preserve the ratio.

decrease.title: Compute the clearing price
decrease.why: Lower prices preserve the desired real stock.

decrease.title: Scale nominal wages downward
decrease.why: W falls 20% while W/P remains unchanged.

edge.title: Change the experiment
edge.why: Permanently faster money growth can alter expected ongoing inflation.
edge.question: Does one higher level of M imply permanently accelerating inflation?
edge.answer: No; levels, growth rates and changes in growth are distinct.

edge.title: Redo the opportunity-cost step
edge.why: Changed πᵉ can affect nominal rates and desired real money holdings.

edge.title: Limit proportionality
edge.why: A fixed-L one-off money-level calculation cannot simply be applied to a new inflation-growth regime; specify the other growth and demand determinants.

rational-expectations.goal: Separate informed forecasting from perfect foresight.

symbols.meaning: relevant information available when the forecast is made
actual outcome minus the conditional forecast

assumptions: Rational expectations uses relevant available information intelligently within the model.
Unforeseeable shocks can still occur; the policy-neutrality claim additionally needs the specified flexible-price information framework.

derive.title: Date the information
derive.why: A forecast cannot condition on information that only arrives after the decision.

derive.title: Use the known structure
derive.why: Known relationships and public policy rules belong in the forecast rather than being deliberately ignored.

derive.title: Allow genuine news
derive.why: An unexpected realization can differ from the forecast without implying irrationality.
derive.question: Can an informed forecast be wrong in one realized period?
derive.answer: Yes; rational expectations does not remove uncertainty.

derive.title: Update when patterns are learned
derive.why: A repeated systematic policy component becomes anticipated, shrinking its surprise component.

graph.title: Date the available information
graph.why: Start with the information set, not tomorrow’s realized outcome.
graph.question: Is a public systematic rule equivalent to random news?
graph.answer: No; its predictable component should be incorporated.

graph.title: Include the public rule
graph.why: Add a public policy rule to the forecast calculation.

graph.title: Separate news from learning
graph.why: Unexpected news can create an error; learning changes future forecasts.

increase.title: Increase credible information
increase.why: A credible forthcoming monetary expansion is announced before decisions.
increase.question: Can the same fully learned announcement remain an unanticipated expansion every period?
increase.answer: No; the systematic pattern is now part of the information set.

increase.title: Adjust the price forecast
increase.why: People can raise expected future prices in response to the known rule.

increase.title: Reduce the surprise channel
increase.why: In the flexible-price misperceptions model, matching actual and expected changes removes the mistaken relative-price incentive.

decrease.title: Announce a credible contraction
decrease.why: The forecast can incorporate lower future nominal demand.
decrease.question: Does a falling actual price necessarily mean agents forecast badly?
decrease.answer: No; it may have been forecast correctly.

decrease.title: Lower the expected price path
decrease.why: Actual lower prices need not be below the new expectation.

decrease.title: Keep error and direction separate
decrease.why: A correctly anticipated decline can produce zero forecast error; an unanticipated decline can produce a negative error.

edge.title: Change the friction
edge.why: In a sticky-price model, contracts can be predetermined even when expectations are informed.
edge.question: Which extra premise is needed for the misperceptions anticipated-policy neutrality result?
edge.answer: The appropriate flexible-price model, not rational expectations by itself.

edge.title: Redo the behavior step
edge.why: Correct forecasts do not automatically allow all wages and prices to reset.

edge.title: Limit neutrality
edge.why: Rational expectations alone does not establish that all anticipated policy has no short-run real effect.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

relative-price-signal.goal: Explain why the same nominal observation can imply different real incentives.

symbols.meaning: the producer’s own selling price or nominal wage

assumptions: Producers observe their own nominal return more clearly than the aggregate price index.
A real relative-price improvement, rather than a change in units alone, motivates the stated production response.

derive.title: Identify the reward
derive.why: The producer earns income from the price of their own output; for a worker it is the nominal wage.

derive.title: Deflate by general prices
derive.why: Purchasing power depends on both numerator and denominator.

derive.title: Separate two explanations
derive.why: An own-price rise could be a genuine relative improvement or merely part of general inflation.
derive.question: If both own price and P rise 6%, what happens to their ratio?
derive.answer: It is unchanged:1.06/1.06=1.

derive.title: Introduce incomplete information
derive.why: If the common price rise is initially missed, the producer can mistakenly infer a stronger relative reward and expand.

graph.title: Observe the own price
graph.why: Begin with the directly observed own price.
graph.question: Why is an own-price observation insufficient to identify real reward?
graph.answer: The general price denominator may have moved too.

graph.title: Compare the general price level
graph.why: Add the aggregate index needed to calculate purchasing power.

graph.title: Identify the mistaken signal
graph.why: The information gap separates true relative changes from misperceived ones.

increase.title: Observe a higher own price
increase.why: A producer sees a higher nominal selling price.
increase.question: What missing information creates the expansion incentive?
increase.answer: The producer does not fully recognize the general-price component of the own-price rise.

increase.title: Underestimate general inflation
increase.why: If the aggregate rise is larger than expected, part may be mistaken for a relative-price gain.

increase.title: Increase production temporarily
increase.why: The perceived reward to working rises even though the common nominal movement need not improve true purchasing power.

decrease.title: Observe a lower nominal return
decrease.why: The producer sees their price or wage fall.
decrease.question: Can a proportional general price decline leave true purchasing power unchanged?
decrease.answer: Yes, if the own price and the general index fall in the same proportion.

decrease.title: Underestimate the common decline
decrease.why: If general prices fell unexpectedly too, the producer may perceive a relative loss that is not fully real.

decrease.title: Reduce work and production
decrease.why: The negative perceived relative reward lowers output until information catches up.

edge.title: Remove the information gap
edge.why: Suppose the producer immediately observes a common six-percent price increase.
edge.question: Does full information imply producers ignore every own-price change?
edge.answer: No; they respond to genuine relative-price changes, but not pure common rescaling.

edge.title: Redo the ratio
edge.why: The nominal scaling cancels exactly.

edge.title: Remove the mistaken incentive
edge.why: The misperception channel produces no extra output; a genuine relative change would still matter.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

misperceptions-sras.goal: Build the supply locus from the price-surprise equation.

symbols.meaning: positive output responsiveness to a price surprise

assumptions: Illustration Y*=100, b=20, Pᵉ=2; prices are flexible but aggregate information is imperfect.
P is a price level here, not the log-price variable used later for the Phillips derivation.

derive.title: Separate baseline and surprise
derive.why: The baseline is capacity; the deviation comes from unexpected price information.

derive.title: Locate zero surprise
derive.why: This identifies a point that anchors every given-expectations SRAS.

derive.title: Solve for the graph’s vertical variable
derive.why: With Y horizontal, the slope is 1/b rather than b.
derive.question: What slope results when b=20?
derive.answer: 1/20=0.05 price units per output unit.

derive.title: Hold expectations fixed
derive.why: Changing actual P traces this line; changing Pᵉ shifts it.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Mark potential Y 100 with LRAS first.
graph.question: If Pᵉ changes, do we stay on this same SRAS?
graph.answer: No; the anchor itself moves vertically.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add SRAS through Y 100, Pᵉ 2 with slope 0.05.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The two sides of the anchor represent positive and negative surprises.

increase.title: Raise actual price at fixed expectation
increase.why: The surprise is positive 0.5.
increase.question: Does positive inflation by itself prove a positive surprise?
increase.answer: No; compare actual price with its forecast using a common baseline.

increase.title: Translate into output
increase.why: Producers increase output in response to the perceived relative improvement.

increase.title: Locate the movement
increase.why: The point moves up/right along original SRAS; no expectation shift was assumed.

decrease.title: Lower actual price below expectation
decrease.why: The surprise is −0.5.
decrease.question: If P and Pᵉ both fell 0.5, would the same negative gap follow?
decrease.answer: No; their difference would remain zero.

decrease.title: Apply the same equation with its sign
decrease.why: The perceived relative deterioration reduces output.

decrease.title: Locate the new point
decrease.why: This is down/left on the unchanged curve, below potential.

edge.title: Change the held-fixed determinant
edge.why: The old curve assumed Pᵉ 2 and is no longer the relevant locus.
edge.question: Does raising expected price imply movement up the old SRAS?
edge.answer: No; it shifts the SRAS itself.

edge.title: Rebuild the anchor
edge.why: The entire SRAS shifts up 0.4 at every Y.

edge.title: Separate shape from shift
edge.why: The expected-price change moves the anchor vertically while leaving the slope 1/b unchanged.

edge.title: Remove surprise responsiveness separately
edge.why: Set b=0 in the original output equation instead of dividing by b. Output is Y*=100 at every price, so the surprise-supply locus becomes vertical. This is a separate change from shifting Pᵉ.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

anticipated-policy.goal: Shift demand and expected-price supply together when the policy is fully known.
assumptions: Start at Y 100, P=Pᵉ 2 in the flexible-price misperceptions model.
Policy is fully credible and correctly anticipated; real determinants stay fixed.
The plot uses exact AD P=M/(2 Y−150) and SRAS Y=100+20(P−Pᵉ).

derive.title: Put the announcement in information
derive.why: People know the nominal-demand change before choosing production.

derive.title: Find the new full-equilibrium price
derive.why: At unchanged real outcomes, M±20% requires P±20% in this calibration.

derive.title: Set a consistent expected price
derive.why: A fully anticipated common nominal change is not mistaken for a relative-price gain.
derive.question: For M 120, what expected price is consistent with unchanged Y 100?

derive.title: Shift both loci
derive.why: AD changes with money; SRAS moves with Pᵉ, so their new intersection stays on LRAS.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Locate the original demand and capacity intersection.
graph.question: Would shifting AD alone represent full anticipation?
graph.answer: No; it would incorrectly hold the known price expectation fixed.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add the SRAS consistent with initial expected P 2.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: For the anticipated expansion, both AD and SRAS move to meet at Y 100, P 2.4.

increase.title: Announce and implement M↑
increase.why: The predictable increase changes nominal demand.
increase.question: Must anticipated money leave AD unmoved?
increase.answer: No; AD moves, but expected-price supply moves consistently.

increase.title: Raise expected prices consistently
increase.why: The supply anchor rises before any mistaken relative-price response is required.

increase.title: Verify neutrality
increase.why: Actual and expected prices coincide at the new equilibrium.

decrease.title: Announce and implement M↓
decrease.why: The known contraction lowers nominal demand.
decrease.question: Does a lower actual price necessarily create a recession here?
decrease.answer: No; a matched lower expected price leaves the surprise term zero.

decrease.title: Lower the expected price
decrease.why: Producers anticipate the common decline rather than interpreting it as a relative loss.

decrease.title: Check the surprise term
decrease.why: Output remains 100 although nominal prices are lower.

edge.title: Remove credibility or advance knowledge
edge.why: If the change is not anticipated, Pᵉ may remain 2 initially.
edge.question: Which assumption distinguishes the two plotted expansion endpoints?
edge.answer: Whether expected prices already changed consistently with the monetary policy.

edge.title: Redo supply at the old expectation
edge.why: The new AD then meets the old SRAS at Y≈102.944, P≈2.147.

edge.title: Limit the original conclusion
edge.why: Full anticipation was essential. Sticky-price models are another distinct reason anticipated policy may have real transition effects.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 7- The New Classical and RBC Models.pdf

unexpected-policy.goal: Separate the immediate price surprise from the later expectation correction.
assumptions: Start at Y 100 and P=Pᵉ 2, holding potential and other real determinants fixed.
Use SRAS Y=100+20(P−Pᵉ) and exact AD P=M/(2 Y−150).

derive.title: Hold the old expectation initially
derive.why: The policy contains genuinely new information rather than a known rule.

derive.title: Shift demand
derive.why: Changing M changes the goods–asset equilibrium at each price.

derive.title: Solve the joint short-run point
derive.why: The actual price adjusts, but its forecast has not yet caught up.
derive.question: For an expansion, must the short-run point be above Y 100 from this initial equilibrium?
derive.answer: Yes; the new intersection has P>Pᵉ and therefore Y>Y*.

derive.title: Update the expectation
derive.why: As information becomes known, the common price rise or decline is no longer mistaken for a relative change.

derive.title: Return to potential
derive.why: Money can remain at its new level while the real gap disappears.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Begin where expected and actual prices match.
graph.question: Why is the immediate point not the final point?
graph.answer: Expected prices initially lag the realized common-price change.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Shift AD while retaining the original SRAS for the unexpected change.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Later shift SRAS when expectations catch up; the new final point lies on the same LRAS.

increase.title: Increase money unexpectedly
increase.why: AD moves right with Pᵉ still 2.
increase.question: Must M return to 100 to remove the output gap?
increase.answer: No; expectations can catch up while M stays 120.

increase.title: Solve the positive surprise
increase.why: The positive difference P−2 induces extra production.

increase.title: Correct the price forecast
increase.why: SRAS shifts up, leaving Y 100 and P 2.4 in full adjustment.

decrease.title: Withdraw money unexpectedly
decrease.why: AD shifts left while the original price expectation remains 2.
decrease.question: Why can output recover although the money stock stays lower?
decrease.answer: The misperception disappears when expected and actual prices match.

decrease.title: Solve the negative surprise
decrease.why: Output falls because actual P is below its forecast.

decrease.title: Revise the expectation down
decrease.why: The lower SRAS restores Y 100 at the lower full-equilibrium price.

edge.title: Change the initial condition
edge.why: Suppose an earlier contraction already left the economy at the plotted negative-surprise point.
edge.question: Does every monetary increase imply Y>Y* regardless of the starting gap?
edge.answer: No; it may merely close part or all of an existing recessionary gap.

edge.title: Increase demand enough to offset it
edge.why: The new intersection returns to Y 100, P 2 rather than exceeding potential.

edge.title: State the qualified sign claim
edge.why: An expansion raises output along SRAS, but an absolute above-potential gap requires the appropriate starting point and magnitude.

lucas-policy.goal: Evaluate policy after allowing expectations and decisions to respond.

symbols.meaning: systematic way policy responds to conditions
observed statistical relation under a particular regime

assumptions: The critique concerns extrapolating policy-dependent behavior as if its historical relationship were invariant.
The Phillips illustration holds natural structure fixed while expectations can change.

derive.title: Identify the old relationship
derive.why: Historical data describe behavior under the policy rule agents actually faced.

derive.title: Change the rule
derive.why: A new systematic policy can alter what people expect and how they choose.

derive.title: Carry the response through behavior
derive.why: Those changed decisions can alter the relationship being extrapolated.
derive.question: What is omitted when a forecast changes systematic policy but freezes πᵉ forever?
derive.answer: The public’s expectation response to the new policy rule.

derive.title: Build a policy counterfactual
derive.why: Use an economic model of expectations and choices under the new regime rather than mechanically reusing the old curve.

graph.title: Identify the old policy regime
graph.why: Start with an estimate from a known historical regime.
graph.question: Does good fit to old data guarantee correct prediction under a new rule?
graph.answer: No; behavior may change with that rule.

graph.title: Change the rule and expectations
graph.why: Insert a policy-rule change and its expectation response.

graph.title: Rebuild the behavioral prediction
graph.why: Only then predict the new relationship and outcome.

increase.title: Try to exploit the old tradeoff
increase.why: A policymaker seeks persistently lower unemployment through systematically higher inflation.
increase.question: Can the old SRPC be held fixed while the new inflation rule becomes widely anticipated?
increase.answer: Not consistently with the expectation mechanism.

increase.title: Let expectations respond
increase.why: Once the higher inflation becomes expected, the short-run curve shifts up.

increase.title: Recompute the endpoint
increase.why: At correct expectations unemployment returns to its natural rate, now with higher inflation.

decrease.title: Adopt credible lower inflation
decrease.why: A changed rule can lower expected inflation rather than merely move along the old curve.
decrease.question: Does the critique imply disinflation is always costless?
decrease.answer: No; it requires modeling responses, not assuming a particular zero-cost outcome.

decrease.title: Rebuild the relation
decrease.why: At each unemployment rate, the conditional inflation rate falls two points.

decrease.title: Avoid extrapolating old costs blindly
decrease.why: The transition still depends on credibility and rigidity; the old fixed-expectations slope is not a complete forecast.

edge.title: Reject the overstatement
edge.why: The critique does not say all historical evidence is useless.
edge.question: Do accounting identities stop holding after a policy reform?
edge.answer: No; the issue is stability of behavioral relationships, not arithmetic identities.

edge.title: Separate identities from behavior
edge.why: Budget and resource identities continue to hold even when expectation-sensitive coefficients change.

edge.title: Retain structural evidence
edge.why: Use data to discipline a model whose decisions and forecasts respond to the new rule.

rbc-evaluation.goal: Separate conditional efficiency, welfare and empirical adequacy.

symbols.meaning: well-being under stated preferences and constraints

assumptions: The strict benchmark combines optimizing competitive agents, flexibility, rational expectations and its efficiency assumptions.
A model’s conditional welfare claim is not evidence that every observed recession satisfies those assumptions.

derive.title: State the benchmark
derive.why: The efficiency argument presumes the relevant market and information conditions, not optimization alone.

derive.title: Separate shock from adaptation
derive.why: A bad productive shock worsens the feasible opportunities before anyone responds.

derive.title: Evaluate the feasible response
derive.why: The best available response can still leave people worse off than before.
derive.question: Does efficient adaptation prove an adverse shock was harmless?
derive.answer: No; the feasible set itself can have worsened.

derive.title: Check the empirical questions
derive.why: Ask whether shocks are sufficiently large/exogenous, labor changes voluntary, money neutral and wages/prices fast to clear.

derive.title: Evaluate intervention conditionally
derive.why: Fiscal output effects, distortionary financing, information limits and lags all matter; a GDP gain alone is not a welfare proof.

graph.title: Trace the feasible response
graph.why: Trace the model’s equilibrium response first.
graph.question: Are “efficient response” and “beneficial shock” the same claim?
graph.answer: No; they answer different questions.

graph.title: State the efficiency conditions
graph.why: Add the conditional efficiency interpretation.

graph.title: Evaluate the evidence
graph.why: Then ask whether observed evidence supports the premises rather than declaring the model universally correct.

increase.title: Improve production opportunities
increase.why: Better usable technology or inputs can raise attainable output and improve feasible welfare.
increase.question: Does higher output alone establish that a tax-financed fiscal intervention improved welfare?
increase.answer: No; taxes, leisure, distribution and other costs also enter the welfare comparison.

increase.title: Observe more flexible adjustment
increase.why: Evidence of fast market clearing would support that particular propagation mechanism.

increase.title: Keep the test conditional
increase.why: Neither one favorable episode nor one GDP increase proves every RBC assumption or every policy conclusion.

decrease.title: Reduce productive opportunities
decrease.why: An energy shortage can lower attainable consumption and production.
decrease.question: Must an efficient response leave welfare equal to its pre-shock level?
decrease.answer: No; optimality is conditional on the available resources.

decrease.title: Optimize within the worse constraint
decrease.why: Agents may choose the best feasible allocation while experiencing a welfare loss.

decrease.title: Test alternative mechanisms
decrease.why: Evidence of involuntary unemployment, sticky prices or short-run monetary effects challenges a strict RBC account.

edge.title: Remove an efficiency premise
edge.why: Market power, externalities, incomplete information or other frictions can break the benchmark welfare argument.
edge.question: Does an empirical objection to RBC establish that all stabilization policies are beneficial?
edge.answer: No; each policy needs its own mechanism and welfare assessment.

edge.title: Redo policy evaluation
edge.why: A possible corrective role requires analyzing that specific friction and the proposed instrument.

edge.title: Avoid the opposite blanket claim
edge.why: Rejecting a strict premise does not prove every intervention helps; implementation and financing still matter.

demand-recessions.goal: Explain how weak spending can reduce jobs without lowering productive capacity.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
Nominal prices are preset locally, firms can meet orders profitably, and employment supports demanded production.
Potential output stays 100 in the pure demand experiment.

derive.title: Begin with desired sales
derive.why: A fall in household or other spending reduces orders at existing prices.

derive.title: Use the quantity margin
derive.why: With prices slow to adjust, firms change production rather than instantly clearing through a new price.

derive.title: Translate production into hiring
derive.why: Producing fewer goods requires less labor when marginal product is positive.
derive.question: Must workers desire more leisure for jobs to disappear?
derive.answer: No; firms can need fewer workers while workers still want employment.

derive.title: Compare with capacity
derive.why: A demand-driven fall in actual Y can leave potential unchanged, creating a negative gap.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start from goods and asset balance at the preset price.
graph.question: Should FE automatically be moved left because sales fell?
graph.answer: No; a pure demand shock does not by itself change productive capacity.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Reduce the IS intercept to represent weaker autonomous demand.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The new intersection Y 90 is left of unchanged FE 100, identifying a demand shortfall.

increase.title: Increase orders
increase.why: Greater autonomous spending shifts IS right at the preset price.
increase.question: Is the higher short-run output necessarily a permanent increase in capacity?
increase.answer: No; productive fundamentals stayed fixed.

increase.title: Raise production
increase.why: Firms meet extra orders when markup, labor and capacity conditions permit.

increase.title: Increase labor needs
increase.why: More production requires more hired labor; a positive gap eventually creates price pressure.

decrease.title: Reduce orders
decrease.why: Consumer pessimism or another spending decline shifts IS left.
decrease.question: What distinguishes this from an RBC capacity contraction?
decrease.answer: Here Y* remains 100; the actual-output fall creates a demand gap.

decrease.title: Cut production
decrease.why: The lower goods–asset intersection is feasible at the old price.

decrease.title: Reduce hiring and diagnose the gap
decrease.why: Employment falls because sales and production fall, not because workers must suddenly prefer unemployment.

edge.title: Introduce a supply disturbance
edge.why: An oil shock can lower the productive benchmark itself.
edge.question: Is every output fall a Keynesian negative output gap?
edge.answer: No; compare actual output with the current potential.

edge.title: Recompute the gap
edge.why: Output is lower than the old 100 but above the new 90 capacity.

edge.title: Reject the old-baseline inference
edge.why: A fall in actual Y is insufficient to identify a negative demand gap once potential changes.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

wage-rigidity.goal: See why optimizing firms may leave excess labor supply at the going wage.
assumptions: Illustrative efficiency wage 6; labor demandw=14−0.1 N and supplyw=1+0.05 N.
The wage can be held above competitive clearing by incentive, turnover or institutional mechanisms.

derive.title: Identify a reason wages resist cuts
derive.why: The lecture considers minimum-wage/union arrangements, turnover and training costs, and effort incentives.

derive.title: Compare quantities at the wage
derive.why: Supply and demand need not coincide when the wage is chosen for more than clearing the market.

derive.title: Compute excess labor supply
derive.why: These workers want jobs at the going wage but are not hired.
derive.question: Does the existence of applicants prove a wage cut improves profit?
derive.answer: No; effort or retention may deteriorate when pay falls.

derive.title: Evaluate effective cost
derive.why: A higher wage per worker can lower cost per effective unit or replacement costs, explaining a privately rational refusal to accept underbids.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: First compare the competitive demand and supply curves.
graph.question: Which wage determines jobs in this illustration?
graph.answer: The imposed efficiency wage 6, not the competitive clearing wage 5⅓.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add the maintained efficiency wage above their competitive intersection.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: At w 6, hiring 80 and willing workers 100 leave excess supply 20.

increase.title: Raise labor demand
increase.why: A stronger demand or productivity schedule raises desired hiring at each wage.
increase.question: Must the wage fall for employment to rise in this case?
increase.answer: No; labor demand itself increases.

increase.title: Keep the wage mechanism fixed
increase.why: The firm expands jobs without changing the maintained wage.

increase.title: Reduce excess supply
increase.why: More employment can reduce unemployment while wage rigidity remains.

decrease.title: Lower labor demand
decrease.why: Fewer profitable jobs are available at each wage.
decrease.question: Does higher unemployment here require lower labor supply?
decrease.answer: No; supply is unchanged while demand falls.

decrease.title: Read hiring at the same wage
decrease.why: The fixed wage prevents the competitive rate of adjustment through pay.

decrease.title: Measure the larger excess supply
decrease.why: Workers can remain willing to work even though job availability falls.

edge.title: Remove the wage-holding mechanism
edge.why: Suppose pay can adjust without effort, turnover or institutional costs.
edge.question: Which premise permitted excess supply in the original graph?
edge.answer: The wage did not adjust solely to equate the quantity supplied and demanded.

edge.title: Redo wage clearing
edge.why: The competitive solution is N 86⅔, w 5⅓.

edge.title: Change the unemployment conclusion
edge.why: Excess supply at w 6 is no longer the maintained equilibrium; the wage and employment adjust together.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

effort-curve.goal: Distinguish worker counts, effort and the incentive response to real pay.
assumptions: Lecture effort rises with real pay through reciprocity or the risk of losing a valuable job.
Original numerical illustration e(w)=w²/(16+w²), w>0; it is not an empirical estimate.

derive.title: Separate effort from headcount
derive.why: The same number of employees can provide different productive effort.

derive.title: Explain the incentive
derive.why: Gift exchange rewards fair treatment; the shirking mechanism values keeping a well-paid job.

derive.title: Read the effort shape
derive.why: The illustrated response is low at small w, rises steeply over an intermediate range and saturates at high w.
derive.question: Does increasing e guarantee that any higher w lowers labor cost?
derive.answer: No; compare proportional effort and wage changes.

derive.title: Introduce the cost comparison
derive.why: The wage buys effort, so cost per worker alone is insufficient.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Plot w horizontally and effort vertically.
graph.question: Why does the highest effort point not necessarily give the cheapest effective labor?
graph.answer: It can require a disproportionately high wage.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: The ray to a point measures effort per wage unit, e/w.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The steepest ray can occur before effort is near its maximum.

increase.title: Raise pay from a low level
increase.why: Effort rises from 0.2 to 0.5 in the stated function.
increase.question: Which ratio determines whether the pay rise is cost-saving?
increase.answer: w/e, or equivalently the reciprocal e/w.

increase.title: Compare proportions
increase.why: Pay doubles, but effort multiplies by 2.5, a larger increase.

increase.title: Calculate effective cost
increase.why: Higher pay per employee buys effective labor more cheaply in this interval.

decrease.title: Cut pay from a high level
decrease.why: Effort falls from 0.8 to 0.5.
decrease.question: Must every pay cut worsen effective labor cost?
decrease.answer: No; the proportional effort loss matters, and it can be smaller than the pay reduction.

decrease.title: Compare the proportional losses
decrease.why: Pay falls 50% while effort falls 37.5%; the wage saving is proportionately larger.

decrease.title: Recompute effective cost
decrease.why: The cut improves cost per effective unit over this upper interval.

edge.title: Remove effort dependence
edge.why: This is a different behavioral assumption, not the same S-curve.
edge.question: Which premise of the S-curve cost-minimum logic failed?
edge.answer: Effort no longer responds to pay.

edge.title: Redo the ratio
edge.why: A lower feasible wage always lowers cost in this stripped-down calculation.

edge.title: Change the optimum
edge.why: There is no interior incentive-based efficiency wage; the lower feasible boundary matters.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

efficiency-wage.goal: Derive the cost minimum, origin-ray tangency and hiring condition.
assumptions: w>0, e(w)>0; an interior candidate must also minimize the relevant cost ratio.
Illustration e=w²/(16+w²); the separate labor-market figure assumes its own stated efficiency wage 6.

derive.title: Hold effective work fixed
derive.why: Greater effort reduces the headcount needed for the same effective input.

derive.title: Rewrite the wage bill
derive.why: For fixed E, minimize q=w/e rather than wage per head.

derive.title: Differentiate the ratio
derive.why: Use the quotient rule; the effort response offsets the direct wage-cost increase.

derive.title: Set the interior condition
derive.why: At tangency the curve slope e′ equals origin-ray slope e/w.
derive.question: Is every solution of w e′=e automatically the global minimum?
derive.answer: No; check curvature, boundaries and the ratio at other feasible wages.

derive.title: Verify the illustrative minimum
derive.why: For w>0, the candidate is w 4 and q″=32/w³>0; costs rise toward both remote boundaries.

derive.title: Then choose headcount
derive.why: Differentiate production with respect to actual N, including the effort multiplier; F′ alone is per effective unit.

derive.title: Write the joint profit problem
derive.why: The firm can choose both the wage per worker and actual headcount. A higher wage raises the cost of every worker but can also raise every worker’s effort.

derive.title: Choose pay at a given headcount
derive.why: Hold N fixed. The output gain from a wage increase is the marginal product per effective unit times N workers times the effort response. The wage bill rises by N for each unit increase in w.

derive.title: Combine the two first-order conditions
derive.why: For positive employment, divide the wage condition by N. Substitute A F′=w/e from the hiring condition. The same effort elasticity condition emerges as in the cost-ratio method.
derive.question: Why must positive employment be stated before dividing?
derive.answer: At N=0 the wage derivative is zero regardless of effort elasticity. The interior two-condition argument then does not determine the wage.

derive.title: Check the optimum before using it
derive.why: The Solow condition is necessary for this positive interior optimum. A global decision still compares feasible wages, output choices and the option of not operating. The S-shaped effort curve selects the highest feasible origin-ray slope when a positive optimum exists.
derive.math: maximize e(w)/w ⇔ minimize w/e(w), for positive e and w

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Plot the effort relation before drawing origin rays.
graph.question: Why is minimizing w/e equivalent to maximizing e/w here?
graph.answer: Both are positive reciprocals, so their order reverses.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Compare e/w as the rays become steeper.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The ray at w 4 is tangent and has maximum slope 0.125, corresponding to minimum cost 8.

increase.title: Start below the optimum
increase.why: The effort elasticity exceeds one, so effort is proportionately responsive.
increase.question: Below this optimum, can a wage increase reduce effective labor cost?
increase.answer: Yes; effort grows proportionately more than the wage.

increase.title: Raise the wage
increase.why: Cost falls to 25/3≈8.333 as effort improves faster than pay.

increase.title: Continue to the minimum
increase.why: At the optimum the first-order proportional gains balance.

decrease.title: Start above the optimum
decrease.why: Effort is relatively saturated, with elasticity below one.
decrease.question: Why not keep cutting pay after reaching w 4?
decrease.answer: Below the minimum the effort loss becomes disproportionately costly.

decrease.title: Reduce the wage
decrease.why: Cost falls to 26/3≈8.667 because wage savings dominate the proportional effort loss.

decrease.title: Stop at the minimum
decrease.why: Further cuts below four would raise the ratio again.

edge.title: Check the failed interior premise
edge.why: A flat effort function, a monotone cost ratio or a constrained wage range can remove the interior optimum.
edge.question: What two separate checks follow the first-order condition?
edge.answer: Verify the cost minimum over feasible wages, then use the correctly measured marginal product for hiring.

edge.title: Return to feasible cost comparisons
edge.why: Evaluate w/e over allowed wages, including endpoints; do not select a tangency merely because it exists.

edge.title: Keep input units straight
edge.why: Whichever feasible wage is chosen, differentiate production with respect to actual worker headcount N: an extra worker supplies e(w) effective units. The hiring condition equates A F′(e(w)N)e(w) to the wage per worker; this algebra is separate from the plotted wage-cost boundary comparison.

edge.title: Use direct comparisons for a wage table
edge.why: Tutorial 10 allows only six wages. There is no continuous wage derivative to set to zero. Compare the effort delivered by each unit of wage spending.
edge.question: Why is the lowest wage not the best choice?
edge.answer: At w=8 each wage unit buys only 0.875 effort units. At w=12 it buys 1.25. The lower wage has a higher cost per effective unit.

edge.title: Hire using marginal product per actual worker
edge.why: Choose w=12 and e=15 from the table. Then set MPN to the wage, using the effort-adjusted marginal product supplied by the tutorial.

edge.title: Separate a surplus from a shortage of workers
edge.why: If 40 workers are willing to work at wage 8 and supply is nondecreasing in the wage, at least 40 are available at 12. Demand is only 6, so availability does not bind and the optimal wage does not fall to clear the market. A genuine labor shortage would require a new constrained hiring problem.
edge.question: Would extra unemployed workers automatically make wage cuts profitable?
edge.answer: No. When labor supply is already ample, cutting pay can reduce effort enough to raise the effective labor cost. Availability and effort incentives are different constraints.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

keynesian-fe.goal: Determine potential employment at the efficiency wage rather than the competitive crossing.

symbols.meaning: production function, with fixed effort absorbed

assumptions: Illustration w_eff 6, NDw=14−0.1 N; supply is initiallyw=1+0.05 N.
For the output calculation use the compatible illustrative F(N)=14 N−0.05 N²; fixed effort is absorbed.

derive.title: Choose the incentive wage first
derive.why: Its determination is an effort-cost problem, not the competitive labor intersection.

derive.title: Read desired hiring
derive.why: Demand at that wage determines jobs while enough workers are available.

derive.title: Check available labor
derive.why: There is excess supply, so labor availability does not constrain those jobs.
derive.question: Would increasing willing workers to 120 force the firm to hire 120?
derive.answer: No; labor demand still calls for 80 at the same wage.

derive.title: Compute capacity
derive.why: The production function converts employed labor, not the entire labor supply, into potential output.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: The competitive crossing is shown only for comparison.
graph.question: Which employment point belongs to this Keynesian FE construction?
graph.answer: N 80 at the efficiency wage, not the competitive 86⅔.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add the maintained wage 6.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Potential jobs 80 occur at the demand–wage intersection, despite 100 willing workers.

increase.title: Increase labor supply
increase.why: More workers wish to work at each wage, with the incentive schedule and labor demand fixed.
increase.question: Why does this supply shift not move FE right?
increase.answer: Employment is pinned by labor demand at fixed w_eff, not by wage clearing.

increase.title: Recheck the constraint
increase.why: Supply was already above demand and remains so.

increase.title: Keep productive employment fixed
increase.why: The additional available workers enlarge excess supply rather than productive input.

decrease.title: Reduce labor supply modestly
decrease.why: Willing workers fall 100→90 at the maintained wage.
decrease.question: Does every fall in available labor reduce this potential output?
decrease.answer: No; a modest fall can merely shrink existing excess supply.

decrease.title: Check that hiring remains feasible
decrease.why: The firm can still obtain its desired workforce.

decrease.title: Keep potential unchanged
decrease.why: Jobs 80 and capacity 800 remain; excess supply falls 20→10.

edge.title: Make labor scarce
edge.why: The original desired 80 jobs can no longer all be filled.
edge.question: Why cannot the old 80-job answer simply be retained?
edge.answer: It requires workers who are not available under the new supply condition.

edge.title: Redo the availability check
edge.why: The assumption that supply is nonbinding fails.

edge.title: Reconsider the closure
edge.why: Wage/incentive adjustment or a binding labor constraint must be modeled; the old rule alone cannot certify the same potential.
