price-setting.goal: Use MR to choose quantity and demand to choose price, then distinguish preset-price sales.
assumptions: Original illustration P=a−b Q, with nonnegative sales and an interior optimum in the stated examples.
Fixed-price order changes require capacity and marginal cost conditions; the markup need not remain constant after a shock.

derive.title: Start from inverse demand
derive.why: A uniform price reduction is needed to sell more along this demand curve.

derive.title: Write revenue and its derivative
derive.why: Extra revenue includes the lower price on existing units, explaining MR<P.

derive.title: Set the interior quantity condition
derive.why: With a 20, b 0.2, MC 8, solve 20−0.4 Q=8.
derive.question: What quantity does this condition select?

derive.title: Read price from demand
derive.why: Price is 14, not the marginal revenue 8.

derive.title: Express the markup
derive.why: The reference price is 75% above marginal cost; a changed demand curve can change this ratio.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw demand in price–quantity space.
graph.question: Should price be read from the MR curve at Q 30?
graph.answer: No; MR=8 selects quantity, while demand gives P 14.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add MR below demand and the cost line; their crossing selects Q.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Move vertically to demand at the selected Q to read the selling price.

increase.title: Raise demand
increase.why: At every Q consumers will pay more.
increase.question: Is meeting new orders at a fixed price the same as cutting price along unchanged demand?
increase.answer: No; one responds to a shifted demand schedule at a maintained posted price.

increase.title: Find the frictionless new optimum
increase.why: Both price and optimal quantity rise when repricing is free.

increase.title: Check the preset-price alternative
increase.why: Extra sales at the fixed posted price earn 14 against MC 8, so they are locally profitable if capacity allows.

decrease.title: Reduce demand
decrease.why: Willingness to pay at each Q falls.
decrease.question: Can a firm rationally sell less at its old price after a small demand loss?
decrease.answer: Yes, if the benefit of repricing is smaller than its menu cost.

decrease.title: Recompute the flexible-price optimum
decrease.why: The profit-maximizing price and quantity both fall.

decrease.title: Keep the old price if resetting is costly
decrease.why: Sales can fall substantially before the posted price changes.

edge.title: Raise marginal cost above the preset price
edge.why: An extra sale now loses two units of operating profit.
edge.question: Which profitability condition failed at the posted price?
edge.answer: Revenue per extra sale no longer covers marginal cost.

edge.title: Redo the marginal decision
edge.why: The earlier “meet every extra order” argument relied on P>MC and no binding capacity limit.

edge.title: If repricing is free, resolve the optimum
edge.why: The firm cannot justify unlimited supply at the old price merely by invoking a markup at the old optimum.

sources.file: [EC2102 Lecture Slides] 8 - the New Keynesian Model.pdf

menu-costs.goal: Derive the reset decision from profits, including the equality and zero-sales boundaries.
assumptions: The curve is an original worked illustration of the lecture’s benefit–cost rule, not a course empirical estimate.
Repricing compares profits over the same horizon. Exit and fixed operating costs are not modeled.

derive.title: Write sales and operating profit
derive.why: This interior expression applies where the stated orders are nonnegative.

derive.title: Find the frictionless best price
derive.why: The optimum is P*=(a+m)/2.

derive.title: Measure the gain from resetting
derive.why: This is the benefit before paying the menu cost, not total profit.

derive.title: Use the illustrative square loss
derive.why: For b 0.2 and feasible old-price orders, the gain is 1.25(Δ a)².
derive.question: For a four-unit intercept change, is gain 20 enough to cover K 25?
derive.answer: No; the firm retains its old price.

derive.title: Apply the decision rule
derive.why: At equality, the two choices yield the same net profit in this simple model.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Draw the profit gain as a function of the demand shift, not as a price curve.
graph.question: Does every change in the frictionless optimum cause repricing?
graph.answer: No; the profit improvement must cover the adjustment cost.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Add the menu cost as a constant benchmark.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Crossings mark indifference; only gains above the cost justify resetting.

increase.title: Raise demand modestly
increase.why: The desired price rises 14→16, but the gain does not cover 25.
increase.question: Why can the firm keep P 14 after the first increase but change it after the second?
increase.answer: The gain crosses the menu-cost threshold; rigidity is conditional.

increase.title: Increase the disturbance
increase.why: The new optimum is P 18; old-price profit 420 becomes 500 before adjustment cost.

increase.title: Compare net gains
increase.why: The larger increase now makes resetting worthwhile.

decrease.title: Reduce demand moderately
decrease.why: Old-price orders remain positive and the best new price would be 12; the gain is too small.
decrease.question: Can a negative demand shock trigger a price cut under the same rule?
decrease.answer: Yes; compare its own reset gain with the same cost.

decrease.title: Reduce demand somewhat more
decrease.why: At a 15 the optimal price is 11.5; resetting produces a greater profit gain.

decrease.title: Pay the cost when justified
decrease.why: A sufficiently valuable price cut is privately rational; menu costs do not imply prices only rise.

edge.title: Check both boundary conditions
edge.why: Equality implies indifference; zero orders invalidate the interior old-profit expression.
edge.question: Why is extending 1.25(Δ a)² to every negative shock wrong?
edge.answer: It would use negative old-price sales; the nonnegativity constraint changes the calculation.

edge.title: Redo the zero-sales example
edge.why: With nonnegative sales, old profit is 0; the new P 10, Q 10 produces 20, not the spurious 80 from extending the interior parabola.

edge.title: Use the corrected gain
edge.why: In this stripped-down example the severe demand contraction does not justify paying 25 to reset. The actual piecewise curve is shown.

keynesian-policy.goal: Compare monetary and fiscal transmission without conflating their interest-rate effects.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: Illustration: IS r=15−0.1 Y, money demand L=Y−10 r, M=100 and initial P=2.
The fixed-price intersection uses downward IS and finite upward LM; expected inflation and other determinants are fixed.
Potential output is fixed under the efficiency-wage closure while available workers remain sufficient.
C=25+0.5 Y−3 r, I=40−2 r, G 10 in the numerical illustration.

derive.title: Name the policy instrument
derive.why: Money policy changes real balances at preset prices; purchases directly change goods demand.

derive.title: Choose the initial curve
derive.why: A monetary expansion shifts LM down; a purchases expansion shifts IS up.

derive.title: Trace the rate difference
derive.why: Both can raise output, but their rate effects oppose.
derive.question: Which expansion directly supports investment through a lower r in the regular model?
derive.answer: Monetary expansion; the G expansion raises r and restrains I.

derive.title: Separate spending components
derive.why: Consumption responds to income as well as interest; its fiscal response is not determined by the rate channel alone.

derive.title: Allow final price adjustment
derive.why: With fixed FE, money ultimately leaves the real allocation unchanged, while fiscal changes alter the private/public spending mix.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Begin with the same initial equilibrium.
graph.question: Do the two new points represent both policies applied together?
graph.answer: No; they are separate one-policy comparisons against the same baseline.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Show the monetary shift separately from the initial LM.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: Then add the separate fiscal scenario; compare their rates without stacking the shocks.

increase.title: Increase money alone
increase.why: Y 105, r 4.5 gives C 64, I 31: both rise in this calibration.
increase.question: Can policies that both raise Y move investment in opposite directions?
increase.answer: Yes; their real-rate changes differ.

increase.title: Increase purchases alone
increase.why: Y 110, r 6 gives C 62, I 28: income raises C despite a higher-rate restraint, while I falls.

increase.title: Compare full adjustment
increase.why: Money eventually restores Y 100, r 5; higher G at fixed FE instead gives Y 100, r 7 and lower total private spending.

decrease.title: Contract money alone
decrease.why: At fixed P, Y 95, r 5.5 reduces C and I.
decrease.question: Does lower r after a G cut guarantee that total consumption rises immediately?
decrease.answer: No; the lower-income effect can dominate.

decrease.title: Cut purchases alone
decrease.why: At fixed P, Y=90 and r=4 reduce income but support investment through the lower rate.

decrease.title: Follow the final composition
decrease.why: After full price adjustment, the money contraction returns to the original real allocation at Y=100 and r=5. The separate G cut instead ends at Y=100 and r=3, releasing resources to C+I.

edge.title: Change the tax assumption
edge.why: A current lump-sum cut is exactly offset in present value by future taxes, with the G path fixed.
edge.question: What is missing from “a tax cut must stimulate” in the Ricardian case?
edge.answer: A change in lifetime resources or a failure of the full saving offset.

edge.title: Apply Ricardian behavior
edge.why: If households fully offset timing through saving, desired consumption does not rise.

edge.title: Remove the presumed IS shift
edge.why: The lecture’s Keynesian tax-stimulus case deliberately uses non-Ricardian behavior; do not import its conclusion into this boundary.

stabilization.goal: Track a policy from diagnosis to its arrival in a changing economy.

symbols.meaning: output response per unit policy change over a specified horizon
delay between decision and economic effect

assumptions: Policy can influence demand, but the current state, response size and arrival time are uncertain.
The lecture’s 6–12-month forecasting discussion is illustrative, not a fixed policy timetable.

derive.title: Diagnose the shock
derive.why: An output decline may reflect deficient demand, lower capacity or both.

derive.title: Estimate the relevant gap
derive.why: Actual output is observed imperfectly and potential is estimated, so even the sign can be uncertain.

derive.title: Choose size and timing
derive.why: A known response direction is insufficient when its magnitude and lag are uncertain.
derive.question: Why is a positive fiscal multiplier alone insufficient to size a successful intervention?
derive.answer: The size of the gap, the multiplier magnitude, its timing and future conditions are also needed.

derive.title: Forecast the arrival state
derive.why: Account for decision, implementation and transmission delays, including political constraints.

derive.title: Judge the later outcome
derive.why: A measure suitable at enactment can become too large or too small when it finally affects spending.

graph.title: Diagnose the current gap
graph.why: Start with the estimate of today’s economy.
graph.question: Can a correct diagnosis today still lead to badly timed stimulus?
graph.answer: Yes; the economy can recover before the main effect arrives.

graph.title: Allow for the policy lag
graph.why: Add instrument choice and the delays before effects arrive.

graph.title: Compare the eventual outcome
graph.why: The outcome depends on the future state, not only the initial diagnosis.

increase.title: Increase demand support in recession
increase.why: A stimulus is selected to close an estimated negative gap.
increase.question: Does the original recession diagnosis prove the eventual stimulus cannot overshoot?
increase.answer: No; the relevant state can change before the effects arrive.

increase.title: Allow recovery during the lag
increase.why: Private demand may rebound before the policy reaches full strength.

increase.title: Recalculate the later gap
increase.why: The same intervention can then produce excess demand and additional inflation pressure.

decrease.title: Reduce demand during apparent overheating
decrease.why: A contraction is chosen based on the estimated positive gap.
decrease.question: Why should the expected future state affect the contraction decision?
decrease.answer: Because the policy acts after the decision, potentially under different conditions.

decrease.title: Allow conditions to weaken
decrease.why: Private spending or external conditions may deteriorate during the delay.

decrease.title: Assess the compounded shortfall
decrease.why: A late contraction can deepen a recession rather than simply restrain the earlier boom.

edge.title: Reject exact fine-tuning
edge.why: Potential output and response parameters are not known precisely enough to guarantee an exact target.
edge.question: Does uncertainty prove stabilization can never help?
edge.answer: No; it limits precision and requires weighing risks rather than asserting perfect control.

edge.title: Compare policy and inaction risks
edge.why: Uncertainty does not automatically mean every response should be zero.

edge.title: State the lecture’s conditional stance
edge.why: The lecture cautions against fine tuning while allowing intervention in major recessions; that is not a guarantee of success.

oil-shocks.goal: Separate lost capacity from a residual demand gap after a cost-driven price change.

symbols.meaning: real interest rate in percentage-point units in the illustration

assumptions: The lecture oil experiment holds IS fixed and allows oil-dependent prices to adjust quickly.
The numerical shock changes potential 100→90; the size and timing of the initial P jump are explicit assumptions.

derive.title: Trace the supply effect
derive.why: Costlier oil reduces usable energy and output at given K, N, lowering potential and shifting FE left.

derive.title: Trace prompt price setting
derive.why: Affected firms may raise their prices quickly, increasing the general price level.

derive.title: Translate prices into asset demand
derive.why: LM shifts up; the unchanged IS then implies lower actual output.

derive.title: Compare with the new potential
derive.why: A fall relative to old Y is not enough to classify the new gap.
derive.question: If new Y*=90 but actual Y=95, is the new gap negative?
derive.answer: No; it is+5, despite the decline from the old 100.

derive.title: Adjust after the initial jump
derive.why: Below-new-potential output creates downward price pressure; above-new-potential output creates upward pressure.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start from Y 100, r 5.
graph.question: Is the initial point below new FE a logical necessity of every oil shock?
graph.answer: No; it depends on the price and demand responses.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Move potential to 90 before deciding whether actual output is excessive or deficient.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The large initial price jump gives Y 87.5 below new FE 90; later price easing restores Y 90.

increase.title: Raise oil costs and cut capacity
increase.why: This real supply loss remains even if demand policy changes.
increase.question: Can prices fall during later adjustment while remaining above their original level?
increase.answer: Yes;4→3⅓ is a fall, but 3⅓ still exceeds the original 2.

increase.title: Let P initially jump to 4
increase.why: Actual output falls farther than potential in this chosen configuration.

increase.title: Undo part of the price overshoot
increase.why: LM moves down until Y 90, r 6, leaving a higher price than before the shock.

decrease.title: Reduce oil costs and improve capacity
decrease.why: This favorable real change raises the productive benchmark.
decrease.question: Does higher actual output after cheaper oil prove demand is above capacity?
decrease.answer: No; potential may have risen even more.

decrease.title: Assume only a partial initial price decline
decrease.why: Actual Y rises to 105 but remains below the new 110 potential.

decrease.title: Allow further price easing
decrease.why: Demand catches up to Y 110 in this scenario. It is not the exact reverse of the adverse-shock path.

edge.title: Use a smaller adverse price jump
edge.why: At the unchanged IS, actual Y is 95.
edge.question: Which assumption generated the earlier downward price adjustment?
edge.answer: The initial price jump was large enough to put output below the new FE.

edge.title: Recompute the gap against 90
edge.why: This is above new potential, unlike the lecture’s overshoot configuration.

edge.title: Reverse the later pressure appropriately
edge.why: P must rise further toward 10/3 rather than fall. Demand stimulus cannot directly restore the physical capacity loss.

wage-evidence.goal: Read the wage illustrations as evidence about mechanisms, not isolated causal experiments.

symbols.meaning: separations relative to a reference workforce
daily pay divided by hours worked
change attributable to one cause under an adequate comparison

assumptions: Ford and mismatch evidence are historical lecture illustrations, not newly estimated data.
Pay, hours and other business conditions changed together; the lecture explicitly notes alternative influences.

derive.title: State a testable prediction
derive.why: A mismatch-only account suggests a particular pattern of vacancies and quits; a demand-shortfall account predicts fewer jobs to fill.

derive.title: Compare the stated pattern
derive.why: The lecture argues that recession vacancy/quit behavior does not support mismatch as the entire explanation.

derive.title: Describe the Ford change
derive.why: Daily pay rose from about 2.30 for nine hours to at least 5 for eight hours; retention and performance changed.
derive.question: Is daily-pay growth the same as hourly-pay growth here?
derive.answer: No; hours fell too, so compute pay per hour separately.

derive.title: Compute meaningful units
derive.why: The hourly comparison incorporates the changed workday instead of treating the daily values as comparable labor units.

derive.title: Separate consistency from attribution
derive.why: The episode fits incentive mechanisms but does not isolate them from Model T success, work changes, union concerns or publicity.

graph.title: Identify the wage intervention
graph.why: Start with the mechanism’s prediction before looking at outcomes.
graph.question: Does a before/after improvement alone prove wages caused all of it?
graph.answer: No; simultaneous changes leave alternative explanations.

graph.title: Trace the observed changes
graph.why: Add the historical wage-and-hours episode.

graph.title: Separate mechanism from proof
graph.why: Then account for concurrent influences before stating a causal conclusion.

increase.title: Increase pay and job value
increase.why: Higher real compensation can strengthen effort or the incentive to retain a valuable job.
increase.question: Can this episode establish that every firm should double wages?
increase.answer: No; effort responses, turnover costs and conditions differ, and causality is not isolated.

increase.title: Examine the observed improvements
increase.why: The lecture reports lower turnover/absence and higher productivity after the change.

increase.title: Keep the interpretation conditional
increase.why: Those observations support a plausible mechanism without establishing its isolated magnitude or proving the chosen wage maximized profit.

decrease.title: Measure an outcome decline correctly
decrease.why: The lecture’s illustrative decline is 7.5 percentage points, or 75% relative to its old value.
decrease.question: Does the historical wage-rise episode identify the exact effect of an equal wage cut?
decrease.answer: No; that unobserved counterfactual can involve different conditions and nonlinear responses.

decrease.title: Do not reverse the experiment
decrease.why: A wage cut is not observed in that comparison; its effect cannot simply be read as the exact negative of the historical gain.

decrease.title: State the counterfactual requirement
decrease.why: To assess lower pay, evaluate how effort, retention and other changing conditions respond under a suitable comparison.

edge.title: Check the turnover denominator
edge.why: Annualized separations per reference workforce can exceed one because replacements can also leave.
edge.question: Why is an annual separation count above 100% arithmetically possible?
edge.answer: The numerator counts separation events, potentially including repeated replacement turnover.

edge.title: Avoid a false population reading
edge.why: The approximate 370% figure is not 370% of distinct people each leaving once.

edge.title: Retain the evidence limit
edge.why: Even a correctly calculated turnover rate does not identify which concurrent change caused it.

other-keynesian-foundations.goal: Explain the two named alternative mechanisms without inventing a formal course model.

symbols.meaning: interdependent decisions can sustain an inefficient collective outcome
different wage or price reset dates
incomplete adjustment of nominal wages or prices

assumptions: Lecture 8 page 47 names these alternatives but does not provide their equations or a unique quantitative solution.
The sequences are labeled intuition; numerical multipliers, welfare rankings and adjustment durations require additional model assumptions.

derive.title: Separate the mechanisms
derive.why: Coordination concerns how one agent’s desired action depends on others; staggering concerns reset timing.

derive.title: Trace the coordination intuition
derive.why: If sales depend on others’ spending, individually cautious choices can reinforce weak demand.

derive.title: Trace the timing intuition
derive.why: When reset dates differ, some wages or prices remain preset while others respond.
derive.question: Does naming staggering specify that all prices adjust in exactly one month?
derive.answer: No; a reset schedule and quantitative model would be needed.

derive.title: Respect the source’s level of detail
derive.why: These are alternatives to the worked efficiency-wage and menu-cost mechanisms, not new equations derived on that slide.

graph.title: Identify the coordination problem
graph.why: Begin with two distinct starting mechanisms.
graph.question: Are these two labels synonymous with the effort-per-dollar problem?
graph.answer: No; they describe different microfoundations.

graph.title: Follow the feedback
graph.why: Follow each into its own reason aggregate adjustment can be incomplete.

graph.title: Separate staggering from coordination
graph.why: End at the explicit limit on quantitative conclusions from a named mechanism alone.

increase.title: Increase desired spending
increase.why: Greater demand can make more production and hiring attractive when firms’ decisions depend on others’ expenditure.
increase.question: Can one calculate a unique output increase from the word “staggering” alone?
increase.answer: No; the relevant equations and reset assumptions are missing.

increase.title: Let some prices reset
increase.why: With staggered timing, newly adjustable prices can respond before still-preset prices.

increase.title: Avoid a numerical leap
increase.why: The signs and speed of a full equilibrium response require the actual coordination and contract model; the slide alone does not fix a multiplier.

decrease.title: Reduce desired spending
decrease.why: Mutually cautious production or spending choices can reinforce a weak-demand situation.
decrease.question: Does the naming of coordination failure prove it caused a particular recession?
decrease.answer: No; application requires model fit and evidence.

decrease.title: Keep some contracts predetermined
decrease.why: Some prices or wages cannot all respond at once, so quantities may bear part of the initial adjustment.

decrease.title: Distinguish illustrative intuition
decrease.why: This possible sequence explains why a formal model is needed; it does not prove that every downturn has the same mechanism.

edge.title: Remove the timing friction
edge.why: Suppose all relevant prices can reset immediately rather than on staggered dates.
edge.question: Does eliminating staggering automatically establish all Classical assumptions?
edge.answer: No; other market and information conditions must also be checked.

edge.title: Redo the adjustment step
edge.why: The specific delay caused by predetermined reset dates disappears.

edge.title: Do not erase other frictions
edge.why: Coordination or information problems could still remain; removing one mechanism does not automatically remove every source of nonneutrality.

symbols.meaning: expected inflation in the same units
positive Phillips slope coefficient,0.5 in the illustration

assumptions: Baseline equation π=πᵉ−h(u−u*) with no additional residual shock.

derive.title: Identify cyclical unemployment
derive.why: Subtract the current natural benchmark rather than treating all unemployment as cyclical.

derive.title: Identify unexpected inflation
derive.why: Compare inflation with what was expected, not simply with zero.

derive.title: Link the gaps
derive.why: Positive h makes their signs opposite.
derive.question: With a two-point unemployment gap and h 0.5, how large is the inflation surprise?
derive.answer: −1 percentage point.

derive.title: Solve for observed inflation
derive.why: Expected inflation determines the anchor, while the gap determines the departure.

derive.title: Read slope and intercept
derive.why: Holding expectations and the natural rate fixed, the slope in π-versus-u space is −h.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Mark u*=5 and expected inflation 3; their crossing anchors the curve.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: Draw the line with slope−0.5 through that anchor.

graph.title: Read the result

increase.title: Raise actual unemployment
increase.why: With u*=5 fixed, cyclical unemployment rises from zero to two points.

increase.title: Apply the negative coefficient

increase.title: Read predicted inflation
increase.why: The movement is down/right along unchanged SRPC.

decrease.title: Lower actual unemployment
decrease.why: The cyclical gap becomes−2 points.

decrease.title: Apply the signed product

decrease.title: Read the new point
decrease.why: The movement is up/left along the same conditional curve.

edge.title: Set the surprise to zero
edge.why: The original equation now has zero on its left-hand gap.

edge.title: Solve the remaining condition
edge.why: This uses h>0 and no extra residual term.

edge.title: Retain the level distinction

symbols.meaning: expected inflation in the same units
positive Phillips slope coefficient,0.5 in the illustration

derive.title: Write the conditional intercept

derive.title: Hold actual unemployment fixed

derive.title: Alternatively hold actual inflation fixed

derive.question: For h 0.5 and πᵉ↑2 points, what is the horizontal shift at fixed π?

derive.title: Preserve the slope

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Start with the curve anchored at u*=5, πᵉ 3.

graph.answer: No; its horizontal location is still u*=5.

graph.title: Add the next relation

graph.title: Read the result

increase.title: Raise expected inflation

increase.title: Compare at the old inflation rate

increase.title: Name the shift

decrease.title: Lower expected inflation

decrease.title: Compare at fixed actual inflation

decrease.title: Preserve interpretation

edge.title: Keep expectations anchored
edge.why: The assumption that expectations automatically follow the latest observation is not part of the baseline equation.
edge.math: πᵉ=3 despite an actual inflation increase
edge.question: Must every rise in actual inflation shift the Phillips curve upward?
edge.answer: No; anchored expectations can leave it unchanged.

edge.title: Use the unchanged curve
edge.why: This can be a movement along the existing SRPC.

edge.title: Specify an update rule before shifting
edge.why: A shift requires an actual change in πᵉ, not merely observing a change in π.

symbols.meaning: expected inflation in the same units
positive Phillips slope coefficient,0.5 in the illustration

derive.title: Locate the natural benchmark
derive.why: The natural-rate location anchors both the short-run and long-run relations.

derive.title: Change the structural rate
derive.why: A higher u* raises the conditional inflation intercept.

derive.title: Hold actual unemployment fixed
derive.why: The vertical shift is scaled by h.
derive.question: If u* rises one point with h 0.5, how far does SRPC shift vertically?
derive.answer: Up 0.5 inflation points at every fixed u.

derive.title: Hold inflation fixed instead
derive.why: The horizontal shift equals the natural-rate change; LRPC moves by the same horizontal amount.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Mark the original natural rate at five.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: A structural rise to six shifts both relevant benchmarks.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: At unchanged actual u 5 inflation rises to 3.5, while correct-expectation unemployment is now 6.

increase.title: Increase structural/frictional unemployment
increase.why: The natural benchmark is higher even if current demand has not changed.
increase.question: Why can unchanged observed u imply a different cyclical condition?

increase.title: Recalculate the same observed rate

increase.title: Update both curves

decrease.title: Improve matching or reduce structural friction

decrease.title: Hold actual u 5 for comparison

decrease.title: Shift the relations

edge.why: A demand recession can increase cyclical unemployment without a structural shift.

edge.title: Redo the gap
edge.why: The old benchmark is still the appropriate one.

edge.title: Keep the curves fixed
edge.why: The economy moves along SRPC; one unemployment observation cannot prove LRPC shifted.

derive.title: Trace sectoral reallocation

derive.title: State the decision limit
derive.why: An uncertain sign cannot support certainty about overheating or deficient demand; additional evidence and risks matter.

graph.title: Choose the axes
graph.why: Put the assumed natural rate on the horizontal axis and inferred gap vertically.
graph.question: Is this graph a time series showing natural unemployment actually changing?
graph.answer: No; it compares alternative estimates for a fixed observed rate.

graph.title: Add the next relation
graph.why: The zero line marks estimates equal to observed u 6.

graph.title: Read the result
graph.why: The historical interval crosses that line, changing the inferred sign.

increase.title: Raise the estimated natural rate
increase.why: Observed unemployment remains 6.
increase.question: Does a higher estimate necessarily mean an actual sudden deterioration in matching?
increase.answer: No; measurement or model revision can change the estimate.

increase.title: Redo subtraction
increase.why: A larger benchmark makes the same observed rate appear less recessionary or more overheated.

increase.title: Distinguish estimate from reality
increase.why: An estimate revision changes the diagnosis without proving a contemporaneous structural shock occurred.

decrease.title: Lower the estimated benchmark
decrease.why: Keep the observed unemployment rate fixed at 6.
decrease.question: Does averaging conflicting estimates eliminate their uncertainty?
decrease.answer: No; it gives another point estimate, not proof of the benchmark.

decrease.title: Recompute the gap
decrease.why: The same actual rate now looks more consistent with deficient demand.

decrease.title: Retain uncertainty
decrease.why: Selecting the smaller estimate does not prove it is the true one; report the range rather than choosing convenient certainty.

edge.title: Change the observation in a counterfactual
edge.why: Now the entire natural-rate range lies below actual unemployment.
edge.question: Does an imprecise estimate always make even the sign unknowable?
edge.answer: No; if all plausible benchmarks are on one side of actual u, the sign can be robust.

edge.title: Redo the interval
edge.why: Every assumed value gives a positive cyclical gap.

edge.title: Separate sign from size uncertainty
edge.why: The sign is robust within this range even though its magnitude remains uncertain. This is a teaching counterfactual, not a new historical claim.

hysteresis.goal: Trace how a temporary downturn can alter the later natural benchmark.

symbols.meaning: persistent effect after the original shock has disappeared

assumptions: This is an alternative persistence hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of the baseline Phillips equation.
The lecture lists possible mechanisms; a persistent graph alone does not identify their causal contribution.

derive.title: Start with a temporary disturbance
derive.why: A demand or labor-demand loss removes jobs during the initial downturn.

derive.title: Identify what survives the shock
derive.why: Skills may decay, attachment may weaken, or laid-off insiders may lose bargaining influence.

derive.title: Trace institutional interactions
derive.why: Benefit arrangements and hiring/firing incentives can affect search or future hiring under the discussed mechanisms.
derive.question: Does slow recovery while the original demand loss is still present establish hysteresis?
derive.answer: No; persistence must be assessed after the originating shock is gone.

derive.title: Re-evaluate the later benchmark
derive.why: If the lasting mechanism changes matching or wage-setting, unemployment can remain higher even when demand has recovered.

derive.title: Separate evidence from explanation
derive.why: The Europe–US historical pattern motivates investigation; it does not by itself prove a unique hysteresis mechanism.

graph.title: Begin with a temporary recession
graph.why: Begin with the temporary job loss.
graph.question: What must remain after the original shock ends for this to be hysteresis?
graph.answer: A lasting employment or natural-rate effect transmitted through a persistence mechanism.

graph.title: Trace structural persistence
graph.why: Add specific mechanisms that can continue beyond the initial disturbance.

graph.title: Identify possible repair
graph.why: A changed later benchmark is the distinguishing conclusion; repair must target the surviving mechanism.

increase.title: Lengthen or deepen unemployment spells
increase.why: Workers can spend more time losing skills, contacts or attachment.
increase.question: Does firm or worker optimization alone rule out persistent outsider unemployment?
increase.answer: No; institutional wage-setting can make individual choices differ from full reintegration.

increase.title: Trace the outsider mechanism
increase.why: A smaller group of remaining insiders may favor wages that protect them rather than rehiring outsiders.

increase.title: Assess persistent unemployment
increase.why: These mechanisms can raise later u*, conditional on their operation; not every recession necessarily produces the same damage.

decrease.title: Reduce the surviving friction
decrease.why: Training, matching support or reintegration may restore skills and opportunities.
decrease.question: Is a positive demand shock guaranteed to reverse a negative shock’s history exactly?
decrease.answer: No; skills and bargaining status can recover asymmetrically or require specific repair.

decrease.title: Rebuild employability and inclusion
decrease.why: The effect depends on the actual persistence mechanism rather than simply reversing the sign of spending.

decrease.title: Allow a lower later benchmark
decrease.why: If the repair succeeds, natural unemployment may fall; a temporary demand rebound alone need not undo previous damage.

edge.title: Consider a purely cyclical recovery
edge.why: Suppose unemployment fully returns after the temporary demand loss disappears, with no lasting structural change.
edge.question: What separates hysteresis from ordinary prolonged weakness?
edge.answer: A lasting effect after the original disturbance ends, with a supported persistence mechanism.

edge.title: Redo the classification
edge.why: That is a temporary gap, even if it was painful or lasted several periods.

edge.title: Avoid identification from persistence alone
edge.why: A long observed spell could also reflect continuing shocks or measurement; evidence is needed to isolate changed u*.

phillips-evidence.goal: Distinguish historical association, variable definitions and a policy-invariant relationship.

symbols.meaning: growth of nominal wages in the original Phillips relationship
growth of the general price level in the later plots

assumptions: The original course charts are historical evidence; no numerical data points are invented in this walkthrough.
A descriptive relationship over one period is not by itself a causal policy menu.

derive.title: Identify the original variable
derive.why: The original Phillips relation concerns nominal wage growth and unemployment, not exactly the same inflation variable as every later plot.

derive.title: Read the later inverse pattern
derive.why: The lecture’s 1960s US price-inflation plot suggested an inverse relation between observed inflation and unemployment.

derive.title: State the theoretical objection
derive.why: Friedman and Phelps emphasized unexpected inflation and cyclical unemployment before the 1970s breakdown.
derive.question: Was expectations augmentation merely a response invented after observing 1970s stagflation?
derive.answer: No; the lecture emphasizes the prediction came beforehand.

derive.title: Compare changing periods
derive.why: High inflation and high unemployment in the 1970s undermine a single fixed observed-level tradeoff.

derive.title: Condition the relation
derive.why: Changing expectations and natural unemployment can shift the curve; a plot alone does not identify which mechanism changed.

graph.title: Identify the measured variables
graph.why: Begin with what was actually measured.
graph.question: Does a negative correlation during one decade establish a permanent policy menu?
graph.answer: No; the determinants and policy regime can change.

graph.title: Compare the historical episodes
graph.why: Keep the theoretical prediction in the correct chronology.

graph.title: Condition the relationship
graph.why: Use the later unstable relation to motivate conditioning, rather than declaring every inverse short-run relation impossible.

increase.title: Observe both rates rising across periods
increase.why: Such a pattern is incompatible with moving along one unchanged downward curve.
increase.question: Must high inflation together with high unemployment imply the entire Phillips framework is impossible?
increase.answer: No; a shifting expectations-augmented curve permits it.

increase.title: Check changing determinants
increase.why: Higher expected inflation or greater mismatch can shift the conditional relationship upward/right.

increase.title: Avoid a single-cause conclusion
increase.why: The pattern permits these mechanisms but does not quantify or isolate each cause without additional evidence.

decrease.title: Observe both rates falling across periods
decrease.why: Improved matching or lower expected inflation can shift the conditional relation down/left.
decrease.question: Why must wage growth and price inflation not be silently treated as identical measurements?
decrease.answer: They are different variables and can respond differently; the historical studies must be identified accurately.

decrease.title: Keep within-curve and cross-curve comparisons separate
decrease.why: A downward within-curve slope does not prohibit both measured levels falling when the curve moves.

decrease.title: Check the measurements
decrease.why: Compare like inflation variables and time conventions before interpreting a change as structural.

edge.title: Hold the conditioning variables approximately stable
edge.why: Within a suitable period, stable πᵉ and u* can support an approximately stable inverse observed-level relationship.
edge.question: Does acknowledging curve shifts mean historical data are useless?
edge.answer: No; they remain evidence, but not automatically invariant causal coefficients.

edge.title: Avoid overrejecting the evidence
edge.why: A later breakdown does not imply the earlier plotted association was fabricated.

edge.title: Limit policy extrapolation
edge.why: Even a real association need not survive a policy rule designed to exploit it, as expectations can respond.

natural-rate-reform.goal: Match policy to structural versus cyclical unemployment mechanisms.
assumptions: Policy effects on skills, matching, location or incentives require the relevant friction to actually improve.
The baseline Phillips comparison holds expectations and h fixed; hysteresis is a separately stated possible extension.

derive.title: Diagnose the source of unemployment
derive.why: Separate temporary deficient demand from frictional/structural barriers to finding or filling jobs.

derive.title: Match instruments to frictions
derive.why: Training targets skills; search information and relocation support target matching and location.

derive.title: Evaluate institutions with tradeoffs
derive.why: Benefit design and hiring/firing rules affect protection as well as incentives; the diagram alone does not establish the best reform.
derive.question: Does cutting a benefit automatically prove that natural unemployment will fall?
derive.answer: No; the net mechanism, implementation and other institutions must be assessed.

derive.title: Move the benchmark only when justified
derive.why: If the structural friction improves, a lower u* shifts LRPC left and SRPC down at fixed πᵉ.

derive.title: Distinguish demand management
derive.why: Stronger spending with unchanged u* moves the economy along SRPC; it is not automatically a structural improvement.

graph.title: Diagnose the structural constraint
graph.why: Start by identifying the type of unemployment.
graph.question: Does every fall in observed u belong on the structural branch?
graph.answer: No; it can be a cyclical movement from stronger demand.

graph.title: Choose a matching or incentive channel
graph.why: Separate structural instruments from the demand-only route.

graph.title: Separate reform from demand stimulus
graph.why: A natural-rate change needs a lasting mechanism, including any explicitly argued hysteresis channel.

increase.title: Increase effective matching or skills
increase.why: Suppose a successful mechanism lowers u*=5→4; the result is an assumption to verify, not an automatic policy label.
increase.question: Why is this different from inflating along the original curve to reach u 4?
increase.answer: The natural benchmark itself changed; it is not merely a negative cyclical gap.

increase.title: Recompute the conditional curve
increase.why: At each fixed actual u, SRPC lies half an inflation point lower.

increase.title: Locate the new long-run benchmark
increase.why: A lasting unemployment reduction can occur at unchanged expected and actual inflation 3.

decrease.title: Reduce matching quality or add a binding friction
decrease.why: Suppose the relevant structural mechanism raises u*=5→6.
decrease.question: Can unchanged actual u conceal a worsening natural benchmark?
decrease.answer: Yes; the structural comparison and the cyclical gap are separate.

decrease.title: Recalculate the same actual rate
decrease.why: The previous unemployment benchmark no longer defines a zero gap.

decrease.title: Shift the structural loci
decrease.why: Restoring the original natural rate requires addressing the friction, not assuming demand alone removed it.

edge.title: Apply demand-only expansion
edge.why: Assume the policy raises spending but leaves matching and other natural-rate determinants unchanged.
edge.question: Does a lower observed unemployment rate prove the reform reduced u*?
edge.answer: No; it may be a cyclical demand effect, so structural success needs separate evidence.

edge.title: Use the old benchmark
edge.why: This is movement along the old curve with a positive inflation surprise.

edge.title: State what would require more evidence
edge.why: If sustained employment is claimed to lower future u* through hysteresis, identify that additional persistence/reversal mechanism and its inflation risks.

early-model.title: Build and test a conditional prediction

nodes.label: Individual decisions
nodes.detail: Households maximize utility; firms maximize present-value profits.

nodes.label: Market consistency
nodes.detail: Combine desired labor, saving/investment and portfolio choices.

nodes.label: Conditional prediction
nodes.detail: Derive output, interest and prices under the specified adjustment rules.

nodes.label: Change an assumption
nodes.detail: Re-solve when wages, prices, information or constraints change.

early-model.note: Original explanatory flow; this is not an empirical curve.

early-variables.title: Inputs, relationship and solved consumption

nodes.label: Given inputs
nodes.detail: Supply the current scenario's a, b and Y; these are inputs to this one-equation model.

nodes.label: Behavioral equation
nodes.detail: C = a + bY converts the given inputs into a consumption prediction.

nodes.label: Solved outcome
nodes.detail: Calculate C from the current inputs. This small equation alone does not determine Y.

nodes.label: Larger model
nodes.detail: Adding a separate output condition can make Y endogenous; the larger system must be solved jointly.

early-variables.note: Symbolic explanatory flow. The walkthrough supplies the numerical scenario; the nodes do not retain an obsolete baseline value after an input change.

early-autonomous.title: Intercept changes and movement along consumption
early-autonomous.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Interest and other determinants are fixed. Y and C are real period flows.

early-real.title: The same nominal wage buys different quantities
early-real.note: Numerical teaching illustration. P is a money price per output unit, not an unnormalized base-100 index. The vertical marker identifies the excluded P = 0 boundary; no real-wage value is assigned there.

early-stocks.title: Reconcile the opening and closing stock

nodes.label: Opening wealth B₀
nodes.detail: A stock measured at the beginning of the chosen period.

nodes.label: Saving S
nodes.detail: Unconsumed income adds to wealth over the period; S can be negative.

nodes.label: Valuation change V
nodes.detail: Asset-price gains or losses change wealth separately from current saving.

nodes.label: Closing wealth B₁
nodes.detail: B₁ = B₀ + S + V + J, where J is any other net stock adjustment. Set J = 0 when the stated scenario excludes such adjustments.

nodes.label: Other net adjustments J
nodes.detail: Examples include an inheritance or another transfer that changes wealth outside the specified saving and valuation terms.

early-stocks.note: Symbolic stock-flow reconciliation. Insert the values given in the current step and include every applicable adjustment once.

early-wealth.title: Assets and liabilities determine net wealth

nodes.label: Assets A
nodes.detail: Value the resources owned at the chosen date, including cash.

nodes.label: Liabilities D
nodes.detail: Value the amounts owed at the same date and in the same currency.

nodes.label: Net wealth NW
nodes.detail: NW = A − D; this can be positive, zero or negative.

nodes.label: Repayment from existing cash
nodes.detail: Subtract the same repayment from A and D. Their difference remains unchanged.

nodes.label: Repayment after new saving
nodes.detail: New unconsumed income first raises net wealth. Repaying debt is one possible use of the resulting resources.

early-wealth.note: Symbolic balance-sheet flow. Use the current scenario's asset and debt values rather than carrying baseline numbers into a changed transaction.

early-profit.title: Profit, a stationary point and a hiring corner
early-profit.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Output is Y = 10N − N² on the specified domain 0 ≤ N ≤ 5, where MPN is nonnegative. The baseline wage is 4; the higher wage is 12. Each profit curve is evaluated only on this feasible production domain.

early-chain.title: Substitution creates one objective
early-chain.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Illustrative u(c, l) = cl and c = 12−2l on 0≤l≤6. The tangent is a local approximation, not the budget.

early-ic-slope.title: Two different constraints give two different slopes

points.label: More leisure at the same utility
Less leisure at the same utility

early-ic-slope.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Illustrative u = ln c+2ln l. The curves meet at (4, 10) but are not tangent there. The plotted budget is not a time-endowment specification.

early-production.title: Productivity and capital shift the production function

curves.label: Zero productivity or zero capital: Y = 0

points.label: Higher A or K, as labelled
Lower A or K, as labelled

early-production.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Y = A√(KN). Productivity experiments fix K = 100; capital experiments fix A = 1. Coincident curves have different causes and are revealed separately.

early-mp.title: Marginal product is the labor-demand curve

points.label: Higher A or K at wage 1
Lower A or K at wage 1

early-mp.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Baseline Y = 10√N uses A = 1 and K = 100. The higher curve can represent A = 1.2 with K = 100, or K = 144 with A = 1, as stated in the walk. The lower curve similarly uses A = 0.8 or K = 64. Curves stop at N = 1 because MPN is unbounded at zero; total output itself is zero there.

early-scale.title: Scale all inputs together
early-scale.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Different technologies are each indexed to 100 at their initial input bundle. z scales both inputs; this is not a one-input marginal-product graph.

early-shares.title: Marginal-product payments and the returns-to-scale test

nodes.label: Output and exponents
nodes.detail: Y = AK^αN^γ. The baseline constant-returns example sets γ = 1−α.

nodes.label: Capital payment
nodes.detail: MPK·K = αY when capital receives its marginal product.

nodes.label: Labor payment
nodes.detail: MPN·N = γY when labor receives its marginal product; γ = 1−α in the baseline.

nodes.label: Check total payments
nodes.detail: Total factor payments are (α+γ)Y. They exhaust output if α+γ = 1; otherwise inspect the residual or shortfall.

early-shares.note: Symbolic explanatory flow. The same expressions accommodate both the constant-returns baseline and the explicitly changed-exponent edge case.

early-labor-market.title: Different shocks have different wage effects
early-labor-market.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Here the production illustration is Y = A(30N−N²/8), distinct from the Cobb–Douglas examples. All points solve the displayed demand and supply equations.

early-leisure.title: Consumption, leisure and a nonlabor-income change

points.label: Below optimal leisure on the baseline budget
Above optimal leisure on the baseline budget
Three more work hours from the baseline optimum

early-leisure.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Utility is u = ln(c) + ln(l), with h = 16. Indifference-curve segments start at l = 4 to avoid divergent plotted values near zero.

early-wage.title: Separate the wage substitution and income effects
early-wage.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Utility is u = ln(c) + ln(l), with h = 16 and m = 20. Compensated lines are tangent to the original cl = 500 indifference curve and parallel to the relevant new wage line. The compensated resource total is hypothetical and serves only to isolate substitution.

early-leisure-corner.title: When desired leisure reaches the time limit
early-leisure-corner.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Utility is u = ln(c) + ln(l), with h = 16 and w = 5. Unrestricted leisure is (80 + m)/10. When this exceeds 16, the constrained solution is l = 16 and c = m.

early-unemployment.title: Classification determines the rate denominators

nodes.label: Adult population POP
nodes.detail: Use the lecture's U.S./BLS illustration: adults aged 16 or above.

nodes.label: Employed E
nodes.detail: Includes qualifying part-time work and temporary absence from an existing job.

nodes.label: Unemployed U
nodes.detail: Not employed, but actively searched for work during the preceding four weeks in the course illustration.

nodes.label: Outside the labor force
nodes.detail: People in POP who are neither employed nor actively searching; count = POP − E − U.

nodes.label: Labor force LF
nodes.detail: LF = E + U. This is the unemployment-rate denominator.

nodes.label: Calculate the three rates
nodes.detail: u = U/LF if LF > 0; p = LF/POP and e = E/POP if POP > 0. When LF = 0, u is undefined.

early-unemployment.note: Symbolic classification flow. Counts and rates are recalculated in each scenario, including job loss, labor-force withdrawal and an empty labor force.

early-okun.title: Growth responds to the change in unemployment
early-okun.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Lecture calibration; an empirical growth-change relation, not an identity or the output-gap version.

early-saving.title: Consolidate private and government saving

nodes.label: Output or income Y
nodes.detail: The current period's real resource total.

nodes.label: Private saving S_p
nodes.detail: S_p = Y − T − C, with T defined consistently as net taxes.

nodes.label: Government saving S_g
nodes.detail: S_g = T − G; a negative amount is a government deficit.

nodes.label: National saving S
nodes.detail: S = S_p + S_g = Y − C − G. Net taxes cancel on consolidation.

nodes.label: Behavioral effects
nodes.detail: A tax change can still affect S through the resulting consumption or income response.

early-saving.note: Symbolic accounting flow. The current step supplies Y, C, T and G; balances are not fixed at their baseline values.

early-desired.title: Separate planned spending from actual accounting

nodes.label: Production Y
nodes.detail: The goods produced in the current period.

nodes.label: Planned purchases
nodes.detail: C + Iᵈ + G is planned spending in the stated fixed-consumption experiment.

nodes.label: Unplanned inventory change
nodes.detail: Y − (C + Iᵈ + G), positive for unsold output and negative for an inventory drawdown.

nodes.label: Actual saving equals actual investment
nodes.detail: I = Iᵈ + unplanned inventory change = Y − C − G = S.

nodes.label: Test desired equilibrium
nodes.detail: Planned goods-market equilibrium additionally requires zero unplanned inventory change, or desired saving equal to desired investment.

early-desired.note: Symbolic explanatory flow. Planned investment changes can create positive, zero or negative inventory surprises without violating the actual accounting identity.

early-life.title: A three-stage life-cycle accounting illustration
early-life.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Illustrative three equal-length stages with zero interest and no initial/final wealth. This motivates smoothing; it does not replace the course’s two-period optimization model. Each changed path is independently recomputed for its stated income or borrowing experiment. The middle-income gain leaves incomes (30,100,20); the retirement-income loss leaves incomes (30,70,5). The no-early-borrowing case keeps the original incomes but changes consumption to (30,45,45) and saving to (0,25,−25).

early-consumption.title: Build the two-period choice diagram
early-consumption.note: Shared numerical budget calibration: R = 1.25, y₁ = 120, y₂ = 75, no initial assets, and present-value resources W = 180. The indifference curves labelled 'Log IC' belong specifically to U = ln(c₁) + 0.8ln(c₂). In the closed-form walk's square-root derivation, only the common budget is revealed: U = √c₁ + 0.8√c₂ happens to share the optimum (100,100) at these same parameters, but its indifference curves are not the displayed log curves. A present-value change of ±18 can arise from current income ±18 or future income ±22.5; their saving effects differ.

early-pv.title: Value a fixed future payment at different real returns
early-pv.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Certain real payment; r>−1. The preference discount factor does not value the resource payment.

early-euler.title: Balance current gain against future loss
early-euler.yLabel: Marginal lifetime utility per current good
early-euler.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Same log preferences and baseline budget as consumption figure. Current consumption changes future consumption through the constraint.

early-interest.title: Interest rotates the endowment budget
early-interest.note: Numerical teaching illustration. U = ln(c₁) + 0.8ln(c₂), with y₁ = 120 and y₂ = 75. This example has substitution dominance for current consumption; a general saver need not.

early-wealth-timing.title: Opening assets, current saving and end assets

nodes.label: Entering asset stock a₀
nodes.detail: Assets are dated before the return earned at the start of period 1.

nodes.label: Current asset income
nodes.detail: ra₀ is new interest income; a₀ itself is existing principal.

nodes.label: Resources available for current spending
nodes.detail: Ra₀ + y₁. If opening wealth is instead defined after its return, call it B₀ = Ra₀ and use B₀ + y₁.

nodes.label: End-of-period assets a₁
nodes.detail: a₁ = Ra₀ + y₁ − c₁.

nodes.label: Current saving s₁
nodes.detail: s₁ = a₁ − a₀ = ra₀ + y₁ − c₁; distinguish this flow from the level of a₁.

nodes.label: Future consumption c₂
nodes.detail: c₂ = Ra₁ + y₂ when terminal assets are zero.

early-wealth-timing.note: Symbolic timing flow. Recompute the quantities when a₀ changes. Use either a₀ before its current return or B₀ after that return consistently; never add the return twice.

early-constraint.title: An affordable lifetime plan may violate a borrowing limit
early-constraint.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Log utility with β = 0.8 and R = 1.25. The initial incomes y₁ = 80 and y₂ = 125 give present-value resources of 180. A current-income gain of 20 or a future-income gain of 25 produces the same new budget, but only the current gain moves the borrowing ceiling. The lower-current-income experiment uses y₁ = 60 and y₂ = 125, so its budget and cap both move. The threshold and slack curves instead hold y₁ = 80 and set y₂ to 80 and 50, respectively; the step states which experiment is active.

early-mpcs.title: Two dated responses to a current-income gain
early-mpcs.yLabel: Increase in consumption at stated date
early-mpcs.note: Numerical teaching illustration. Square-root utility with β = 0.9 and R = 2. Current and future quantities are not directly additive; discount future consumption before adding it to current consumption.

early-cw-supply.title: Current versus future wages: movement and shift

curves.label: Current supply with future wage w₂ = 8

points.label: No current work when w₁ = 2, w₂ = 8

early-cw-supply.note: Numerical teaching illustration. U = ln(c₁) + ln(l₁) + 0.8[ln(c₂) + ln(l₂)], with R = 1.25 and h = 10. The interior solution is used only when l₁ ≤ h. Otherwise the no-current-work boundary is imposed and the remaining choices are re-solved. Future leisure stays interior throughout the displayed parameter range. Curves use current wages from 0.5 to 5.5 so that the lowest plotted future wage, two, never reaches its future-leisure corner.

early-cw-budget.title: One constraint links four chosen quantities

nodes.label: Time at each date
nodes.detail: n₁ = h − l₁ and n₂ = h − l₂, with 0 ≤ l₁,l₂ ≤ h.

nodes.label: Endogenous labor earnings
nodes.detail: y₁ = w₁(h − l₁); y₂ = w₂(h − l₂).

nodes.label: Saving transfers resources
nodes.detail: a₁ = Ra₀ + y₁ − c₁ and s₁ = a₁ − a₀. In the baseline a₀ = 0, so a₁ = s₁ = y₁ − c₁.

nodes.label: Future consumption
nodes.detail: c₂ = y₂ + Ra₁. In the baseline a₀ = 0, this becomes c₂ = y₂ + Rs₁.

nodes.label: Full-income representation
nodes.detail: c₁ + w₁l₁ + (c₂ + w₂l₂)/R = W. With no initial assets, W = w₁h + w₂h/R; add Ra₀ under the stated opening-asset convention.

early-cw-budget.note: Original explanatory flow of the joint budget, not an empirical curve. Insert the wages, time endowment, gross return and initial assets stated in the current step. The baseline numerical example has h = 10, w₁ = 2, w₂ = 4, R = 1.25 and no initial assets, giving W = 52.

early-cw-trade.title: Value both leisure costs at the same date
early-cw-trade.note: Numerical teaching illustration. A fixed future-valued leisure-expenditure slice of the four-good budget. Its slopes illustrate opportunity-cost ratios, not final wage-shock optima: actual wage changes also alter full income and consumption choices.

early-cw-current-choice.title: Illustrative current consumption–leisure slice
early-cw-current-choice.note: Derived numerical slice of the full consumer-worker problem: hold the optimal future consumption and leisure fixed, with w₁ = 2, w₂ = 4, R = 1.25, β = 0.8, h = 10. The remaining current full-expenditure budget is 260/9. This slice isolates the current intratemporal condition; it is not a separate no-saving worker problem.

early-cw-euler.title: Illustrative Euler comparison holding both leisure choices fixed
early-cw-euler.yLabel: Marginal utility per current consumption unit
early-cw-euler.note: Derived illustration using optimal baseline leisure l₁ = 65/9 and l₂ = 65/18, held fixed for the Euler marginal comparison. Then labor incomes are y₁ = 50/9 and y₂ = 230/9, and c₂ = 32.5 − 1.25c₁. A wage shock also changes leisure, so its final effect requires the full four-good solution.

early-mpcs-future-loss.title: Square-root utility: a signed future-income loss
early-mpcs-future-loss.xLabel: Change in future income Δy₂ (future goods)
early-mpcs-future-loss.yLabel: Signed consumption change at the labelled date
early-mpcs-future-loss.note: Derived numerical illustration with U = √c₁ + 0.9√c₂, R = 2 and no borrowing restriction. Initial y₁ = 262 and y₂ = 524 imply c₁ = 200 and c₂ = 648. Reducing y₂ by 262 leaves y₂ = 262 and gives c₁ = 150 and c₂ = 486, so all incomes and consumption remain positive. The horizontal axis is a signed change in FUTURE income. Add RΔc₁ to Δc₂ when checking the budget in future units; do not directly add current- and future-dated goods.

early-sqrt-constraint.title: Square-root utility with a binding borrowing limit
early-sqrt-constraint.note: Derived numerical illustration with U = √c₁ + 0.9√c₂, R = 2, y₁ = 100 and y₂ = 500. Present-value resources are 350. The unrestricted current consumption 350/2.62 exceeds y₁, so the no-borrowing solution is c₁ = 100 and c₂ = 500. The curve segment starts at c₁ = 40 to keep the finite plot readable.

early-kink.title: An optimum without a smooth indifference-curve slope

curves.label: u = min(c,l): vertical arm at l = 20/3
u = min(c,l): horizontal arm at c = 20/3

early-kink.note: Derived boundary illustration with a DIFFERENT utility function u = min(c,l), budget c + 2l = 20 and 0 ≤ l ≤ 10. The optimal bundle is where c = l = 20/3. Moving either way along the budget reduces the smaller argument. At this kink there is no unique smooth MRS; this is not the original logarithmic utility curve.

early-linear-mp.title: Linear technology: a flat marginal product

points.label: No hiring when wage exceeds MPN

early-linear-mp.note: Derived alternative-technology illustration. For Y = AN with A = 1, MPN is the constant 1 and its derivative with respect to N is zero. At w = 1 every feasible employment quantity yields the same profit; at w > 1 the optimum is zero; at w < 1 profit keeps increasing if there is no employment cap. For Y = K + N, the same MPN = 1 is independent of K. This replaces the original diminishing-MPN technology.

early-one-input-scale.title: One-input change compared with proportional scaling
early-one-input-scale.xLabel: Labor multiplier z, with K fixed for the curved line

curves.label: Reference experiment: both K and N scale by z

early-one-input-scale.note: Derived illustration for a Cobb–Douglas technology with capital and labor exponents both 0.5. The curved line holds capital fixed and changes only labor. The dashed line is a separately labelled all-input scaling experiment from the same initial bundle. The common horizontal multiplier does not mean the two experiments change the same inputs.

early-wage-zero-income.title: Zero nonlabor income: wage effects cancel in work hours
early-wage-zero-income.note: Derived edge case for u = ln(c) + ln(l), h = 16 and m = 0. The budget is c = w(16 − l). Tangency c = wl gives l = 8 at every positive wage, so work stays eight hours while consumption varies with w. These are new m = 0 budgets, not the original m = 20 budgets.

early-mp-boundary.title: Marginal product near zero labor
early-mp-boundary.note: Zoomed derived illustration for Y = 10√N. The curve is plotted only for N ≥ 0.01, while the boundary marker identifies the excluded zero denominator. The derivative grows without bound as N tends to zero from above; no finite marginal-product point is assigned at N = 0. Total output is a different quantity and tends to zero.

early-pv-boundary.title: Present value near a zero gross return
early-pv-boundary.xLabel: Net real rate r; the boundary r = −1 is excluded
early-pv-boundary.note: Derived boundary illustration. The curve stops at r = −0.9 for a finite plotting window; the marked r = −1 boundary is not a valid input to the formula. Approaching it from the right sends PV to infinity. The formula is never evaluated at a zero or negative gross return.

early-interest-zero-saving.title: A rate change from an initially zero-saving optimum
early-interest-zero-saving.note: Derived zero-saving illustration, explicitly changing the income endowment to y₁ = y₂ = 100. Utility is ln(c₁) + 0.8ln(c₂). At R = 1.25, the optimum is the endowment (100,100), so initial saving is zero. Higher or lower R rotates the budget through that endowment but changes the optimal choice. This replaces the original saver example with incomes 120 and 75.

early-linear-utility.title: Linear utility: corners or an entire line of optima

The three lines use β = 1, 0.8 and 0.6 to demonstrate βR greater than, equal to and less than one. Nonnegative consumption allows both endpoint allocations.

late-fe.title: Constructing the full-employment locus
late-fe.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Potential output is independent of the plotted real rate in this labor-market closure. The 90/100/110 levels are stated capacity scenarios.

late-loanable.title: Tracing IS from desired saving and investment

late-is-tax.title: Tax leakage changes the IS slope

late-money-market.title: Deriving LM in the money market
late-money-market.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Expected inflation is fixed at zero for this illustration. At fixed supply, higher Y raises the demand schedule at each r; r adjusts so final demanded balances still equal the unchanged supply.

late-bond.title: Fixed payoff and inverse price–yield relation
late-bond.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Certain one-year total payoff is 110. Nominal yields are plotted in percent; the underlying discount factor uses decimal i. Above payoff, the mathematical yield is negative; feasibility depends on the asset model.

late-adas.title: AD–AS consistent with the IS–LM illustration
late-adas.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. AD is exactly P=M/(2 Y−10 a), derived from r=a−0.1 Y and L=Y−10 r. Only positive-denominator portions are shown. Baseline a=15, M=100; a 17/a 13 represent G±10, while M 120/M 80 represent money±20%.

late-sensitivity.title: Change money-demand interest sensitivity, not just a drawn slope
late-sensitivity.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. IS r=a−0.1 Y and L=Y−hr. Only h differs across the two baseline economies, so their baseline intersections differ. Compare changes within each economy; keep units and shock sizes identical.

late-vertical-lm.title: The h=0 limit: output fixed by real balances
late-vertical-lm.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Here L=Y, so R=100 is needed for baseline Y 100. This h=0 calibration intentionally differs from the regular L=Y−10 r example; no division by h is used.

late-trap.title: A flat branch with an explicit exit
late-trap.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Piecewise illustration: r=max(−πᵉ, (Y−R)/10−πᵉ). It implements a nominal zero bound with sufficient balances on the flat branch. Baseline πᵉ=0, R=100. G shocks are IS intercept changes, not arbitrary shifts of the rate floor.

late-surprise.title: Surprise demand with flexible prices and imperfect information
late-surprise.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. SRAS Y=100+20(P−Pᵉ); original Pᵉ=2. AD P=M/(2 Y−150) is unchanged from the linked monetary example. Recomputed SR points are intersections, not arbitrary arrows. Price levels here are not log prices.

late-effort.title: Effort, origin rays and the tangency
late-effort.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. The smooth S-shaped e=w²/(16+w²) is an original illustrative effort function, not an estimated or official lecture equation. Its origin-ray slope e/w is maximized at w 4. The constant-effort boundary uses a different stated incentive assumption.

late-effort-cost.title: Cost per effective unit and the reciprocal ratio
late-effort-cost.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. For the stated illustrative effort function, q=w/e=w+16/w, q′=1−16/w² and q″=32/w³>0 for w>0. The flat-effort boundary has no interior cost minimum.

late-labor-rigid.title: Hiring at the efficiency wage
late-labor-rigid.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. This separate labor illustration assumes w_eff=6, rather than borrowing w 4 from the effort-function example. ND follows a marginal-product schedule. At fixed w 6, supply 100 exceeds jobs 80; the competitive clearing pair would be N=86⅔, w=5⅓.

late-price-setting.title: Find quantity with MR, then price with demand
late-price-setting.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Linear demand P=a−0.2 Q and constant MC 8 give Q*=(a−8)/0.4 and P*=(a+8)/2. At fixed P 14, demand shifts change orders, not the price along a fixed demand schedule. Capacity is assumed adequate for plotted orders.

late-menu.title: Menu cost versus the gain from resetting
late-menu.note: Original numerical teaching illustration, not data. Demand Q=max((a−P)/0.2,0), MC 8, initial a 20, P 14, menu cost 25. When Δ a≥−6, both relevant order quantities are nonnegative and resetting gain=1.25(Δ a)². For −10≤Δ a<−6, old-price orders are zero and gain=(12+Δ a)²/0.8. The plotted kink and different formula explicitly enforce nonnegative sales; symmetry is local to the interior-order region.

late-oil.title: A price overshoot can deepen an oil-shock contraction
late-oil.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. M 100 and unchanged IS. The stated capacity decline is 100→90. An initial P 4 gives R 25 and Y 87.5 below new potential; later P 10/3 restores Y 90. A smaller P 2.5 jump gives Y 95 above the new potential, illustrating why the gap sign is not logically fixed. A separate favorable illustration raises potential to 110: an initial price fall to 5/3 gives R 60, Y 105, still below the new potential; a further fall to 10/7 restores Y 110. This is explicitly not a universal mirror-image response.

late-phillips.title: Movements and shifts of the expectations-augmented curve
late-phillips.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. Baseline πᵉ 3, u*=5, h 0.5. Rates are expressed in percentage points, so a two-point unemployment gap changes inflation by one point. These illustrative lines are not fitted historical US data.

late-log-sras.title: The same surprise translated through output
late-log-sras.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. p=ln(price index), common known p_previous=0, pᵉ 0.03, Y*=100, b=1000 output units per log-price unit. Okun illustration Y−100=−5(u−5) maps this line to the baseline Phillips line with h 0.5. Raw price levels are not relabeled as inflation.

late-natural-estimate.title: Changing the estimate changes the diagnosed gap
late-natural-estimate.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not estimated data. The lecture’s historical 1994 illustration reports observed u≈6, point estimate 5.75 and 95% interval 4.8–6.6. This plotted mapping is arithmetic across alternative estimates, not a probability density or observed time-series curve. The additional observed u 7 line is a counterfactual teaching case showing a robust gap sign; it is not another historical observation.

late-expectations-flow.title: Information arrives before and after choices

nodes.label: Information set
nodes.detail: What relevant information was available when decisions were made?

nodes.label: Conditional forecast
nodes.detail: Use that information and the model to form expectations.

nodes.label: Predictable policy
nodes.detail: A public systematic response belongs in the forecast.

nodes.label: Unanticipated news
nodes.detail: A genuinely new shock can still produce a forecast error.

nodes.label: Update
nodes.detail: Once the policy pattern is learned, repeating it no longer creates the same surprise.

nodes.label: Separate friction
nodes.detail: Even correct forecasts do not eliminate preset contracts in a different model.

late-expectations-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-relative-flow.title: From nominal observation to perceived relative reward

nodes.label: Observe own price or wage
nodes.detail: The worker/producer sees their nominal return clearly.

nodes.label: Assess general prices
nodes.detail: The true purchasing power uses the overall price index.

nodes.label: Compute relative price
nodes.detail: True real reward is own price divided by the general index.

nodes.label: Information error
nodes.detail: An unexpected common price movement may be mistaken for a relative-price movement.

nodes.label: Adjust work/output
nodes.detail: Respond to the perceived relative reward, not nominal units themselves.

nodes.label: Full-information boundary
nodes.detail: Proportionate own/general price changes cancel, leaving no relative incentive.

late-relative-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-lucas-flow.title: A changed rule changes the relationship being forecast

nodes.label: Old regime and data
nodes.detail: Estimate an association under the policy rule people faced.

nodes.label: Change the policy rule
nodes.detail: Agents know or learn the new systematic behavior.

nodes.label: Expectations respond
nodes.detail: Forecasts and choices can adjust to new incentives.

nodes.label: Observed relation changes
nodes.detail: The old reduced-form coefficient or Phillips curve need not remain invariant.

nodes.label: Evaluate structurally
nodes.detail: Model the expectation and choice response; retain useful evidence without freezing old behavior.

late-lucas-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-ford-flow.title: Use evidence without inventing causality

nodes.label: Mechanism prediction
nodes.detail: Mismatch, deficient demand and incentive wages make different observable predictions.

nodes.label: Vacancies and quits
nodes.detail: The lecture rejects mismatch as the complete recession story using their pattern.

nodes.label: Ford changed pay and hours
nodes.detail: Daily pay rose while hours fell; turnover, absence and productivity changed.

nodes.label: Other conditions changed
nodes.detail: Model T success, production conditions, publicity and union motives complicate attribution.

nodes.label: Qualified evidence
nodes.detail: The episode is consistent with incentives but does not isolate their causal contribution.

late-ford-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-stabilization-flow.title: A policy acts on the economy that exists when it arrives

nodes.label: Estimate today’s gap
nodes.detail: Actual and potential output are imperfectly measured.

nodes.label: Choose size and instrument
nodes.detail: The multiplier and its timing are uncertain.

nodes.label: Decision and transmission
nodes.detail: Political/implementation delays and variable transmission separate choice from effect.

nodes.label: Forecast the arrival state
nodes.detail: The economy may already be recovering or may have weakened further.

nodes.label: Judge the resulting gap
nodes.detail: Stimulus can close a recession or overshoot; contraction can restrain demand or deepen weakness.

late-stabilization-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-other-nk-flow.title: Two alternative mechanisms named, not fully derived

nodes.label: Coordination failure
nodes.detail: Desired action can depend on demand created by others.

nodes.label: Mutual response
nodes.detail: Individually cautious production/spending can reinforce weak demand.

nodes.label: Different reset dates
nodes.detail: Some wages/prices remain predetermined while others change.

nodes.label: Incomplete aggregate adjustment
nodes.detail: The collection need not jump instantly to all desired new prices.

nodes.label: Scope limit
nodes.detail: Lecture 8 names these mechanisms; a quantitative model needs added assumptions.
