late-phillips-evidence-flow.title: From a historical association to a conditional relation

nodes.label: Original variable
nodes.detail: Phillips related nominal wage growth to unemployment.

nodes.label: Later price-inflation plot
nodes.detail: A 1960s inverse pattern suggested a policy menu.

nodes.label: Friedman–Phelps objection
nodes.detail: Expected inflation and the natural rate matter; prediction preceded the 1970s breakdown.

nodes.label: High inflation and unemployment
nodes.detail: Oil shocks and changing conditions can shift the relation.

nodes.label: Test a conditional relation
nodes.detail: Distinguish surprise inflation from expected inflation and cyclical from natural unemployment.

late-phillips-evidence-flow.note: Original teaching flow based on the cited course mechanism; not an empirical curve.

late-hysteresis-flow.title: A temporary shock can leave a lasting labor-market change

nodes.label: Temporary demand loss
nodes.detail: Jobs disappear during the original downturn.

nodes.label: Skills and attachment
nodes.detail: Long unemployment can erode skills, search attachment or employability.

nodes.label: Insiders become outsiders
nodes.detail: Laid-off workers can lose wage-bargaining influence.

nodes.label: Hiring and benefit incentives
nodes.detail: Rules and support arrangements can interact with search and hiring decisions.

nodes.label: Natural benchmark changes
nodes.detail: Even after the original shock ends, matching or wage-setting may keep employment lower.

nodes.label: Mechanism-specific repair
nodes.detail: Training, matching, reintegration or prevention can reduce persistence; recovery is not automatic symmetry.

late-reform-flow.title: Choose the policy for the unemployment mechanism

nodes.label: Cyclical or structural?
nodes.detail: A fall in actual unemployment does not by itself identify a lower natural rate.

nodes.label: Improve matching
nodes.detail: Training, information and relocation target skills, search and location barriers.

nodes.label: Evaluate institutions
nodes.detail: Benefit design and hiring/firing rules involve incentives and protection tradeoffs.

nodes.label: Lower u* if the friction improves
nodes.detail: A lasting improvement shifts the long-run benchmark.

nodes.label: Demand-only route
nodes.detail: With unchanged u*, stronger demand moves along the short-run curve.

nodes.label: Hysteresis extension
nodes.detail: Demand history may affect u* through an additional mechanism; that claim needs evidence.

late-tutorial9.title: Tutorial 9 calibration: full Classical equilibrium
late-tutorial9.note: Source-calibrated worked exercise, not empirical data. This uses the Tutorial 9 equations and decimal r, distinct from the percentage-point teaching economy in other figures. L=10+Y−200 r, not 10 Y−200 r.

late-tutorial9-ad.title: Tutorial 9: money scales prices at fixed capacity
late-tutorial9-ad.note: Source-calibrated Classical exercise with fully flexible prices. AD comes from substituting IS into L=10+Y−200 r; real outcomes remain fixed and P scales with M. No sustained fixed-price boom is claimed.

late-deflation-surprise.title: Deflation can be a positive inflation surprise
late-deflation-surprise.note: Numerical illustration with the same h 0.5 and natural rate 5 as the main Phillips graph, but expected inflation−3. Actual inflation−1 exceeds expectation by 2 points, so the cyclical unemployment gap is −4 points. No historical observations are fabricated.

late-is-construction.title: Construct IS from market equilibria
late-is-construction.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not data. Goods balance uses C=25+0.5Y−3r, I=40−2r and G=10. The horizontal coordinate here is output, not the saving/investment quantity in the source diagram. Coordinate guides are construction aids, not additional equilibrium restrictions; all three pairs trace one unchanged locus.

late-lm-construction.title: Construct LM from market equilibria
late-lm-construction.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not data. Money balance uses L=Y−10r and fixed M/P=50. The horizontal coordinate here is output, not the money stock in the source diagram. Coordinate guides are construction aids, not additional equilibrium restrictions; all three pairs trace one unchanged locus.

late-is-boundaries.title: Separate vertical, horizontal and coincident boundaries

curves.label: Separate h=0 money case: LM Y=100

points.label: One feasible rate on coincident loci
Another feasible rate on coincident loci

late-is-boundaries.note: Numerical teaching boundary cases, not data. Goods equilibrium is DY=A₀−Hr, with A₀=75. H=0,D=0.5 gives Y=150; D=0,H=5 gives r=15 and regular LM then gives Y=200. D=0 is a separate limiting consumption/tax specification, not the interior c=0.5 calibration. Vertical-LM comparisons are explicitly separate: LM fixes Y=100 and conflicts with IS Y=150, or, after separately changing the goods intercept to A₀=50 with D=0.5 and H=0, coincides with IS Y=100; coincident loci leave r undetermined by these two equations.

late-lm-boundary.title: Remove rate sensitivity at the same real money stock
late-lm-boundary.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not data. Keep L=Y−hr, R=M/P=50 and IS r=15−0.1Y. Removing h leaves Y=50 directly from money balance; goods balance supplies r=10. The money stock and axes are not silently renormalized.

late-ad-price-experiments.title: Vary P while keeping nominal M fixed
late-ad-price-experiments.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not data. Every experiment holds M=100, IS and money-demand behavior fixed. Only P changes, so M/P changes. These are three price experiments used to construct one AD curve; the nominal money stock is never changed.

late-ad-construction.title: Transfer price experiments to construct AD
late-ad-construction.note: Numerical teaching illustration, not data. Each (Y,P) pair comes from a separate goods-and-money equilibrium with M=100. The r coordinate in the source diagram is replaced by the price P used in that experiment. The reference lines are coordinate guides, not SRAS or LRAS. The positive-denominator AD branch follows from M/P=2Y−150.
